8.heading: Day 8 · UX/UI basics: structure, visual hierarchy, interaction

intro.about: Today is about how a learning platform is built before it is made to look good. You learn the three parts of a structure (information architecture, navigation and orientation), how size, colour and position steer attention, how a clear button and a quick response guide action, and how to weigh structure against surface when a platform has grown without a plan.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is StructLearn, a learning platform that has grown without a plan: users cannot find content, many visual elements compete without structure, and many beginners give up. The puzzle: with limited money and little time, what do you fix first, and how do you decide when you cannot test first?

story.question: Which of three mistakes does each of the eight facts show, where does a beginner lose orientation, and which four of nine measures fit €40,000 and ten weeks?
As the Chief UX Architect, how is the platform structured, which principles and which guidance keep it clear, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Tell navigation, overload and inconsistency apart
wiifm.payoff: “Where am I, what is the main thing, does it work like the last screen?” are three questions you can ask of any screen, form or intranet page at your own desk.

wiifm.skill: Say what a visual change can and cannot fix
wiifm.payoff: A new colour scheme cannot repair a menu in which one item sits in three places. Knowing this protects a budget from being spent on the look first.

wiifm.skill: Weigh a design measure on three questions
wiifm.payoff: User impact, effort and risk work for any proposal on the table: a website relaunch, a new form, a new report layout.

wiifm.skill: Plan a structure before you build it
wiifm.payoff: A card sort with real people shows how others group your content. You can run one for a team wiki or a product catalogue in an afternoon.

wiifm.skill: Write design principles that can say no
wiifm.payoff: “One main action per screen” turns a taste argument into a check, in a product team, a department or a client meeting.

wiifm.skill: Decide when you cannot test first
wiifm.payoff: A decision with an unknown, a reversal figure, a date and something given up is a form you can reuse for any change you cannot test beforehand.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Assess the interface, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight facts into three mistakes, say where a beginner is confused and what you would improve, then choose four of nine measures within €40,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 8 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application

brief1.heading: The case: StructLearn, a cluttered learning platform
brief1.paragraph: StructLearn is a learning platform that has grown without a plan. Users cannot find content, many visual elements compete without any structure, and the drop-out rate is high. A first analysis points to a lack of hierarchy and no clear navigation. The users are beginners. You are part of the UX team, you have three weeks, and you are asked to work out what is wrong and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four StructLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three design options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €40,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 10 weeks for the case study (Case assumption); the options in Block 1.2 have 3 weeks, as in the plan
The users are beginners.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: users cannot find content, many visual elements without structure, a high drop-out rate, a lack of hierarchy, no clear navigation, many colours, no clear structure, several buttons without priority, beginners, three weeks. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €40,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight facts into three mistakes, say where confusion arises, what you would improve (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

p2.title: Choose design measures within the limits

cats.label: Unclear navigation
cats.hint: Can the learner tell where they are and what comes next?
cats.test: Can the learner tell where they are, where something is and what comes next? If one item has several homes, or the marked place and the page disagree, or there is no next step, it is navigation.

cats.label: Visual overload
cats.hint: Is there a main thing, or does everything compete?
cats.test: Is there one main thing on the screen, or do many elements of the same weight compete? Many colours, sizes, banners and equal buttons are overload.

cats.label: Inconsistent design
cats.hint: Does the same function look and work the same everywhere?
cats.test: Does the same function look and work the same on every screen? If a link, a button or a back arrow changes between screens, it is inconsistency.

facts.text: The menu has four levels, and the same course can be reached under “Learn”, “Library” and “Archive”.
facts.short: Four menu levels; one course under three entries
facts.clue: A beginner looks for one course. How many places could it be, and which is the real one?
facts.why: The same item has several homes, so the learner cannot tell where it is: unclear navigation.

facts.text: While a learner is inside a course, the menu still marks “Home”.
facts.short: The menu marks “Home” inside a course
facts.clue: The learner looks at the menu to see where they are. What does it tell them?
facts.why: The marked entry and the page disagree, so the learner cannot tell where they are: unclear navigation.

facts.text: At the end of a lesson there is no “Next” link; the learner must go back up three levels.
facts.short: No “Next” link at the end of a lesson
facts.clue: A learner has just finished a lesson. What can they see to do next?
facts.why: The learner does not know what comes next, which is the third orientation question: unclear navigation.

facts.text: The course page uses nine colours, four font sizes and three animated banners at the same time.
facts.short: Nine colours, four sizes, three banners
facts.key: nine colours, four font sizes and three animated banners
facts.clue: Where does the eye go first on this page, and is there one clear answer?
facts.why: Many elements compete and nothing leads: visual overload.

facts.text: Five buttons of the same size and colour sit in a row: “Start”, “Save”, “Share”, “Report”, “Delete”.
facts.short: Five equal buttons in a row
facts.key: Five buttons of the same size and colour
facts.clue: Which of the five is the one the learner is meant to press, and how can they tell?
facts.why: There is no main action: several buttons without priority, which is a hierarchy problem and so visual overload.

facts.text: Links are blue on one screen, orange on another and plain black on a third.
facts.short: Links in three different colours
facts.key: blue on one screen, orange on another and plain black on a third
facts.clue: A learner has learned what a link looks like on one screen. Can they rely on that on the next?
facts.why: The same function looks different in different places: inconsistent design.

facts.text: “Submit” is a filled button on the quiz, a grey link in the profile and a small icon in the editor.
facts.short: “Submit” looks different on three screens
facts.key: a filled button on the quiz, a grey link in the profile and a small icon in the editor
facts.clue: Is it the same action each time? Does it look as if it is?
facts.why: One function with three looks: inconsistent design.

facts.text: The “Back” arrow returns to the previous page on some screens and goes up one level on others.
facts.short: “Back” does different things on different screens
facts.key: returns to the previous page on some screens and goes up one level on others
facts.clue: The same arrow does two different things. What can a learner expect when they press it?
facts.why: The same control works differently on different screens: inconsistent design (it touches navigation, but the test is that one function behaves in two ways).

8.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto the mistake it shows, or select it and then a mistake. Select a placed one to move it again. One mistake per fact: Unclear navigation, Visual overload or Inconsistent design.
8.sortKeyTitle: Eight facts into Unclear navigation, Visual overload, Inconsistent design
8.sortTeaching: The sort is objective: each fact breaks one of the three mistakes the plan names, and the test is what the learner cannot do. Fact 8 touches navigation too, but the printed phrase is that one control behaves in two ways: inconsistency. A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. The confusion, the improvements and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, describe 5 problems from the user's side, where confusion arises, what to improve intuitively.
8.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A4 and A1 to A3

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight facts: navigation, overload or inconsistency?
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight facts and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · describe the problems from the user's side, where confusion arises, what you would improve intuitively.

fields.label: Which fact would confuse you most as a beginner?
fields.help: Choose one. Any of the eight defends if the reason below says what the learner wants to do at that point.
fields.missing: choose the fact that would confuse a beginner most

options.label: 1 · Four menu levels, one course under three entries
options.why: Defends: the learner cannot tell which entry is the real one.

options.label: 2 · The menu marks “Home” inside a course
options.why: Defends: the menu says the wrong place.

options.label: 3 · No “Next” link at the end of a lesson
options.why: Reference choice: a beginner who has just finished does not know what to do and has to go back up three levels.

options.label: 4 · Nine colours, four sizes, three banners
options.why: Defends: nothing leads the eye.

options.label: 5 · Five equal buttons
options.why: Defends: no main action.

options.label: 6 · Links in three colours
options.why: Defends, but a smaller confusion: a link is usually still recognised.

options.label: 7 · “Submit” looks different on three screens
options.why: Defends: the learner may not find the button in the editor.

options.label: 8 · “Back” does different things
options.why: Defends: the learner is taken somewhere unexpected.

fields.model: f3
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The fact that confuses a beginner most
fields.teaching: Any of the eight defends. Look at the reason: it should say what the learner wants to do at that point and what they cannot tell. The plan's goal is to develop an understanding of structural problems.

fields.label: Where does the confusion arise, and why?
fields.help: Say what the learner wants to do at that point, and what they cannot tell. Refer to the fact by number. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say where the confusion arises: what the learner wants to do and what they cannot tell
fields.model: Fact 3: at the end of a lesson there is no “Next” link. A beginner who has just finished a lesson wants to carry on, cannot see how, and has to go back up three levels; many will stop there.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, fact 2 confuses me most: while I am inside a course, the menu still marks “Home”. I want to know where I am, and the menu tells me the wrong place, so I stop trusting it.
guide.why: Any of the eight facts defends if the reason says what the learner wants to do at that point and what they cannot tell (Materi A1: where am I, where can I go, what comes next).
lookFor: Says what the learner wants to do.
Says what they cannot tell.
Refers to a fact by number.

clue.refValue: where am I · where can I go · what comes next
steps: Pick the fact, then say what the beginner wants to do at that point.
Say which of the three orientation questions the screen does not answer.

fields.label: What would you improve intuitively?
fields.help: Name the fact (by number) that each improvement answers, and start each with a verb. At least 60 characters in all.
fields.missing: write what you would improve, naming the fact each improvement answers
fields.model: 1. Add a “Next lesson” button at the end of every lesson (fact 3). 2. Mark the real place in the menu, so that inside a course it shows “Learn” (fact 2). 3. Make one button the main button and turn the other four into quiet links (fact 5).

guide.example: 1. Give every course one place in the menu and remove the two copies (one course under three entries). 2. Use one colour for links on all screens (links in three colours). 3. Make the back arrow always return to the previous page (one arrow, two behaviours).
guide.why: The plan asks for intuitive improvements. Each should name the fact it answers and improve structure before decoration (Materi A1, A2).
lookFor: Names the fact each improvement answers.
Starts each with a verb.
Improves structure before decoration.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Making design decisions: three options under three weeks
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to improve a learning interface. You have three weeks, the users are beginners and the drop-out rate is high (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A and option C change how the platform looks; option B changes how it is organised.

criteria.label: User impact
criteria.help: How much it helps the learner find, choose and carry on.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could be added or lost, for example more clutter.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your decision: weigh structure against design
opts.whyHelp: Say which option fixes what the learner cannot do, and which only changes how it looks. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Simplify the design visually: fewer colours, fewer banners, one button style
options.keyWhy: It calms the page but does not fix a menu in which one course sits in three places.

options.name: Restructure the navigation: fewer levels, one place per course, a path and a “Next” link
options.keyWhy: It answers what the learner cannot do: find, place themselves and carry on. It needs all three weeks.

options.name: Add more visual elements: icons, illustrations and animations on every course page
options.keyWhy: Rejected: it adds things to look at and helps nobody find anything; more clutter.

model.why: I put B first: beginners are lost because they cannot find content and do not know what comes next, and only the navigation answers that. A comes second: a calmer page helps, but a calm page with the same course under three entries still loses them. C comes last: it only changes how the platform looks.

guide.example: For LearnLoop I would put the navigation first: learners cannot find their course, and a calm page does not change that. Fewer colours come second, because they make the main button visible. Animated illustrations come last: they add more to look at.
guide.why: The plan asks for a prioritisation with a justification. Structure beats visual design. A first also defends if the reason says that calming the page is the fastest win and what it leaves open.
lookFor: Says which option fixes what the learner cannot do.
Says which only changes the look.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Three design options under three weeks
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €8,000 Low, €8,000 to €15,000 Mid, above €15,000 High), so the check can flag it; user impact and risk are judgements. The plan's goal is to weigh structure against design: structure beats visual design. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: design is decision architecture
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: UI is not about making it pretty but about making it understandable; structure beats visual design; good UX reduces the user's wrong decisions.

questions.q: What really guides the user?
Where does uncertainty arise in the interface?
Which design decision has the greatest effect?

model.a: A path, a marked place in the menu and one main button.
model.b: Where the menu and the page disagree and where there is no next step.
model.c: Giving every item one home and every lesson a next step.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: UI is not about making it pretty but about making it understandable; structure beats visual design; good UX reduces the user's wrong decisions. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four structural problems
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight facts of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A structural problem is something a learner cannot do because of how the platform is built, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it stops a learner from doing something, or is only a matter of price, length or taste.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at a fact by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: Learners cannot find content: one item sits in several places under different names.
items.why: Fact 1 and the case: users cannot find content.

items.text: There is no clear visual hierarchy: everything competes for attention.
items.why: Facts 4 and 5; the case names a lack of hierarchy.

items.text: The navigation is not unambiguous: learners cannot tell where they are.
items.why: Facts 2 and 3; the case names no clear navigation.

items.text: There is no clear guidance for action: no main button and no next step.
items.why: Facts 3 and 5.

items.text: The courses are too long.
items.why: No printed fact says so.

items.text: The subscription price is too high.
items.why: A business matter; nothing printed.

items.text: There are too few courses.
items.why: A content matter; the case is about structure.

causes.whyModel: Fact 1: the same course can be reached under “Learn”, “Library” and “Archive”, so learners do not know which entry is the real one.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “Learners cannot tell where they are” rests on one printed fact, that inside a course the menu still marks “Home”. It blocks every beginner who looks at the menu to find their place.
guide.why: A structural problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the main problem as a lack of structure.
lookFor: Points at a fact by number or quotes the case.
Names what the learner cannot do.

causes.teaching: A structural problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the main problem as a lack of structure. The three rejected options are real business or content matters, but none of them stops a learner from doing something.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four improvements, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which fact it answers (by number), what the learner notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the chain structure, orientation, use: say how your first measure leads to orientation and then to use. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could be added or lost, for example more clutter.

impact.label: User impact
impact.help: How much it helps the learner find, choose and carry on.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: clear information architecture, reduction of visual complexity, unambiguous navigation, clear action guidance; rationale structure → orientation → usage. The reference set costs €41,000, €1,000 over the printed budget by plan fidelity; the worksheet allows going over with a reason. A set within budget is M3, M4, M2 and M5 (€38,000), but it leaves the architecture unchanged: whoever picks it should say why. Reference order: M1, M3, M2, M4; M3 first also defends (a quick win in four weeks).

measures.name: A clear information architecture
measures.what: One place per item, grouped into four sections named after what the learner does.
measures.notice: A course is in one place under one name.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1 to 3: one place per item.

measures.name: Reduce visual complexity
measures.what: At most three colours and two text sizes; remove the banners.
measures.notice: The page is calm.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 4 (and fact 5 with M4).

measures.name: Unambiguous navigation
measures.what: The menu marks where the learner is; a path above the page; a “Next” link after every lesson.
measures.notice: The learner knows where they are and what comes next.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 2 and 3 and the case's no clear navigation.

measures.name: A clear action guidance
measures.what: One main button per screen; secondary actions as quiet links.
measures.notice: The learner sees what to do.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 5: several buttons without priority.

measures.name: Consistent components
measures.what: A style guide for buttons, links, dates and “Back”, applied to every screen.
measures.notice: The same thing looks the same.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: answers facts 6, 7 and 8. A second wave: consistency matters once the structure is fixed.

measures.name: More visual elements
measures.what: Animated illustrations on every course page.
measures.notice: More pictures and movement.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: adds decoration; effort High, risk High (more clutter).

measures.name: A dark mode
measures.what: An alternative dark colour scheme.
measures.notice: A switch for light and dark.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: the look; no printed fact asks for it.

measures.name: A new logo and brand name
measures.what: A new name, logo and colours.
measures.notice: The platform is called something new.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: the brand; learners who are lost need a structure, not a new name.

measures.name: A search with AI suggestions
measures.what: A search box that suggests courses with an algorithm.
measures.notice: A new search bar appears.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: adds technology on top of a structure that is not clear; effort High.

reasons.m1: It answers facts 1 to 3: one place per item, grouped into four sections. At €16,000 it is above €15,000, so effort is High. User impact High: it fixes the cause of the lost orientation. Risk Mid, because it is a large change that touches every page.
reasons.m2: It answers fact 4: at most three colours, no banners. €8,000 is the lower edge of the €8,000 to €15,000 band, so effort is Mid. User impact Mid: it calms the page but does not fix the menu. Risk Low, it removes things.
reasons.m3: It answers facts 2 and 3: the menu marks the real place and every lesson ends with “Next”. €11,000, so effort is Mid. User impact High: where am I and what comes next are answered. Risk Low, it adds a path and a link and removes nothing.
reasons.m4: It answers fact 5: one main button, the others become quiet links. At €6,000 it is under €8,000, so effort is Low. User impact High for its cost: the learner sees what to do. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: structure leads to orientation, and orientation leads to use. As long as the same course sits in three places, a calmer page or a better button only decorates a menu the beginner cannot read. The four measures cost €41,000, €1,000 over the €40,000; I accept that because the structure cannot be cut.
model.missingInfo: I do not know where beginners actually get lost: the facts say what is there, not which step makes them stop. I would watch five beginners find one course in a tree test before I rebuild the architecture.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, a “Next” link after every lesson costs €5,000, so effort is Low. It answers the missing next step, so user impact is High for every learner who finishes a lesson. Risk is Low: it adds a link and removes nothing.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). User impact and risk are judgements: they must name the fact the measure answers, what the learner notices, and what could go wrong, for example that a measure adds more clutter (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed fact the measure answers.
Says what the learner notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop the navigation goes first: it costs €18,000, learners cannot find their course, and every other fix works better once they know where they are.
order.why: The plan's rationale: structure → orientation → usage. A different first priority defends if the reason names the group it reaches, the cost, or what the others depend on.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Uses the chain structure, orientation, use.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know whether learners fail because of the menu or because of the names in it. I would run a tree test with five beginners before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

brief2.heading: The situation: StructLearn's Chief UX Architect
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief UX Architect of StructLearn. The platform has grown and become cluttered, users lose orientation, and a redesign is necessary, but the budget is limited. Management wants the basic UX/UI structure of the platform for the next 12 months and expects you to take responsibility for the design decisions.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €210,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Data: you have no user tests of a new structure yet.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: a platform that has grown and become cluttered, users who lose orientation, a necessary redesign, a limited budget. Everything else is made up: the €210,000, the twelve content items, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the basic structure (a card sort), the principles for visual design and the concept for user guidance (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised design measures, the risk analysis (too complex against too reduced), one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · Basic structure, principles for visual design and user guidance
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the card sort of twelve items below, then the lists of principles and guidance and the fields. Answer in the grid, the lists and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 3 · a basic structure (information architecture), principles for visual design, a concept for user guidance.

fields.help: A closed card sort checks a structure before you build it. Use each section at least once, and decide where an item belongs for the learner, not for the system.
fields.missing: place every one of the twelve items in a section

items.label: Continue where I stopped
items.why: It is the learner's way back into the course.

items.label: Course catalogue
items.why: Finding a course.

items.label: Search
items.why: Finding.

items.label: My certificates
items.why: A certificate is the result of progress.

items.label: Progress in each course
items.why: Progress.

items.label: My notes
items.why: Open item: Progress or Help also defend; notes belong to the lesson the learner is in.

items.label: Reminder settings
items.why: Open item: it also supports progress.

items.label: Help centre
items.why: Help.

items.label: Profile and password
items.why: Account.

items.label: Create a course (for trainers)
items.why: Trainer area.

items.label: Learner list of my course (for trainers)
items.why: Trainer area.

items.label: Messages from my trainer
items.why: Open item: Trainer area or Help defend; decide by where the learner looks for it.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The basic structure: a closed card sort of twelve items
fields.teaching: A card sort has no single right answer. Items 6, 7 and 12 are the open ones; any placement with a reason from the learner's side defends. Each section must be used at least once. Plan: item 1, basic structure of the platform (information architecture).

fields.label: Name one item that was hard to place, say why, and how you would check it with learners
fields.help: For example a card sort or a tree test. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one item that was hard to place and how you would check it with learners
fields.model: “Reminder settings” (7) was hard to place: it is a setting, so Help and account, but it also supports progress. I would give the twelve cards to ten learners in an open card sort and see where most of them put it.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, “Download receipt” was hard to place: it is a document, but also part of the account. I would run a tree test with eight learners: where would they look for it first?
guide.why: The plan asks for a basic structure. Naming the hard item and a cheap check (card sort, tree test) shows the learner knows a structure is checked with people (Materi A1).
lookFor: Names one item.
Says why it is hard.
Names a check with learners.

fields.label: Principles for visual design
fields.help: Choose at least three that you would put on a one-page list, so that they can be used to say no to a proposal.
fields.missing: choose at least three principles for visual design

options.label: One main action per screen
options.why: Answers fact 5.

options.label: At most three colours and one accent colour
options.why: Answers fact 4.

options.label: The same function always looks the same (a style guide)
options.why: Answers facts 6 to 8.

options.label: Text contrast of at least 4.5 : 1 and no information by colour alone
options.why: A rule that can be checked.

options.label: Group with space and proximity, not with boxes everywhere
options.why: A hierarchy rule.

options.label: New courses may choose their own colours for variety
options.why: Rejected: it creates the inconsistency of facts 6 to 8.

options.label: Add animation to keep learners interested
options.why: Rejected: decoration; the case already has three animated banners.

options.label: Every screen shows a banner for current offers
options.why: Rejected: competes with the main action.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · Principles for visual design
fields.teaching: A principle is good if it can be used to say no to a proposal. Ask the learner which proposal each principle would reject. At least three; any three of the five reference principles defend. Plan: item 2, principles for visual design.

fields.label: Concept for user guidance
fields.help: Choose at least three elements that together answer “where am I, and what comes next?”.
fields.missing: choose at least three elements for the user guidance

options.label: A path above the page and a marked menu entry
options.why: Answers facts 1 and 2.

options.label: A “Next” or “Continue” button after every lesson
options.why: Answers fact 3.

options.label: A “Continue where you stopped” entry on the home screen
options.why: Orientation on the first screen.

options.label: Progress shown on each course page
options.why: Tells the learner how far they are.

options.label: Plain labels named after what the learner does
options.why: Names sections by what the learner does.

options.label: A pop-up tour on every page
options.why: Rejected: interrupts and adds noise.

options.label: Tooltips on every element
options.why: Rejected: explains a structure that should explain itself.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The concept for user guidance
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference elements defend if together they answer where am I and what comes next. Plan: item 3, concept for user guidance.

fields.label: In one or two sentences: how does a learner always know where they are and what comes next?
fields.help: Answer both questions, and use at least two of the guidance elements you chose. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say how a learner always knows where they are and what comes next
fields.model: A path above the page and the marked menu entry say where they are; a “Next” button after each lesson and “Continue where you stopped” on the home screen say what comes next.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a line above the lesson reads “Learn › Negotiation › Lesson 3 of 8”, which says where the learner is, and a button “Next: lesson 4” says what comes next.
guide.why: Both orientation questions need an answer: where am I, and what comes next (Materi A1, B1).
lookFor: Answers both questions.
Uses at least two of the chosen guidance elements.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 4 and 5 and the additional requirement · prioritised design measures, a risk analysis (too complex against too reduced), a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: too complex against too reduced
fields.help: Imagine the redesign has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the redesign fails

options.label: The new structure is still too complex, and learners are still lost.
options.why: Action: a tree test before release; notice it in the first weeks by support questions.

options.label: We removed so much that learners and trainers lost help and functions they needed.
options.why: The too-reduced failure. Action: test with trainers as well as learners; notice it in support requests in the first four weeks.

options.label: The new section names did not make sense to beginners.
options.why: Action: name sections after what the learner does and test the names.

options.label: The style guide was ignored and the platform drifted back to inconsistency.
options.why: Action: components in the design system and a review gate.

options.label: The budget was spent on the look before the structure was fixed.
options.why: Action: order the work: structure first.

fields.model: r2
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: too complex against too reduced
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the learner would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007).

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I run a tree test with learners and trainers before the release and watch the support requests in the first four weeks; if trainers cannot find their functions, I restore them in the trainer area at once.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would test the new menu with five learners and two trainers before release and read the support requests in the first month; if more than a handful ask where something went, I bring it back.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without user tests)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to rebuild the information architecture into five sections named after what the learner does (D1) before any visual redesign.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example how beginners will group the items. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know how beginners will group the twelve items.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of week 8, fewer than 80% of 20 tested learners find a given course in under a minute in a tree test.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to move the course list into one section first. I do not know whether learners will understand the new section names. I reverse if fewer than 7 of 10 tested learners find their course in under a minute by the end of week 6.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I postpone the full visual rebrand (D6) and the animated elements (D7) to next year. The marketing team will miss the new look in this year's campaign.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I give up the new logo for this year and postpone the dark mode. The brand team will miss the launch picture they planned.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say what it does for orientation and for the learner's behaviour. At least 30 characters.

items.name: Rebuild the information architecture and navigation
items.what: Four or five sections, one place per item, a path and a next step on every page.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: structure first, the cause of the lost orientation.

items.name: A design system with a style guide
items.what: Shared components and rules for buttons, links, dates and “Back”.
items.keyWhy: Defends as the second wave: consistency after structure. In place of D4 if the reason says why tests can wait.

items.name: Redesign the home and course pages around one main action
items.what: A clear visual hierarchy and a “Continue” button.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: hierarchy and guidance on the pages learners meet first.

items.name: Tests of the new structure with learners
items.what: A closed card sort, a tree test and a usability test with beginners.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: the structure is decided without user tests; D4 is how it is checked later.

items.name: A guided first visit for beginners
items.what: A short, skippable first-visit guide to the new structure.
items.keyWhy: Defends, but guiding learners through a confusing structure treats the symptom; it follows D1.

items.name: A full visual rebrand
items.what: New logo, colours, fonts and illustrations.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: the look before the structure; one of the risks the worksheet names.

items.name: Animated elements everywhere
items.what: Movement and illustrations on every page.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: decoration; more things competing for attention.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: the structure is the reason learners lose orientation, and with it fixed every later measure (hierarchy, guidance, tests) has something solid to work on. The learner will find their course and see what comes next, instead of giving up.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the new navigation goes first: it costs the most and removes the cause of the drop-out, and every later fix works on a menu people can read.
guide.why: Structure leads to orientation and orientation to use. A different first measure defends if the reason names what it does for orientation and behaviour (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says what it does for orientation.
Says what it does for the learner's behaviour.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D3, D4 (€135,000 of €210,000, longest 20 weeks). D1 first because structure leads to orientation and orientation to use. D4 third, run next to the build, so the decision made without tests is checked early. D1, D2, D3 also defends. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The basic UX/UI structure of the platform for the next twelve months

8.caseExport: StructLearn is a learning platform that has grown without a plan: users cannot find content, many visual elements compete without structure and the drop-out rate is high. The users are beginners, the budget is €40,000 and the time is limited.

memoSections.title: Risk analysis: too complex against too reduced
What I give up or postpone

8.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 clear information architecture, M2 reduce visual complexity, M3 unambiguous navigation, M4 clear action guidance) and cost €41,000 of the case's €40,000 (a Case assumption), longest 5 weeks of 10. The plan's rationale: structure → orientation → usage.

9.heading: Day 9 · Information architecture, navigation and interaction

intro.about: Today is about how learners find their way, and how a platform gets them to act once they have found it. You learn how information architecture and navigation answer “where am I, and what comes next?”, when a quiz or a task really helps learning and when it becomes a burden, and how to weigh structure against interaction on a platform that has grown without a plan.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is NavLearn, a platform whose learners cannot find content, rarely interact and are losing motivation. The puzzle: with limited money and little time, which comes first, a clear structure or more interaction, and how do you decide when you have no behaviour data yet?

story.question: Which navigation problem does each of the eight facts show, where does a learner lose orientation, and which four of nine measures for structure and interaction fit €45,000 and ten weeks?
As Head of UX Architecture, which sections and navigation does the platform get, where does interaction belong and how, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Tell too many options, unclear labels and missing orientation apart
wiifm.payoff: Count the choices at one point, read each label as a stranger, and ask where you are and what comes next: three quick checks for any menu, intranet or app at your own desk.

wiifm.skill: Tell an interaction that teaches from one that only clicks
wiifm.payoff: A question with feedback makes the learner think; a badge for opening a page does not. The same test works for a training course, a survey or an onboarding flow.

wiifm.skill: Weigh structure against interaction
wiifm.payoff: “More features” and “a clearer order” compete for the same budget in every project. Rating both on user impact, effort and risk gives you a fair comparison.

wiifm.skill: Design the sections and the navigation of a platform
wiifm.payoff: Four sections named after what people do, a short menu and a path above the page are a pattern you can reuse for a website, a knowledge base or an internal tool.

wiifm.skill: Say where interaction belongs, and where it does not
wiifm.payoff: Deciding at the start, inside or at the end of a lesson, and what to leave out, makes a design review concrete instead of a debate about taste.

wiifm.skill: Decide when you have no behaviour data
wiifm.payoff: An unknown, a reversal figure, a date and something given up is a form you can use for any change you cannot measure beforehand.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Analyse the navigation, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight facts into three navigation problems, say where a learner loses orientation and how you would improve it, then choose four of nine measures within €45,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 9 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application
route1.h1: Information architecture and interaction: analyse the navigation, then choose structure and interaction measures
route1.order: Materi A (all five cards, four are core) → the UX Analysis task, one case in two parts (analyse the navigation, choose measures), with two core blocks. Every section stays open, so you can start anywhere.
route1.taskSub: UX Analysis File: analyse the navigation, choose the measures

route2.title: Design the structure and the interaction
route2.blurb: Level 3 in the Head of UX Architecture's chair: the main sections of a new information architecture, a navigation concept, an interaction strategy (where and how), three prioritised measures, the biggest risk (too much structure against too much interaction), one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up.
route2.h1: Structure as steering: sections, navigation, interaction, three measures, the risk, and what you give up
route2.order: Materi B (three cards) → the UX Strategy task, one frame with two core blocks and a memo that builds below. Route 1 is a good start but not needed; every section stays open.
route2.taskSub: UX Strategy Memo: decide as Head of UX Architecture

brief1.heading: The case: NavLearn, a platform learners cannot find their way in
brief1.paragraph: NavLearn is a learning platform with many courses. Users cannot find content, they rarely interact with what they do find, and their motivation is declining. A first analysis points to a poor information architecture and to a lack of activation. The menus have many entries in no clear order, the content is complex, and users lose interest quickly. You are part of the UX team, time is limited, and you are asked to work out what is wrong and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four NavLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options for an interaction strategy (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible structural problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €45,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 10 weeks for the case study (Case assumption); the options in Block 1.2 have 4 weeks (Case assumption: the plan says “time is limited”)
Users quickly lose interest, and the content is complex.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: users cannot find content, low interaction, declining motivation, a poor information architecture, a lack of activation, many menu items without a clear order, users who lose interest quickly, complex content and limited time. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €45,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight facts into three navigation problems, say where a learner loses orientation and how you would improve the navigation (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

p2.title: Choose structure and interaction measures within the limits

cats.label: Too many options
cats.hint: Does the learner face more choices than they can weigh?
cats.test: Count the choices at one decision point. If the learner must pick from many entries or results with no grouping and no order, it is too many options.

cats.label: Unclear labels
cats.hint: Can the learner tell from the name what is behind it?
cats.test: Read the name as a stranger would. If the learner cannot tell what a button or an entry will open, or two names look alike, the label is unclear.

cats.label: No orientation
cats.hint: Can the learner tell where they are and what comes next?
cats.test: Can the learner tell where they are and what comes next? If the page does not say which lesson of how many, or ends without a next step, or looks the same everywhere, orientation is missing.

facts.text: The home menu shows 24 entries in one row, with no grouping.
facts.short: 24 menu entries in one row
facts.clue: A learner looks for one entry. How many must they weigh, and is there a hint where to start?
facts.why: The learner must weigh 24 choices with no grouping: too many options.

facts.text: The course page shows two menus side by side, one with 24 entries and one with 11.
facts.short: Two menus side by side, 24 and 11 entries
facts.clue: Which of the two menus should a learner use, and how can they tell?
facts.why: Two long menus double the choices at one decision point: too many options.

facts.text: Entries are named “Hub”, “Stream”, “Vault” and “Space”.
facts.short: Entries named Hub, Stream, Vault, Space
facts.clue: A newcomer reads these four words. Can they say what is behind each one?
facts.why: The names are the system's words, not what the learner does, so the learner cannot tell what is behind them: unclear labels.

facts.text: Two buttons are named “Go” and “Run”: one opens the quiz, the other the video.
facts.short: Buttons named “Go” and “Run”
facts.clue: Which button opens the quiz? Could the learner know before pressing?
facts.why: Two names that look alike and say nothing about the result: unclear labels.

facts.text: Nothing on the lesson page says which lesson of how many it is.
facts.short: No sign which lesson of how many
facts.key: Nothing on the lesson page says which lesson
facts.clue: A learner is in the middle of a course. Can they tell how far they are?
facts.why: The learner cannot tell where they are in the course: no orientation.

facts.text: After a quiz, the page shows a score and no next step.
facts.short: A score and no next step after a quiz
facts.key: shows a score and no next step
facts.clue: The learner has just seen their score. What can they see to do next?
facts.why: The learner does not know what comes next, the second orientation question: no orientation.

facts.text: A search for “negotiation” returns 140 results in no particular order, with no filters.
facts.short: 140 search results, no order, no filters
facts.clue: The learner wants one good course on the topic. How do they choose among 140?
facts.why: 140 results with no order and no filters: too many options.

facts.text: The title above every page of the platform is just “NavLearn”.
facts.short: The same title “NavLearn” on every page
facts.clue: A learner looks at the title to see where they are. What does it tell them?
facts.why: The title says nothing about the page, so the learner cannot tell where they are: no orientation.

9.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto the problem it shows, or select it and then a problem. Select a placed one to move it again. One problem per fact: Too many options, Unclear labels or No orientation.
9.sortKeyTitle: Eight facts into Too many options, Unclear labels, No orientation
9.sortTeaching: The sort is objective: each fact breaks one of the three navigation problems the plan names (too many options, unclear labels; orientation is the plan's own question “where am I, what comes next”). Fact 8 could be read as a label problem (a poor title); the test is that the learner cannot tell where they are, so orientation; a learner who argues the other reading with a reason defends the choice. The place where orientation is lost, the improvements and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, identify 5 problems, where the user loses orientation, how the navigation could be improved.
9.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A2

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight facts: too many options, unclear labels or no orientation?
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight facts and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · identify the problems, where the user loses orientation, how the navigation could be improved.

fields.label: Where does a learner lose orientation first?
fields.help: Choose one fact. Any of the eight defends if the reason below says what the learner wants to do at that point.
fields.missing: choose the fact where a learner loses orientation first

options.label: 1 · 24 menu entries in one row
options.why: Defends: the learner cannot tell where to start.

options.label: 2 · Two menus side by side
options.why: Defends: it is unclear which menu to use.

options.label: 3 · Entries named Hub, Stream, Vault, Space
options.why: Defends: the names say nothing.

options.label: 4 · Buttons named “Go” and “Run”
options.why: Defends: the learner cannot tell which opens what.

options.label: 5 · No sign which lesson of how many
options.why: Reference choice: in the middle of a course the learner cannot tell how far they are.

options.label: 6 · A score and no next step after a quiz
options.why: Defends: the learner stops at the score.

options.label: 7 · 140 results, no order, no filters
options.why: Defends: the learner cannot choose.

options.label: 8 · The same title on every page
options.why: Defends: the title cannot say where the learner is.

fields.model: f5
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · Where a learner loses orientation first
fields.teaching: Any of the eight defends. Look at the reason: it should say what the learner wants to do at that point and what they cannot tell (where am I, where can I go, what comes next). The plan's goal is to develop an understanding of structural problems.

fields.label: Why do they lose orientation there?
fields.help: Say what the learner wants to do at that point, and what they cannot tell. Refer to the fact by number. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why a learner loses orientation at that fact: what they want to do and what they cannot tell
fields.model: Fact 5: a learner in the middle of a course wants to know how far they are and how much is left. Nothing on the lesson page says it, so they cannot tell, and a learner who cannot see an end tends to stop.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, fact 6 would stop me: after the quiz I see 6 of 10 and nothing else. I want to carry on or fix my mistakes, but I cannot tell what the platform wants me to do next, so I close the tab.
guide.why: Any of the eight facts defends if the reason says what the learner wants to do at that point and what they cannot tell (Materi A2: where am I, where can I go, what comes next).
lookFor: Says what the learner wants to do.
Says what they cannot tell.
Refers to a fact by number.

clue.refValue: where am I · what comes next
steps: Pick the fact, then say what the learner wants to do at that point.
Say which orientation question the screen does not answer.

fields.label: How could the navigation be improved?
fields.help: Name the fact (by number) that each improvement answers, and start each with a verb. At least 60 characters in all.
fields.missing: write how the navigation could be improved, naming the fact each improvement answers
fields.model: 1. Group the 24 entries into four sections and keep one menu (facts 1 and 2). 2. Name the entries after what the learner does, such as “Learn” and “Find” (fact 3). 3. Show “Lesson 3 of 8” and a “Next” button after the quiz (facts 5 and 6).

guide.example: 1. Cut the menu to six entries and put the rest under “More” (a menu with 20 entries). 2. Rename “Go” to “Start the quiz” (an unclear button). 3. Add the page name to the title (the same title on every page).
guide.why: The plan asks how the navigation could be improved. Each improvement should name the fact it answers and answer one of the three problems (Materi A2).
lookFor: Names the fact each improvement answers.
Starts each with a verb.
Answers all three problems, or says why not.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Deciding on an interaction strategy: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to improve a learning platform. Users quickly lose interest, the content is complex and time is limited (four weeks, Case assumption). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A adds interaction, option B builds a clear structure, and option C changes only the look.

criteria.label: Learning impact
criteria.help: How much it helps the learner find the content and then learn from it.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example that interaction becomes a burden.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your decision: weigh structure against interaction
opts.whyHelp: Say which option makes interaction useful and which only adds clicks or looks. At least 30 characters.

options.name: More interactions: a quiz or a click on every page
options.keyWhy: It activates learners who are already in the right place; on a platform where they cannot find content it adds clicks to a lost learner. Risk: interaction becomes a burden.

options.name: Build a clear learning structure: groups, a path and a next step
options.keyWhy: It answers the cause: learners find content and see what comes next. Without structure, interaction has no effect.

options.name: Leave the content as it is and improve only its look
options.keyWhy: It leaves the cause in place: a better look on a menu nobody can read.

model.why: I put B first: users quickly lose interest because they cannot find content, and without structure interaction has no effect. A comes second: once learners find their way, interaction activates them, but on its own it adds clicks to a lost learner and can become a burden. C comes last: it only changes how the platform looks.

guide.example: For LearnLoop I would build the structure first: learners cannot find their course, and a quiz on every page would only add clicks. Interaction comes second, once they can find their way. Only changing the look comes last.
guide.why: The plan's coaching: without structure, interaction has no effect. B first defends; A first also defends if the reason says how the interaction would be targeted and what it leaves open.
lookFor: Says which option makes interaction useful.
Says which only adds clicks or changes the look.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Three options for an interaction strategy
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €7,000 Low, €7,000 to €14,000 Mid, above €14,000 High), so the check can flag it; learning impact and risk are judgements. The plan's goal is to weigh structure against interaction: without structure interaction has no effect. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: structure guides, interaction activates
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: without structure, interaction has no effect; navigation is decision guidance; interaction must be goal-oriented, not an end in itself; engagement arises from meaningful activation.

questions.q: Where does the user lose orientation?
Which interaction brings real added value?
When does interaction become a burden?

model.a: Where the menu has too many entries and where a page does not say which lesson it is.
model.b: A short question after a lesson section, with an answer and a next step.
model.c: When it blocks the next page or rewards a click that teaches nothing.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: without structure interaction has no effect; navigation is decision guidance; interaction must be goal-oriented; engagement arises from meaningful activation. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four structural problems
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight facts of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A structural problem is something a learner cannot do because of how the platform is built or what it asks of them, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it stops a learner from finding or doing something, or is only a matter of price, length or staffing.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at a fact by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: Learners cannot find content: the structure has no clear groups and too many entries.
items.why: Facts 1, 2 and 7 and the case: users cannot find content.

items.text: Learners cannot tell where they are or what comes next: there are no orientation cues.
items.why: Facts 5, 6 and 8.

items.text: The names of entries and buttons do not say what is behind them.
items.why: Facts 3 and 4.

items.text: Lessons activate nobody: there is little interaction, and what exists ends in a score with no next step.
items.why: Fact 6 and the case: low interaction, a lack of activation.

items.text: The courses are too long.
items.why: No printed fact says so.

items.text: The subscription price is too high.
items.why: A business matter; nothing printed.

items.text: There are too few trainers.
items.why: A staffing matter; the case is about structure and activation.

causes.whyModel: Fact 1: the home menu shows 24 entries in one row with no grouping, so a learner who looks for one entry has nothing to guide them.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “Learners cannot tell where they are” rests on one printed fact, that no lesson page says which lesson of how many it is. It blocks every learner in the middle of a course.
guide.why: A structural problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the main problem as a lack of orientation.
lookFor: Points at a fact by number or quotes the case.
Names what the learner cannot do.

causes.teaching: A structural problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names a poor information architecture and a lack of activation; the Musterlösung names the main problem as a lack of orientation. The three rejected options are real business or staffing matters, but none of them stops a learner from finding or doing something.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four measures for structure and interaction, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which fact it answers (by number), what the learner notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the chain orientation, activation, engagement: say how your first measure leads to the next. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example that an interaction becomes a burden.

impact.label: Learning impact
impact.help: How much it helps the learner find the content and then learn from it.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: clear structure, reduced navigation, targeted interactions, feedback mechanisms; rationale orientation → activation → engagement. The reference set costs €42,000 of €45,000 and takes at most 5 weeks of 10. M5 (renaming entries) defends in place of M2 if the reason names the unclear labels (facts 3 and 4). Reference order: M1, M2, M3, M4; M2 first also defends (the quickest orientation gain).

measures.name: A clear information structure
measures.what: Four sections named after what the learner does, one place per item, grouped logically.
measures.notice: Content has one clear place.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1, 2 and 7: groups instead of 24 entries.

measures.name: Reduced navigation
measures.what: At most six entries in the main menu, a path above every page and the lesson number on every lesson page.
measures.notice: The learner always sees where they are.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1, 2, 5 and 8.

measures.name: Targeted interactions
measures.what: One short question after each lesson section, tied to what the section teaches.
measures.notice: The learner answers, not only reads.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers the case's lack of activation; interaction tied to a goal.

measures.name: Feedback and a next step
measures.what: After every interaction an explained result and a button for what to do next, plus a progress bar.
measures.notice: The learner knows how they did and what to do next.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 6; feedback closes each interaction.

measures.name: Names after what the learner does
measures.what: Rename the entries and buttons: “Learn”, “Find”, “Start the quiz”.
measures.notice: The names say what is behind them.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: answers facts 3 and 4, a cheap quick win. A learner who picks it instead of M2 should name the unclear labels.

measures.name: Points and badges for every click
measures.what: A reward for opening a page or pressing a button.
measures.notice: Badges appear all the time.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: interaction as an end in itself; it rewards clicks that teach nothing and adds noise.

measures.name: A drag-and-drop exercise in every lesson
measures.what: A new interactive exercise on every lesson page.
measures.notice: Every lesson asks for activity.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: more interaction without structure; effort High, and a lost learner meets more clicks.

measures.name: A new visual theme
measures.what: New colours and fonts for every course page.
measures.notice: The platform looks different.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: the look; no printed fact asks for it.

measures.name: An AI assistant that tells learners where to go
measures.what: A chat assistant that answers where content is.
measures.notice: A chat button appears.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: technology laid over a structure that is not clear; effort High.

reasons.m1: It answers facts 1, 2 and 7: groups instead of 24 entries and two menus. At €15,000 it is above €14,000, so effort is High. Learning impact High: it fixes the cause that learners cannot find content. Risk Mid, because it is a large change that touches every page.
reasons.m2: It answers facts 1, 2, 5 and 8: six entries, a path and the lesson number. €7,000 is the lower edge of the €7,000 to €14,000 band, so effort is Mid. Learning impact Mid: it helps orientation but does not create the groups. Risk Low, it removes entries and adds a path.
reasons.m3: It answers the lack of activation: one question after each section, tied to what it teaches. €11,000, so effort is Mid. Learning impact Mid: it makes the learner think, but only once they can find the lesson. Risk Mid, because a question that does not fit the lesson would be a burden.
reasons.m4: It answers fact 6: a result, an explanation and a next step after every interaction. €9,000, so effort is Mid. Learning impact High: feedback closes the loop for every learner after every question. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: orientation comes before activation, and activation before engagement. As long as 24 entries sit in one row, a quiz after each section only adds clicks to a learner who has not found the lesson. The four measures cost €42,000 of €45,000, with the longest at five weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know where learners drop out: before they find a lesson or after they have found it. I would check where sessions end in the analytics and watch five learners look for a course in a tree test before I spend the last €3,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, a progress bar and “Lesson 3 of 8” on every lesson page cost €4,000, so effort is Low. It answers the missing sign of where the learner is, so learning impact is Mid for every learner. Risk is Low: it adds one line.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). Learning impact and risk are judgements: they must name the fact the measure answers, what the learner notices, and what could go wrong, for example that an interaction becomes a burden (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed fact the measure answers.
Says what the learner notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop the new menu structure goes first: it costs €13,000, learners cannot find their course, and a quiz on every page would only add clicks until they can.
order.why: The plan's rationale: orientation → activation → engagement. A different first priority defends if the reason names the group it reaches, the cost, or what the others depend on.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Uses the chain orientation, activation, engagement.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know whether learners leave before or after they find a lesson. I would read where sessions end and test the menu with five learners before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

brief2.heading: The situation: NavLearn's Head of UX Architecture
brief2.paragraph: You are the Head of UX Architecture of NavLearn. The platform is growing without a structure, users lose orientation, and engagement is declining. Management wants a new information architecture, a navigation concept and an interaction strategy for the next 12 months, and it expects you to take responsibility for guiding the users.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €190,000 (Case assumption: the plan does not give one)
Data: you have no behaviour data on a new structure yet.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: a platform that grows without a structure, users who lose orientation, declining engagement. Everything else is made up: the €190,000, the section candidates, the interaction types, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the main sections of the information architecture, the navigation concept and the interaction strategy, where and how (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk analysis (too much structure against too much interaction), one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · Information architecture, navigation and interaction strategy
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the list of sections below, then the navigation elements, the interaction map and the fields. Answer in the lists, the grid and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 3 · a new information architecture, a navigation concept, an interaction strategy (where and how).

fields.label: The new information architecture: choose the four main sections
fields.help: Sections are named after what the learner does and are few. Choose exactly four.
fields.missing: choose exactly four main sections

options.label: Learn: my current course and the next step
options.why: The entry for the learner who comes back to carry on.

options.label: Find: catalogue, search and filters
options.why: Where a learner finds something new.

options.label: Progress: what I have done and earned
options.why: Orientation over time and certificates.

options.label: Help and account
options.why: Help, settings and profile in one place.

options.label: Community: forum and groups
options.why: Defends if learners ask for exchange; a fifth section raises the choices, so it goes under Learn or waits.

options.label: News and offers
options.why: Rejected as a main section: it competes with the learner's goal; one banner or a line in Find is enough.

options.label: Archive of old course versions
options.why: Rejected: a second home for content that already has one.

options.label: Partners and press
options.why: Rejected: a business matter, not something a learner does.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The four main sections
fields.teaching: Four sections named after what the learner does (Learn, Find, Progress, Help) answer where am I, where can I go. A fifth, Community, defends if the reason says who asked for it and what it replaces. Plan: item 1, a new information architecture.

fields.label: Which section does a new learner meet first, and what does it show?
fields.help: Name the section and the one main thing it shows. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say which section a new learner meets first and what it shows
fields.model: A new learner meets Find first: it shows a short catalogue with filters and one recommended starting course. A returning learner meets Learn, which shows “Continue: lesson 3”.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a new learner meets Learn first, because it shows one starter course and one big button “Start”. Find is one click away for learners who want to browse.
guide.why: The first section should show one main thing and answer what to do next (Materi A1, B1).
lookFor: Names a section.
Names one main thing it shows.

fields.label: The navigation concept: choose at least three elements
fields.help: Choose elements that together answer “where am I, where can I go, what comes next?”.
fields.missing: choose at least three elements for the navigation concept

options.label: A main menu with at most six entries
options.why: Answers where can I go, and keeps the choices small.

options.label: A path above the page: Learn › Course › Lesson 3 of 8
options.why: Answers where am I.

options.label: A progress indicator on every course page
options.why: Answers how far, and what is left.

options.label: A “Continue where you stopped” entry
options.why: Answers what comes next for a returning learner.

options.label: Labels named after what the learner does
options.why: Answers what is behind an entry.

options.label: A mega menu that lists every page of the platform
options.why: Rejected: it recreates the 24 entries.

options.label: A menu that hides itself on desktop screens
options.why: Rejected: it hides the answer to where can I go.

options.label: A different menu layout for every course
options.why: Rejected: it breaks consistency and orientation between courses.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The navigation concept
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference elements defend if together they answer where am I, where can I go, what comes next. Plan: item 2, a navigation concept.

fields.label: In one or two sentences: how does a learner always know where they are and what comes next?
fields.help: Answer both questions, and use at least two of the elements you chose. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say how a learner always knows where they are and what comes next
fields.model: The path above each page and the lesson number say where they are; the progress bar shows how much is left, and “Continue where you stopped” on the home screen says what comes next.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a line “Learn › Negotiation › Lesson 3 of 8” says where the learner is, and a button “Next: lesson 4” at the end of the lesson says what comes next.
guide.why: Both orientation questions need an answer: where am I, and what comes next (Materi A2, B1).
lookFor: Answers both questions.
Uses at least two of the chosen elements.

fields.label: The interaction strategy, where: place eight interactions
fields.help: Decide for each interaction where in a lesson it belongs, or that it would be a burden and is not used. Interaction must serve a goal, not be an end in itself.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight interactions

bins.label: At the start of a lesson
At the end of a lesson
Not used: it would be a burden

items.label: A one-question warm-up that recalls the last lesson
items.why: Recall at the start activates what the learner already knows.

items.label: A short quiz question after each section
items.why: Active use right where the idea was taught.

items.label: A task: apply the idea to the learner's own work
items.why: Transfer after the idea is understood.

items.label: A click-through scenario with two choices
items.why: Practice of a decision in context.

items.label: A pop-up quiz that blocks the next page
items.why: A burden: it interrupts and blocks.

items.label: A reflection note: what will I do differently?
items.why: Closes the lesson with meaning.

items.label: A badge for opening a page
items.why: Rewards a click that teaches nothing: interaction as an end in itself.

items.label: A poll: how confident do you feel about this topic?
items.why: Open item: end also defends; at the start it activates and frames.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · Where interactions belong
