fields.teaching: There is no single right map. Items 1 to 4 and 6 are well-defended; items 5 and 7 are the burdens (a blocking pop-up, a reward for a click). Item 8 defends at the start or at the end. Each bin must be used at least once. Plan: item 3, an interaction strategy (where and how).

fields.label: The interaction strategy, how: which interaction goes first, and what does it add beyond clicking?
fields.help: Name one interaction and say what the learner does with their mind, and what feedback they get. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say which interaction goes first and what it adds beyond clicking
fields.model: The short question after each section goes first: the learner has to recall and apply the idea, not only click, and gets an explained answer and a next step, so the interaction teaches and closes the loop.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a one-question check after each section goes first: the learner thinks before the next section and sees why an answer is right, which a badge for opening the page never would.
guide.why: Interaction brings value when it makes the learner think and answers back (Materi A3).
lookFor: Names one interaction.
Says what the learner thinks or does.
Says what feedback they get.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 4 and 5 and the additional requirement · prioritised measures, a risk analysis (over-structuring against over-interaction), a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: over-structuring against over-interaction
fields.help: Imagine the redesign has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the redesign fails

options.label: We over-structured: learners lost the freedom to jump straight to what they already know.
options.why: The over-structuring pole. Action: keep a search and a direct link for experienced learners; notice it in how often they skip the path.

options.label: We over-interacted: every screen asked for a click, and learners felt pushed.
options.why: The over-interaction pole. Action: cap interactions per lesson and make most skippable; notice it in skip and drop-out rates per lesson.

options.label: Structure and interaction were built separately and do not fit.
options.why: Action: one owner for both and a joint review.

options.label: The new section names did not make sense to beginners.
options.why: Action: test the names with a tree test.

options.label: Learners clicked more and learned no more: engagement without learning.
options.why: Action: measure results, not clicks.

fields.model: r2
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: over-structuring against over-interaction
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the learner would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007).

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I cap the interactions at one question per lesson section and make all but the first skippable, and I read the skip and drop-out rates per lesson in the first month.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would limit each lesson to two interactions and watch how many learners skip them in the first four weeks; if more than a third skip, I remove one.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without behaviour data)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to rebuild the structure into four sections and add one targeted question per lesson section (D1 and D2) before any other interaction.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example how learners react to a question after every section. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know whether learners will find a question after every section helpful or intrusive.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of week 8, more than 40% of learners skip the question in a lesson, and I make it optional there.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to add one question per lesson first. I do not know whether learners find it helpful. I reverse if more than 30% skip it by the end of week 6, and I make it optional.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I give up the points and badges for every click (D6) and the AI assistant (D7) this year. The community team will miss the engagement figures that badges would have produced.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I give up the new chat assistant this year and postpone the guided learning path. The sales team will miss the demo feature they planned.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.pickLabel: measures for your structure and interaction
decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say how it leads to orientation, and from there to activation. At least 30 characters.

items.name: Rebuild the information architecture and navigation
items.what: Four sections, a short menu, a path and a lesson number on every page.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: orientation first, the cause of the lost orientation.

items.name: Five targeted interaction patterns
items.what: A warm-up question, a section question, a scenario, a task and a reflection note, each tied to a lesson goal.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: activation, tied to goals, after the structure.

items.name: A progress and feedback system
items.what: An explained result and a next step after every interaction, and progress shown on every course page.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: feedback turns interaction into engagement.

items.name: Tests of the structure and the interactions with learners
items.what: A card sort, a tree test and a usability test with learners.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D3: the decision is made without behaviour data, and D4 is how it is checked later.

items.name: A guided learning path through every course
items.what: A recommended order with a skip option for experienced learners.
items.keyWhy: Defends as a second wave: it builds on a clear structure and keeps freedom with the skip option.

items.name: Points and badges for every click
items.what: A reward for every page opened and every button pressed.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: interaction as an end in itself; it rewards clicks that teach nothing.

items.name: An AI assistant that tells learners where to go
items.what: A chat assistant that answers where content is.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: technology on top of a structure that is not clear; the most expensive and the longest.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: orientation comes before activation. Once learners can find their lesson and know where they are, the targeted interactions of D2 have something to work on, and the feedback of D3 turns them into engagement. In that order each measure makes the next one effective.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the new menu structure goes first: learners cannot find their course, and the questions and feedback that follow only work once they can. Orientation, then activation, then engagement.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: orientation → activation → engagement. A different first measure defends if the reason names what it does for orientation and behaviour (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says how it leads to orientation.
Says how it leads on to activation.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D2, D3 (€125,000 of €190,000, longest 20 weeks). D1 first because orientation comes before activation and engagement. D1, D2, D4 also defends: the decision is made without behaviour data, so tests come early. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The information architecture, navigation and interaction strategy for the next twelve months

9.caseExport: NavLearn is a learning platform whose learners cannot find content, rarely interact and are losing motivation. Menus have many entries in no clear order, the content is complex and users lose interest quickly. The budget is €45,000 and the time is limited.

memoSections.title: The interaction strategy: where and how
What I give up or postpone

9.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 clear information structure, M2 reduced navigation, M3 targeted interactions, M4 feedback and a next step) and cost €42,000 of the case's €45,000 (a Case assumption), longest 5 weeks of 10. The plan's rationale: orientation → activation → engagement.

10.heading: Day 10 · Feedback, progress tracking and responsive design

intro.about: Today is about telling learners how they are doing, on whatever device they use. You learn what makes feedback useful, how a progress display raises or kills motivation, how a layout changes on a phone, and how accessibility makes all of it work for more people. You then weigh these measures on a platform where learners do not know how far along they are.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is TrackLearn, a platform where learners do not know how far along they are, where most learners use a phone and the experience there is poor, and where motivation is low. The puzzle: with a limited budget, what do you build first, and how do you decide when you cannot yet measure retention by device?

story.question: Which of three problems does each of the eight facts show, how does that affect a learner's motivation, and which four of nine measures fit €45,000 and ten weeks?
As the Chief UX Systems Officer, what feedback and progress tracking does the platform get, how does it adapt to devices and stay accessible, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Spot missing feedback, unclear progress and poor phone use
wiifm.payoff: “What happened when I pressed that, how far am I, does it work on my phone?” are three questions you can ask of any form, app or portal at your own desk.

wiifm.skill: Tell honest progress from misleading progress
wiifm.payoff: A bar that jumps to 90% after one click makes people feel cheated later. The same test works for an onboarding checklist or a project status page.

wiifm.skill: Weigh feedback, progress and mobile against a budget
wiifm.payoff: Impact, effort and risk give you a fair comparison when three good-sounding measures compete for the same money.

wiifm.skill: Design feedback and progress as one system
wiifm.payoff: Choosing which feedback exists, which progress is shown and what a risk looks like is a pattern you can reuse for any product that users return to.

wiifm.skill: Put a phone first without leaving other devices behind
wiifm.payoff: Deciding what is the same everywhere, what comes first on a phone and what only fits a large screen makes a design review concrete.

wiifm.skill: Decide when you cannot measure retention by device
wiifm.payoff: An unknown, a reversal figure, a date and something given up is a form you can use for any change you cannot measure beforehand.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Assess feedback and progress, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight facts into three problems, say how they affect motivation and what you would improve, then choose four of nine measures within €45,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 10 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application
route1.h1: Feedback, progress and responsive design: assess the platform, then choose the measures
route1.order: Materi A (all five cards, four are core) → the UX Analysis task, one case in two parts (assess feedback and progress, choose measures), with two core blocks. Every section stays open, so you can start anywhere.
route1.taskSub: UX Analysis File: assess feedback and progress, choose the measures

route2.title: Design the feedback and tracking system
route2.blurb: Level 3 in the Chief UX Systems Officer's chair: a concept for feedback, a strategy for progress tracking, a responsive concept with accessibility built in, three prioritised measures, the biggest risk, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up.
route2.h1: UX as a steering and feedback system: feedback, progress, devices, accessibility, three measures, the risk, and what you give up
route2.order: Materi B (three cards) → the UX Strategy task, one frame with two core blocks and a memo that builds below. Route 1 is a good start but not needed; every section stays open.
route2.materiSub: Level 3 · UX as a feedback system
route2.taskSub: UX Strategy Memo: decide as Chief UX Systems Officer

brief1.heading: The case: TrackLearn, a platform where learners do not know where they stand
brief1.paragraph: TrackLearn is a learning platform whose users do not know how far along they are. Most of them use a phone, but the experience there is poor, and their motivation is low. A first analysis points to missing feedback and no mobile optimisation. There is no progress bar, nothing answers a finished task, and the learning status is unclear. You are part of the UX team, the budget is limited and the drop-out rate is high.

have.title: What you have
items: Four TrackLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible central problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €45,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 10 weeks (Case assumption: the plan gives none)
Most users use the platform on a phone, and many drop out.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: users do not know how far along they are, high mobile use but poor UX, low motivation, missing feedback, no mobile optimisation, no progress bar, no response to completed tasks, an unclear learning status, a limited budget and a high drop-out rate. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €45,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight facts into three problems, say how they affect motivation and what you would improve (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

cats.label: Missing feedback
cats.hint: Does the platform answer what the learner does?
cats.test: When the learner finishes a task or gives an answer, does the platform answer, and does the answer say something useful? Silence, or a bare mark with no reason, is missing feedback.

cats.label: Unclear progress
cats.hint: Can the learner tell how far along they are?
cats.test: Can the learner tell how far along they are, which lessons are done and what is left? No bar, no status, or a number that says nothing about what it measures, is unclear progress.

cats.label: Poor use on a phone
cats.hint: Does the screen work on a small display?
cats.test: Does the screen work on a phone? Text that runs off the edge, sideways scrolling or tiny buttons mean the layout was not adapted to the device.

facts.text: When a learner finishes a task, nothing on the screen changes.
facts.short: Nothing changes when a task is finished
facts.clue: A learner has just finished a task. What tells them it counted?
facts.why: The platform does not answer what the learner did: missing feedback.

facts.text: A wrong quiz answer shows only a red cross, with no reason.
facts.short: A red cross and no reason
facts.key: only a red cross, with no reason
facts.clue: The learner sees the cross. What do they know about why, and about what to do?
facts.why: The platform answers, but with a bare mark that explains nothing: missing feedback.

facts.text: Saving a task gives no message, so learners press Save again to be sure.
facts.short: No message after saving
facts.clue: A learner saves a task. How do they know it worked?
facts.why: No answer to an action, so the learner presses again to be sure: missing feedback.

facts.text: The course page shows no progress bar and no count of finished lessons.
facts.short: No progress bar, no count of lessons
facts.key: no progress bar and no count
facts.clue: A learner is half way through a course. What tells them so?
facts.why: The learner cannot see how far along they are: unclear progress.

facts.text: Finished lessons look the same as lessons not yet started.
facts.short: Finished lessons look like unstarted ones
facts.key: look the same as lessons not yet started
facts.clue: Can a learner tell by looking at the list which lessons they have done?
facts.why: The status of a lesson is not shown: unclear progress.

facts.text: The dashboard shows “Level 7” and does not say what it measures.
facts.short: “Level 7” with no meaning
facts.key: does not say what it measures
facts.clue: The learner sees a level number. What does it tell them about their progress?
facts.why: A number that says nothing about what it measures is not transparent progress: unclear progress (and a risk of a misleading display).

facts.text: On a phone, the lesson text is cut off at the right edge, and the learner must scroll sideways.
facts.short: Text cut off on a phone, sideways scrolling
facts.key: cut off at the right edge
facts.clue: A learner reads on a phone. Does the text fit the screen?
facts.why: The layout was not adapted to the small screen: poor use on a phone.

facts.text: On a phone, the Next button is 20 px high and sits at the very bottom of a long page.
facts.short: A 20 px Next button at the page bottom
facts.clue: A learner uses a thumb. Can they reach and hit the button easily?
facts.why: A small target far from the thumb: poor use on a phone, and an accessibility problem too (target size).

10.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto the problem it shows, or select it and then a problem. Select a placed one to move it again. One problem per fact: Missing feedback, Unclear progress or Poor use on a phone.
10.sortKeyTitle: Eight facts into Missing feedback, Unclear progress, Poor use on a phone
10.sortTeaching: The sort is objective: each fact breaks one of the three areas of the day (feedback, progress, responsive design). Fact 8 touches accessibility too (target size), and fact 6 could be argued as feedback; the test is what the learner cannot do (hit the button; tell how far along they are). A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. The effect on motivation, the improvements and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, describe 5 problems from the user's perspective, how this affects motivation, which improvements.
10.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A1 to A3

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight facts: feedback, progress or phone?
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight facts and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · describe the problems from the user's perspective, how they affect motivation, which improvements you suggest.

fields.label: Which fact would take away a learner's motivation first?
fields.help: Choose one. Any of the eight defends if the reason below says what the learner feels and what they stop doing.
fields.missing: choose the fact that would take away a learner's motivation first

options.label: 1 · Nothing changes when a task is finished
options.why: Reference choice: effort with no sign that it counted is the quickest way to lose motivation.

options.label: 2 · A red cross and no reason
options.why: Defends: a mistake with no explanation feels like a verdict.

options.label: 3 · No message after saving
options.why: Defends: insecurity about whether work is safe.

options.label: 4 · No progress bar, no count of lessons
options.why: Defends: no sense of getting somewhere.

options.label: 5 · Finished lessons look like unstarted ones
options.why: Defends: finished work is invisible.

options.label: 6 · “Level 7” with no meaning
options.why: Defends: a number that cannot be interpreted.

options.label: 7 · Text cut off on a phone
options.why: Defends: most learners use a phone.

options.label: 8 · A 20 px Next button at the page bottom
options.why: Defends: friction at every lesson.

fields.model: f1
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The fact that would take motivation first
fields.teaching: Any of the eight defends. Look at the reason: it should say what the learner feels and what they stop doing. The plan's goal is to develop an understanding of feedback systems; the coaching says making progress visible raises motivation.

fields.label: How does this affect motivation?
fields.help: Say what the learner feels and what they stop doing. Refer to the fact by number. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say how that fact affects motivation: what the learner feels and what they stop doing
fields.model: Fact 1: a learner finishes a task and nothing changes on the screen. They put in effort and get no sign that it counted, so they feel unseen, wonder if it was worth it and, after a few tasks, stop.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, fact 4 would hurt most: with no progress bar I cannot tell if I am a tenth or nine tenths through the course. Without a sense of getting somewhere I start to wonder how much more there is, and I stop.
guide.why: Any of the eight facts defends if the reason says what the learner feels and what they stop doing (Materi A1, A2: feedback and progress as a tool for motivation).
lookFor: Says what the learner feels.
Says what they stop doing.
Refers to a fact by number.

clue.refValue: a sign that it counted · a sense of getting somewhere
steps: Pick the fact and say what the learner has just done.
Say what the screen does not tell them back, and what that feels like.

fields.label: Which improvements do you suggest?
fields.help: Name the fact (by number) that each improvement answers, and start each with a verb. At least 60 characters in all.
fields.missing: write which improvements you suggest, naming the fact each improvement answers
fields.model: 1. Show a message and a tick when a task is finished, and say what it counted towards (facts 1 and 3). 2. Add a progress bar and a status for every lesson: not started, in progress, done (facts 4 and 5). 3. Adapt the layout to a phone: text that fits and a Next button at least 44 px high within thumb reach (facts 7 and 8).

guide.example: 1. Explain every wrong answer in one sentence and show the next step (a red cross with no reason). 2. Show “3 of 8 lessons done” on the course page (no count of lessons). 3. Make the text wrap to the phone width (text cut off on a phone).
guide.why: The plan asks which improvements you suggest. Each should name the fact it answers and answer one of the three problems (Materi A1 to A3).
lookFor: Names the fact each improvement answers.
Starts each with a verb.
Answers all three problems, or says why not.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Prioritising UX systems: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to optimise a learning platform. Users use it on a phone, the drop-out rate is high and the budget is limited (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A shows progress, option B adapts the platform to phones, and option C builds a detailed feedback system.

criteria.label: Impact
criteria.help: How much it does for motivation and for finishing a course.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example a display that misleads or feedback that overloads.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your decision: make a systemic UX decision
opts.whyHelp: Say what each option does for most of your users, who use a phone, and what it leaves open. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Introduce a progress indicator
options.keyWhy: It answers how far along am I at a low price, but only helps if it also works on a phone.

options.name: Optimise the platform for mobile
options.keyWhy: Most users are on a phone, so everything else has to work there first: responsive design is a prerequisite.

options.name: Develop a detailed feedback system
options.keyWhy: It is valuable, but costs the most and risks overloading learners; it comes after the basics.

model.why: I put B first: most of our users are on a phone, so a progress indicator or feedback that does not work there reaches nobody; responsive design is a prerequisite. A comes second: it is the cheapest way to show learners how far along they are. C comes last: detailed feedback costs the most and risks overloading learners before the basics work.

guide.example: For LearnLoop, where most learners are on a phone, I would adapt the platform to phones first, because a progress bar that cannot be read there helps nobody. The bar comes second, and a detailed feedback system comes last.
guide.why: The plan's coaching: responsive design is not an option but a prerequisite. A first also defends if the reason says that transparency is the cheapest quick win and what it leaves open.
lookFor: Names what each option does for phone users.
Says what it leaves open.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Prioritising UX systems: three options
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €8,000 Low, €8,000 to €16,000 Mid, above €16,000 High), so the check can flag it; impact and risk are judgements. The plan's goal is to make systemic UX decisions. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: UX as a steering and feedback system
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: users need orientation and feedback; making progress visible raises motivation; responsive design is not an option but a prerequisite; accessibility means scalability and reach.

questions.q: Where does the user lack orientation?
Which information is decisive for motivation?
Which UX decision works on all devices?

model.a: In the middle of a course, where nothing says how far along they are.
model.b: A sign that their work counted and how much is left.
model.c: A layout that adapts and a progress display that does not depend on screen size.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: users need orientation and feedback; visible progress raises motivation; responsive design is a prerequisite; accessibility is scalability and reach. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four central problems
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight facts of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A central problem is something that stops a learner from knowing how they are doing or from using the platform, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it stops a learner from seeing their progress or using a phone, or is only a matter of price, length or choice.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at a fact by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: Learners do not know how far along they are: progress is not shown.
items.why: Facts 4, 5 and 6 and the case: users do not know how far along they are.

items.text: Feedback is missing or says nothing: tasks get no answer, or only a bare mark.
items.why: Facts 1, 2 and 3 and the case: missing feedback.

items.text: The platform works badly on a phone, where most learners are.
items.why: Facts 7 and 8 and the case: high mobile use but poor UX, no mobile optimisation.

items.text: Information is hard to use for many people: tiny targets and text that does not fit.
items.why: Facts 7 and 8; the plan's Musterlösung names poor accessibility.

items.text: The courses are too long.
items.why: No printed fact says so.

items.text: The subscription price is too high.
items.why: A business matter; nothing printed.

items.text: The platform has too few courses.
items.why: A content matter; the case is about feedback, progress and mobile use.

causes.whyModel: Fact 4: the course page shows no progress bar and no count of finished lessons, so a learner half way through a course has nothing that tells them so.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “Feedback says nothing” rests on one printed fact, that a wrong answer shows only a red cross. It blocks every learner who wants to know why they were wrong.
guide.why: A central problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the main problem as a lack of transparency and poor accessibility.
lookFor: Points at a fact by number or quotes the case.
Names what the learner cannot do.

causes.teaching: A central problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names missing feedback and no mobile optimisation; the Musterlösung names a lack of transparency and poor accessibility. The three rejected options are real business or content matters, but none of them stops a learner from seeing their progress or using a phone.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four measures for feedback, tracking and phones, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which fact it answers (by number), what the learner notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the chain transparency, motivation, usage: say how your first measure leads to the next. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example a display that misleads or feedback that overloads.

impact.label: Impact
impact.help: How much it does for motivation and for finishing a course.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: progress indicator, direct feedback, mobile optimisation, clear presentation; rationale transparency → motivation → usage. The reference set costs €40,000 of €45,000 and takes at most 5 weeks of 10. M5 (accessible targets and contrast) defends in place of M4 if the reason names facts 7 and 8. Reference order: M1, M2, M3, M4; M3 first also defends (most users are on a phone, so it is a prerequisite).

measures.name: A progress indicator
measures.what: A bar on every course page and a status for every lesson: not started, in progress, done, with “3 of 8”.
measures.notice: The learner always sees how far along they are.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 4, 5 and 6: honest transparency.

measures.name: Direct feedback
measures.what: A message and a tick when a task is finished, and an explained result with a next step after every quiz answer.
measures.notice: Every action gets an answer that says something.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1, 2 and 3: feedback that counts and explains.

measures.name: Mobile optimisation
measures.what: A phone-first layout: text that fits, large targets within thumb reach, the main action at the bottom.
measures.notice: The platform is easy to use on a phone.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 7 and 8; most users are on a phone.

measures.name: A clear presentation
measures.what: One main thing per screen, a short result line and plain words, so that progress and feedback are read at a glance.
measures.notice: The screens are calm and easy to read.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Keeps information from overloading; supports facts 6 and 7.

measures.name: Accessible targets and contrast
measures.what: Targets of at least 44 px, contrast of at least 4.5 : 1, and status shown with a word as well as a colour.
measures.notice: Buttons are easy to hit and text is easy to read.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: answers fact 8 and the plan's poor accessibility. A learner who picks it instead of M4 should name facts 7 and 8.

measures.name: Levels and points for every action
measures.what: A level number and points for every click and every lesson opened.
measures.notice: Numbers and levels appear everywhere.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: a display that does not say what it measures (fact 6) and rewards activity, not progress; a risk of misleading learners.

measures.name: A detailed learning analytics dashboard
measures.what: Fourteen charts about time spent, clicks and scores for every learner.
measures.notice: A dense page of charts.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: more information than a learner can use; information density against clarity; effort High.

measures.name: A separate native mobile app
measures.what: A second product for phones, built and maintained alongside the website.
measures.notice: A second thing to install.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: the cost of a second product when the website itself can be made responsive; effort High and over the limits.

measures.name: Daily reminder emails
measures.what: An email every day to every learner who has not logged in.
measures.notice: More emails arrive.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: it pushes learners back to a platform that still does not tell them where they stand; effort Low, but it treats a symptom.

reasons.m1: It answers facts 4, 5 and 6: a bar, a status for each lesson and “3 of 8”. At €7,000 it is under €8,000, so effort is Low. Impact High: it answers the question “how far along am I?” for every learner. Risk Mid, because a progress display that is wrong would mislead and demotivate.
reasons.m2: It answers facts 1, 2 and 3: a message and a tick after a task, and an explained result with a next step. €9,000, so effort is Mid. Impact High: every learner gets a sign that their work counted. Risk Low, it adds answers and removes nothing.
reasons.m3: It answers facts 7 and 8: text that fits, large targets in thumb reach. At €16,000 it is the upper edge of the €8,000 to €16,000 band, so effort is Mid. Impact High: most learners are on a phone. Risk Mid, because it changes the layout of every screen.
reasons.m4: It keeps feedback and progress readable: one main thing per screen and plain words. €8,000 is the lower edge of the €8,000 to €16,000 band, so effort is Mid. Impact Mid: it supports the other three rather than answering a fact alone. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: transparency leads to motivation, and motivation leads to use. A learner who sees “3 of 8” knows they are getting somewhere, and then the direct feedback of M2 and the phone layout of M3 keep them going. The four measures cost €40,000 of €45,000, with the longest at five weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know how many learners use a phone and where they drop out: before they see their progress or after. I would split the analytics by device and watch five phone learners work through one course before I spend the last €5,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, a message and a tick after each task cost €6,000, so effort is Low. It answers the missing sign that work counted, so impact is High for every learner who finishes a task. Risk is Low: it adds a line and removes nothing.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). Impact and risk are judgements: they must name the fact the measure answers, what the learner notices, and what could go wrong, for example a display that misleads or feedback that overloads (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed fact the measure answers.
Says what the learner notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop the progress bar goes first: it costs €6,000, learners cannot tell how far along they are, and every other fix works better once they can.
order.why: The plan's rationale: transparency → motivation → usage. A different first priority defends if the reason names the group it reaches, the cost, or what the others depend on (for example M3, because most users are on a phone).
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Uses the chain transparency, motivation, usage.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know whether phone learners leave before or after they see their progress. I would split the analytics by device and watch five phone learners before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

brief2.heading: The situation: TrackLearn's Chief UX Systems Officer
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief UX Systems Officer of TrackLearn. The platform is growing, but user retention is declining. Most users are on a phone, and feedback systems are missing. Management wants a strategy for feedback and UX systems for the next 12 months and expects you to take responsibility for guiding the users.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €200,000 (Case assumption: the plan does not give one)
Data: you cannot yet measure retention by device.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: a platform that grows while retention declines, high mobile use, missing feedback systems. Everything else is made up: the €200,000, the feedback and tracking elements, the device cards, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the concept for feedback, the strategy for progress tracking, the responsive concept and the accessibility integration (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk analysis, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · Feedback, progress tracking, devices and accessibility
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the lists of feedback and tracking elements, the device grid, the accessibility list and the fields. Answer in the lists, the grid and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 4 · a concept for feedback systems, a strategy for progress tracking, a responsive design concept, accessibility integration.

fields.label: The concept for feedback: choose at least three elements
fields.help: Choose elements that together tell the learner that their work counted, why a result is what it is, and what to do next.
fields.missing: choose at least three elements for the feedback concept

options.label: An explained result after every task, with a next step
options.why: Direct feedback that explains and leads on.

options.label: A message and a tick when a task is saved or finished
options.why: Confirms that the work counted.

options.label: A short note at a milestone: half the course done
options.why: Indirect feedback: visible progress at the moments that matter.

options.label: An error hint that says what to change
options.why: Turns a mistake into a next step.

options.label: A pop-up after every single click
options.why: Rejected: feedback that overloads and interrupts.

options.label: A badge for every login
options.why: Rejected: rewards activity, not progress.

options.label: Feedback only at the end of the course
options.why: Rejected: too late to steer anything.

options.label: A red or green mark with no words
options.why: Rejected: a bare mark that explains nothing and fails for colour-blind learners.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The concept for feedback
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the four reference elements defend if together they say that the work counted, why, and what next. The rejected ones overload, reward activity or come too late. Plan: item 1, a concept for feedback systems.

fields.label: The strategy for progress tracking: choose at least three elements
fields.help: Choose elements that answer “how far along am I?” honestly, without misleading or overwhelming.
fields.missing: choose at least three elements for the progress tracking strategy

options.label: A progress bar for each course, based on lessons finished
options.why: Transparent and based on something real.

options.label: A status for every lesson: not started, in progress, done
options.why: Makes finished work visible.

options.label: A “Continue where you stopped” entry
options.why: Turns progress into the next step.

options.label: An estimate of the time left in the course
options.why: Helps a learner decide whether to start now.

options.label: One overall score that hides the details
options.why: Rejected: not transparent; the learner cannot tell what it means.

options.label: A level number that does not say what it measures
options.why: Rejected: a misleading display (the plan's risk).

options.label: A ranking against all other learners
options.why: Rejected: demotivates the many who are not at the top.

options.label: A bar that fills fast at the start and slowly at the end
options.why: Rejected: a misleading display that feels like a cheat later.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The strategy for progress tracking
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the four reference elements defend if the display is honest and based on something real. The rejected ones mislead (an unexplained level, a bar that cheats) or demotivate (a ranking). Plan: item 2, a strategy for progress tracking.

fields.label: Name one way the progress display could mislead or demotivate, and how you prevent it
fields.help: The plan names two risks: a misleading display and demotivation when overwhelmed. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one way the progress display could mislead or demotivate, and how you prevent it
fields.model: A bar based on clicks would show 90% after the first lesson and then crawl, so learners feel cheated. I base it on lessons finished out of lessons in the course, and label it “3 of 8”, so the number always means something.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, a long course shown as “2 of 40 lessons” could overwhelm a beginner. I show the first module as its own small goal, “2 of 5”, so the first steps feel reachable and the whole course stays visible.
guide.why: The plan's risks of progress tracking: a misleading display, and demotivation when the learner is overwhelmed (Materi A2).
lookFor: Names one risk (misleading or overwhelming).
Says how the design prevents it.

fields.label: The responsive concept: place eight pieces of content by device
fields.help: Decide for each piece whether it is the same on every device, comes first on a phone, only fits a larger screen, or is not shown on a phone because it distracts. Content is prioritised by device.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight pieces of content

items.label: “Continue where you stopped”
items.why: The most common phone use is a few minutes on the next lesson.

items.label: The progress bar and the lesson status
items.why: Transparency must not depend on the device.

items.label: The lesson text
items.why: The core content on every device, with a layout that fits.

items.label: A video with captions
items.why: Open item: on a phone it may come after the text; captions on every device.

items.label: A short quiz question after a section
items.why: Open item: same on every device also defends; short questions suit phones.

items.label: Notes next to the lesson, side by side
items.why: Needs width; on a phone notes open as a separate layer.

items.label: The full course catalogue with filters
items.why: Browsing many courses suits a larger screen; on a phone a shorter list with search.

items.label: A banner for current offers
items.why: On a small screen it pushes the lesson down and competes with the main action.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · Content by device
fields.teaching: There is no single right grid. Items 4 and 5 are the open ones; any placement with a reason from the learner's use defends. Each bin must be used at least once. Plan: item 3, a responsive design concept (content prioritised by device).

fields.label: The accessibility integration: choose at least three measures
fields.help: Choose measures that make the progress and feedback usable on every device and by more people (Day 7).
fields.missing: choose at least three accessibility measures

options.label: Touch targets of at least 44 px
options.why: Operable with a thumb or a tremor.

options.label: Contrast of at least 4.5 : 1 for text and the progress bar
options.why: Legible in sunlight and for low vision.

options.label: Text that reflows to the phone width without sideways scrolling
options.why: Works zoomed and on small screens.

options.label: Status and feedback in words and not by colour alone
options.why: Works for colour-blind learners and in a bright light.

options.label: A name and value for the progress bar for screen readers
options.why: Makes the progress readable for blind learners.

options.label: A separate accessible version of the site
options.why: Rejected: a second site that drifts; build it into the one site.

options.label: A fixed 11 px font so that more fits on a phone
options.why: Rejected: unreadable for many; fact 7 and the target of legibility.

options.label: Colour alone to show a lesson as done
options.why: Rejected: fails for colour-blind learners.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The accessibility integration
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference measures defend. The plan's coaching: accessibility is scalability and reach, and it belongs in the responsive concept, not in a separate version. Plan: item 4, accessibility integration.

fields.label: In two sentences: how do feedback, progress and a phone-first layout work together so that a learner always knows how they are doing?
fields.help: Use at least one element from each of the three parts. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say how feedback, progress and the phone-first layout work together
fields.model: Every task ends with an explained result and a tick, and the course page shows “3 of 8” with the status of each lesson, so the learner sees that their work counted and how far along they are. On a phone the same information comes first, in large, readable form, with “Continue where you stopped” as the first button.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, a tick and a short explanation after each answer say that the work counted, “2 of 5” on the module says how far along the learner is, and on a phone both sit at the top in large type.
guide.why: The three parts form one system: feedback says it counted, progress says how far, the layout makes both reachable on the device the learner uses (Materi B1).
lookFor: Uses an element of feedback, one of progress and one of the layout.
Says what the learner knows as a result.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, item 5 and the additional requirement · prioritised measures and a risk analysis, a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: the biggest risk of the plan
fields.help: Imagine the plan has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the plan fails

options.label: Too much feedback: learners felt interrupted and overloaded, and turned it off.
options.why: The feedback against overload pole. Action: cap the messages per lesson and test with learners; notice it in how often they dismiss or skip them.

options.label: The progress display misled learners, and they felt cheated when it slowed down.
options.why: Action: base it on lessons finished and label it; notice it in complaints and drop-out at the slow part.

options.label: The phone-first layout removed functions that desktop users needed.
options.why: Action: keep the full set on larger screens; check task success by device.

options.label: Accessibility was added late and broke the new components.
options.why: Action: build it into the components from the start and test every release.

options.label: We measured clicks, not retention, so we could not tell whether it worked.
options.why: Action: measure retention and completion by device.

fields.model: r1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk of the plan
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the learner would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007). The plan's conflict feedback against information overload is r1.

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I allow at most one message per task and keep the rest on a result page, and I watch how often learners dismiss feedback in the first month; if more than a third dismiss it, I cut the messages.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would show feedback only once per task and test it with six learners before release; if they say it interrupts, I move the detail to a “Why?” link.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without retention data by device)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to build the progress tracking and the direct feedback first (D2 and D1) and to make the course page phone-first as part of D3.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example how retention differs between phone and desktop. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know how much of the drop-out happens on phones and how much on desktops.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of month 4, the seven-day return rate of phone learners has not risen from 25% to 32%, and I put the money into a phone usability test first.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to add the progress display and one feedback message per task first. I do not know whether phone learners return more often because of it. I reverse if the seven-day return rate has not risen from 20% to 26% by the end of month 3.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I give up the levels and points (D6) and the separate mobile app (D7) this year. The product team will miss the app they have wanted, and the community team the badges.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I give up the native app this year and postpone the detailed analytics. The data team will miss the dashboard they planned.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.pickLabel: measures for your feedback and tracking system
decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say what it does for transparency and for motivation. At least 30 characters.

items.name: A feedback system
items.what: Explained results, milestone messages and error hints across all tasks.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: motivation, feedback that counts and explains.

items.name: A progress tracking system
items.what: A bar, a status per lesson, a resume entry and a time estimate on every course.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: transparency first, the cheapest answer to how far along am I.

items.name: A phone-first responsive redesign
items.what: Layouts for phone, tablet and desktop with content prioritised by device.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: usage; most users are on a phone, so it is a prerequisite.

items.name: Accessibility built into the components
items.what: Targets, contrast, reflow and screen reader names in every shared component.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D1: accessibility is scalability and reach; best built into D3.

items.name: Tests on real phones with learners
items.what: Usability tests of progress and feedback with learners on their own phones.
items.keyWhy: Defends: the decision is made without retention data by device; D5 is how it is checked.

items.name: Levels and points for every action
items.what: A level system and points for every click and lesson opened.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: a display that misleads and rewards activity, not progress.

items.name: A separate native mobile app
items.what: A second product for phones alongside the website.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: the most expensive and the longest, when the website itself can be made responsive.

model.orderWhy: D2 goes first: transparency leads to motivation, and motivation to use. Once learners can see how far along they are, the feedback of D1 gives them a reason to carry on, and the phone-first redesign of D3 makes both reachable on the device most of them use. The three cost €165,000 of the €200,000.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the progress display goes first: it is the cheapest way to answer how far along am I, and the feedback and the phone layout that follow only help once learners can see where they stand.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: transparency → motivation → usage. A different first measure defends if the reason names what it does for most users (for example D3, because most are on a phone) (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says what it does for transparency.
Says what it does for motivation.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D2, D1, D3 (€165,000 of €200,000, longest 20 weeks). D2 first because transparency leads to motivation and usage. D3 first also defends: most users are on a phone, so responsive design is a prerequisite. D2, D1, D5 also defends: tests early, since there is no retention data by device. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The feedback and UX systems strategy for the next twelve months

10.caseExport: TrackLearn is a learning platform whose users do not know how far along they are. Most use a phone, but the experience there is poor, there is no progress bar, nothing answers a finished task and motivation is low. The budget is €45,000.

memoSections.title: Accessibility integration and how the system works together
What I give up or postpone

10.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 progress indicator, M2 direct feedback, M3 mobile optimisation, M4 clear presentation) and cost €40,000 of the case's €45,000 (a Case assumption), longest 5 weeks of 10. The plan's rationale: transparency → motivation → usage.

11.heading: Day 11 · Gamification and motivation

intro.about: Today is about when game elements help people learn and when they only make them busy. You learn what points, badges, levels and leaderboards are, what intrinsic and extrinsic motivation mean, how Self-Determination Theory explains what people need to stay motivated, and why a reward can crowd out interest. You then weigh gamification measures on a platform where learners collect points and learn little.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is GameLearn, a platform with a lot of activity and little learning: learners collect points, and the reward has become more important than the content. The puzzle: with a limited budget, which mechanics do you keep, which do you drop, and how do you decide when competitors use gamification heavily and you have no proof yet that it works?

story.question: What does each of the eight elements of GameLearn do to a learner's motivation, which one would last longest, and which four of nine measures fit €45,000 and ten weeks?
As the Chief Engagement Officer, do you use gamification at all, which mechanics are meaningful and how do they serve learning goals, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Tell a reward from real progress
wiifm.payoff: A point for logging in and a bar that shows what you have mastered look alike and work very differently. The same test works for a loyalty scheme, a sales contest or a fitness app.

wiifm.skill: Use the three needs of Self-Determination Theory
wiifm.payoff: Autonomy, competence and relatedness give you a checklist for motivating a team, a class or a customer, far beyond games.

wiifm.skill: Weigh a gamification measure
wiifm.payoff: Motivation, effort and risk give you a fair comparison when a flashy idea competes with a plain one for the same budget.

wiifm.skill: Decide whether to gamify at all
wiifm.payoff: “Everybody does it” is not a reason. Asking what a mechanic changes in behaviour, and what learning it serves, protects a budget from fashion.

wiifm.skill: Link a mechanic to a learning objective
wiifm.payoff: Placing each element against an objective, and dropping what serves none, is a review you can run on any incentive scheme.

wiifm.skill: Name the perverse incentive before it happens
wiifm.payoff: Asking how people could game a reward is a habit worth having in any target, bonus or KPI design.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Assess the game elements, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight elements of GameLearn by what they do to motivation, say which would last longest and what you would change, then choose four of nine measures within €45,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 11 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application
