brief1.heading: The case: GameLearn, a platform with high activity and low learning
brief1.paragraph: GameLearn is a learning platform full of game elements. Users collect points, but they learn little, and the focus has shifted from the content to the reward. A first analysis points to a wrong gamification strategy, in which extrinsic motivation dominates. Users drop out early, the content is complex and the budget is limited. You are part of the UX team and asked to work out which elements help, which only reward activity, and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four GameLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €45,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 10 weeks (Case assumption: the plan gives none)
Users drop out early, and the content is complex.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: users collect points but learn little, the focus is on reward instead of content, a wrong gamification strategy, extrinsic motivation dominates, early drop-out, a limited budget and complex content. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €45,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight elements by what they do to motivation, say which one would last longest and what you would change (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

cats.label: Extrinsic: reward or pressure
cats.hint: Does it push the learner from outside, with a reward or a threat?
cats.test: Would the learner still do it if the reward or the threat were taken away? If they do it for the point, the prize, the rank or to avoid a loss, it is extrinsic.

cats.label: Competence: progress and feedback
cats.hint: Does it show the learner that they are getting better?
cats.test: Does it tell the learner how they are doing and how they are improving: a result, what to practise, a step that fits their level? If so, it supports the need to feel competent.

cats.label: Intrinsic: interest and choice
cats.hint: Does it make the content itself worth doing, or give the learner a say?
cats.test: Does it make the content itself interesting or meaningful, or let the learner choose? That feeds interest and autonomy, which keep a learner going without a reward.

facts.text: Every login gives 10 points, whether or not the learner opens a lesson.
facts.short: 10 points for every login
facts.clue: Would a learner log in if the points were taken away? What do the points reward?
facts.why: The points reward showing up, not learning: extrinsic reward.

facts.text: A leaderboard ranks all 5,000 learners by points, and the top three get a prize.
facts.short: A leaderboard of 5,000 with prizes for the top three
facts.key: the top three get a prize
facts.clue: A learner who is number 4,200 sees the list. What does it ask of them, and what for?
facts.why: Rank and prize push from outside, and most learners cannot win: extrinsic reward and pressure.

facts.text: A daily streak counter turns red and “breaks” when a day is missed.
facts.short: A streak counter that breaks
facts.clue: A learner is ill for a day. What does the screen say to them?
facts.why: The fear of losing the streak is pressure, not interest: extrinsic pressure.

facts.text: A bar shows the share of lessons finished in each unit.
facts.short: A bar of lessons finished per unit
facts.clue: Does it tell a learner how far they have come in what they are learning?
facts.why: It shows progress in the learning itself: competence.

facts.text: After each task, a result line says what was right and what to practise.
facts.short: A result line: what was right, what to practise
facts.key: what was right and what to practise
facts.clue: Does the learner know how they are doing and what to do next?
facts.why: It tells the learner how they are improving: competence.

facts.text: Tasks come in three steps of difficulty, and the learner moves up after two correct answers.
facts.short: Three difficulty steps, moving up after two correct answers
facts.key: moves up after two correct answers
facts.clue: Is the task matched to what the learner can do now?
facts.why: The challenge grows with the learner's ability: competence.

facts.text: A short story case runs through each unit, so tasks are about a situation the learner cares about.
facts.short: A story case through every unit
facts.key: a situation the learner cares about
facts.clue: Is the task worth doing for its own sake, with no reward?
facts.why: It makes the content itself meaningful: intrinsic interest.

facts.text: A learner may choose which of three topics to start with.
facts.short: A choice of three starting topics
facts.key: may choose which of three topics
facts.clue: Who decides what the learner does first?
facts.why: The learner has a say, which feeds autonomy: intrinsic motivation.

11.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto what it does to motivation, or select it and then a heading. Select a placed one to move it again. One heading per fact: Extrinsic, Competence or Intrinsic.
11.sortKeyTitle: Eight elements into Extrinsic, Competence, Intrinsic
11.sortTeaching: The sort is objective in its core: points for a login, a leaderboard with prizes and a breaking streak are extrinsic; a bar, a result line and stepped difficulty support competence; a story case and a choice feed intrinsic motivation. Fact 6 could also be argued as autonomy or flow; the test is whether it matches the challenge to the learner's ability. A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. Which element lasts longest, the improvements and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, which elements increase motivation, the differences between platforms.
11.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A1 and A2

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight elements: reward, competence or interest?
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight elements and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · which platform and which elements are more motivating and why, the differences, which elements increase motivation.

fields.label: Which element would keep a learner motivated for the longest time?
fields.help: Choose one. Any of the eight defends if the reason below says what it gives the learner that does not depend on a reward.
fields.missing: choose the element that would keep a learner motivated longest

options.label: 1 · 10 points for every login
options.why: Rejected: rewards showing up, and fades once the points stop mattering.

options.label: 2 · A leaderboard with prizes for the top three
options.why: Rejected: most learners cannot win, and it pushes from outside.

options.label: 3 · A streak counter that breaks
options.why: Rejected: pressure and fear of loss, not interest.

options.label: 4 · A bar of lessons finished per unit
options.why: Defends: visible progress in the learning itself.

options.label: 5 · A result line: what was right, what to practise
options.why: Reference choice: feedback that tells the learner how they are improving lasts because it serves the learning.

options.label: 6 · Three difficulty steps
options.why: Defends: keeps challenge and ability in balance.

options.label: 7 · A story case through every unit
options.why: Defends: the content itself is meaningful.

options.label: 8 · A choice of three starting topics
options.why: Defends: autonomy, though a small one.

fields.model: f5
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The element that lasts longest
fields.teaching: Elements 4 to 8 all defend; 1 to 3 do not, because their effect depends on the reward. Look at the reason: it should say what the element gives the learner that does not depend on a reward. The plan's goal is to understand the effect of gamification.

fields.label: Why would it last, and why not the others?
fields.help: Say what the element gives the learner that does not depend on a reward, and name one element that would fade, with the reason. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why that element would last and why a reward-based one would not
fields.model: Element 5, the result line, tells the learner what was right and what to practise, so it helps them improve, and that has value whether or not a point is given. Element 1, points for a login, would fade: it rewards showing up, and once the points stop mattering nothing else holds the learner.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would pick the choice of starting topic: it gives learners a say, which people value without a prize. A badge for every lesson opened would fade, because it rewards a click and says nothing about what was learned.
guide.why: Intrinsic and competence-supporting elements last because they serve the learning; extrinsic ones fade when the reward stops mattering (Materi A2).
lookFor: Names what the element gives that does not depend on a reward.
Names an element that would fade, with the reason.

clue.refValue: would they do it without the reward?
steps: Pick the element and ask: would the learner still do this if the reward were taken away?
Name one element that would stop working, and say why.

fields.label: Which elements increase motivation, and what would you change?
fields.help: Name the element (by number) that each change answers, and start each with a verb. At least 60 characters in all.
fields.missing: write which elements increase motivation and what you would change, naming the element each change answers
fields.model: Keep and build on elements 4, 5 and 6 (progress, a result line, stepped difficulty) and 7 and 8 (a story and a choice): they support competence and interest. 1. Replace the points for a login with points for a correct task (element 1). 2. Drop the prize for the top three and show learners their own progress instead (element 2). 3. Remove the streak penalty and let a missed day pause it (element 3).

guide.example: 1. Give the badge only when a task is applied at work (a badge for opening a page). 2. Show a learner their rank among their own group, not among thousands (a leaderboard of thousands). 3. Let a learner choose the order of topics (a fixed order).
guide.why: The plan asks which elements increase motivation. A good answer keeps what supports competence and interest, and changes what only rewards activity (Materi A1 to A3).
lookFor: Names which elements to keep.
Names the element each change answers.
Starts each change with a verb.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Deciding on a gamification strategy: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to improve a learning platform. Users drop out early, the content is complex and the budget is limited (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A adds a points and reward system, option B shows the learning progress, and option C makes the content more interesting without gamification.

criteria.label: Motivation
criteria.help: How much it keeps the learner going, and for how long.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example that learners chase the reward and learn little.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your decision: assess gamification critically
opts.whyHelp: Say what each option does to motivation in the short and the long term, and what risk it carries. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Introduce a points and reward system
options.keyWhy: A short-term lift with the highest risk: learners learn to chase the reward and the content becomes an afterthought.

options.name: Visualise the learning progress
options.keyWhy: Cheap, and it supports competence in the learning itself; the lowest risk.

options.name: Make the content more interesting, without gamification
options.keyWhy: It builds intrinsic interest, which lasts; it costs more and works more slowly.

model.why: I put B first: users drop out early and the content is complex, so showing learners how far they have come is cheap and supports competence in the learning itself. C comes second: interesting content builds interest that lasts, but it costs more and works slowly. A comes last: points lift activity for a while, but they invite learners to chase the reward and risk superficial motivation.

guide.example: For LearnLoop I would show progress first: it is cheap and it tells learners they are improving. Better content comes second. A point system comes last, because learners may chase the points and learn less.
guide.why: The plan's goal is to assess gamification critically. A first also defends if the reason says that points can lift early drop-out quickly and what it risks.
lookFor: Says what each option does short term and long term.
Names the risk of a reward system.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Three options for a gamification strategy
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €7,000 Low, €7,000 to €14,000 Mid, above €14,000 High), so the check can flag it; motivation and risk are judgements. The plan's goal is to assess gamification critically: learning > reward system. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: using gamification correctly
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: gamification only works in the right context; there is a difference between real motivation and a short-term reward; there is a danger of overstimulation; ask when gamification makes sense, and when it does not.

questions.q: Which mechanic really changes behaviour?
Where does only superficial motivation arise?
Which risks arise in the long term?

model.a: Feedback that says how the learner is improving, and a progress display that is based on what they mastered.
model.b: Where points are given for logging in or opening a page.
model.c: Learners chasing the reward, losing interest in the content, and feeling pressure from streaks and ranks.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: gamification only works in the right context; real motivation against a short-term reward; the danger of overstimulation; when it makes sense and when not. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four problems
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight elements of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A problem is something that makes learners collect points and learn little, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it explains why learners collect points and learn little, or is only a matter of how many badges there are, or of price.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at an element by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: Points reward activity, not learning: learners collect points without learning.
items.why: Element 1 and the case: users collect points but learn little.

items.text: Extrinsic motivation dominates: rewards, ranks and streaks push, and nothing makes the content itself worth doing.
items.why: Elements 1, 2 and 3 and the case: extrinsic motivation dominates.

items.text: The mechanics are not linked to learning objectives: nothing says what a point or a level means for what was learned.
items.why: Elements 1 and 2; the case: the focus is on reward instead of content.

items.text: Most learners cannot win and some feel pressure: the leaderboard and the streak create pressure, not interest.
items.why: Elements 2 and 3.

items.text: There are too few badges.
items.why: More badges would add more reward, which is the problem, not the remedy.

items.text: The subscription price is too high.
items.why: A business matter; nothing printed.

items.text: There are too few courses.
items.why: A content matter; the case is about incentives.

causes.whyModel: Element 1: every login gives 10 points whether or not the learner opens a lesson, so the points reward showing up and not learning.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “Rewards are not linked to learning” rests on one printed fact, that a badge is given for opening a page. It tells the learner nothing about what they learned.
guide.why: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the main problem as wrong incentives.
lookFor: Points at an element by number or quotes the case.
Says why it explains points without learning.

causes.teaching: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names a wrong gamification strategy with dominating extrinsic motivation; the Musterlösung names wrong incentives as the main problem. The rejected options include the tempting “too few badges”, which would add more of the problem; none of them explains why learners collect points and learn little.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four improvements, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which element it answers (by number), what the learner notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the plan's rationale, learning before the reward system: say how your first measure puts learning first. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example that learners chase the reward or feel pressure.

impact.label: Motivation
impact.help: How much it keeps the learner going, and whether that lasts.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: focus on learning progress instead of points, meaningful feedback systems, balance between motivation and content; rationale learning > reward system. The reference set costs €37,000 of €45,000 and takes at most 4 weeks of 10. M5 (a team goal without ranking) defends in place of M4 if the reason names relatedness. Reference order: M3, M1, M2, M4; M1 first also defends (progress by learning is the plan's first measure).

measures.name: Progress by learning, not by points
measures.what: Replace the point total with a bar of objectives mastered, based on correct answers to tasks.
measures.notice: The learner sees what they can now do.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers elements 1 and 4: progress that means learning.

measures.name: Meaningful feedback
measures.what: After every task a result line that says what was right, what to practise and what to do next.
measures.notice: Every task teaches something.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Extends element 5 to every task.

measures.name: Link every mechanic to a learning objective
measures.what: Remove points for logging in and badges for opening pages; give a reward only when an objective is shown to be reached.
measures.notice: Points mean something again.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers the plan's main problem, wrong incentives (elements 1 to 3).

measures.name: A say for the learner
measures.what: Let learners choose the order of topics and switch badges off.
measures.notice: The learner decides how to play.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Feeds autonomy (element 8) at the lowest cost.

measures.name: A group goal without ranking
measures.what: A study group works towards a shared goal; the board shows what the group finished, not who is first.
measures.notice: The learner belongs to a group.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: feeds relatedness without the pressure of a ranking. A learner who picks it instead of M4 should name relatedness.

measures.name: More badges and more levels
measures.what: Twenty new badges and ten more levels for every kind of activity.
measures.notice: More rewards appear.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: more of the problem; extrinsic reward with no link to learning; effort High.

measures.name: A daily streak with a penalty
measures.what: Points are lost when a day is missed.
measures.notice: A warning appears each evening.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: pressure and loss aversion; over-motivation and anxiety; cheap but harmful.

measures.name: Prizes for the top ten of the leaderboard
measures.what: A monthly prize pool for the ten learners with the most points.
measures.notice: A prize banner appears.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: a contest most learners cannot win; extrinsic; invites gaming the points; effort High.

measures.name: An AI that optimises rewards per learner
measures.what: An algorithm that adjusts points and prompts to keep each learner clicking.
measures.notice: Prompts arrive at odd times.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: optimises for clicks, not learning; a manipulation risk; effort High.

reasons.m1: It answers elements 1 and 4: a bar of objectives mastered instead of a point total. €9,000 lies between €7,000 and €14,000, so effort is Mid. Motivation High: the learner sees what they can now do, which lasts. Risk Low, it shows something real.
reasons.m2: It extends element 5 to every task: what was right, what to practise, what next. €10,000, so effort is Mid. Motivation High: every task teaches something. Risk Low, it adds answers and removes nothing.
reasons.m3: It answers the plan's main problem, wrong incentives (elements 1 to 3): no points for a login, a reward only when an objective is shown to be reached. €12,000, so effort is Mid. Motivation High: points mean something again. Risk Mid, because removing points that learners are used to may upset them at first.
reasons.m4: It feeds autonomy (element 8): learners choose the order of topics and can switch badges off. At €6,000 it is under €7,000, so effort is Low. Motivation Mid: a small but lasting gain. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M3 goes first: the main problem is wrong incentives, and as long as points are given for logging in, every other fix competes with the reward. Learning comes before the reward system: with the incentives right, the progress of M1 and the feedback of M2 show real learning, and M4 adds choice. The four measures cost €37,000 of €45,000, with the longest at four weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know whether the learners who collect the most points learn anything, because the platform does not link points to results. I would compare task results of the top and the average learners and ask ten learners what keeps them coming before I spend the last €8,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, rewarding only a task that is applied at work costs €11,000, so effort is Mid. It answers points that were given for clicks, so motivation is High and it lasts. Risk is Mid: learners used to easy points may complain.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). Motivation and risk are judgements: they must name the element the measure answers, what the learner notices, and what could go wrong, for example that learners chase the reward (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed element the measure answers.
Says what the learner notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop the link between rewards and learning goes first: while points are given for clicks, every other fix competes with the points. Learning comes before the reward system.
order.why: The plan's rationale: learning > reward system. A different first priority defends if the reason names what it does for learning and why it can wait or go first.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Puts learning before the reward.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know whether learners with the most points learn the most. I would compare their task results with the average learner's before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

brief2.heading: The situation: GameLearn's Chief Engagement Officer
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief Engagement Officer of GameLearn. User retention is low, competitors make heavy use of gamification, and the budget is limited. Management wants a gamification strategy for the next 12 months, and it expects you to decide whether to use gamification at all and to take responsibility for what it does to behaviour.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €150,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Data: you have no proof yet that any mechanic improves learning here.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: low user retention, competitors that make heavy use of gamification, a limited budget. Everything else is made up: the €150,000, the mechanic cards, the objective grid, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the decision on gamification, the meaningful mechanics, and the link to learning objectives (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk analysis (perverse incentives, over-motivation), one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · The decision, the mechanics and the link to learning objectives
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the decision below, the list of mechanics, the objective grid and the fields. Answer in the lists, the grid and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 3 · the decision whether to use gamification, a definition of meaningful mechanics, the link to learning objectives.

fields.label: The decision: use gamification or not?
fields.help: Choose the position you will take to management. A decision with a clear reason counts, whichever you choose.
fields.missing: choose whether to use gamification or not

options.label: Yes, selectively: only mechanics that serve a learning objective
options.why: Reference position: gamification as a strategic tool, tied to learning.

options.label: Yes, fully, as our competitors do
options.why: Weak: “everybody does it” is not a reason, and the case shows where it leads.

options.label: No gamification at all
options.why: Defends if the reason says that the learners' interest in the content is enough and that mechanics would add risk; it ignores what progress and feedback can do.

options.label: Not yet: test one mechanic against a control group first
options.why: Defends: a decision under uncertainty with an evidence step; slower, but cheap.

fields.model: g1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The decision on gamification
fields.teaching: The plan's question is whether to use gamification at all. Position 1 is the reference; position 4 also defends (test first); position 3 defends with a reason; position 2 is the weakest because its only reason is what competitors do. A decision with a clear reason exports whichever is chosen (CLAUDE.md #38). Plan: item 1, the decision.

fields.label: Why this position, and not the others?
fields.help: Give the reason in terms of what the mechanics change in behaviour and in learning, not in terms of what competitors do. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why you chose that position and not the others
fields.model: I use gamification selectively: retention is low and some mechanics (visible progress, explained feedback) do support competence, so dropping everything would waste them. But points and leaderboards would only invite learners to chase the reward, as GameLearn's own history shows, so I keep only mechanics that serve a learning objective, and I do not copy competitors for their own sake.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would gamify selectively: visible progress helps learners see they are improving, so I keep it. A competitor's leaderboard would reward the few at the top and discourage the rest, so I would not copy it just because others have it.
guide.why: The reason must rest on what a mechanic changes in behaviour and learning, not on what competitors do (Materi B1).
lookFor: Gives a reason about behaviour or learning.
Does not rest on what competitors do.
Names what is kept and what is not.

fields.label: Meaningful mechanics: choose at least three
fields.help: A mechanic is meaningful when it serves a learning objective, is transparent and fair, and keeps challenge and ability in balance.
fields.missing: choose at least three meaningful mechanics

options.label: Progress shown as objectives mastered
options.why: Competence: progress that means learning.

options.label: Explained feedback with a next step after each task
options.why: Competence: tells the learner how they improve.

options.label: The learner chooses the order of topics
options.why: Autonomy: a say in what to do.

options.label: A study-group goal with no ranking
options.why: Relatedness without the pressure of a rank.

options.label: A level of challenge that rises as the learner improves
options.why: Balance between challenge and ability.

options.label: A leaderboard of all learners with prizes
options.why: Rejected: most cannot win; extrinsic; invites gaming.

options.label: Points for logging in every day
options.why: Rejected: rewards activity, not learning.

options.label: A streak that breaks when a day is missed
options.why: Rejected: pressure and loss aversion.

options.label: Badges for opening pages
options.why: Rejected: rewards a click, says nothing about learning.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The meaningful mechanics
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference mechanics defend if each serves a learning objective and one of the three needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness). The rejected ones reward activity or create pressure. Plan: item 2, a definition of meaningful mechanics.

fields.label: The link to learning objectives: place eight mechanics
fields.help: Place each mechanic under the learning objective it serves, or under “linked to no objective” if it serves none. A mechanic that serves no objective is dropped.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight mechanics

items.label: A short check question after each section
items.why: Retrieval practice serves remembering and understanding.

items.label: A task: apply the idea to the learner's own work
items.why: Transfer to work.

items.label: A weekly goal that the learner sets, such as one unit
items.why: Keeps practice going; the learner owns the goal.

items.label: A progress bar of objectives mastered
items.why: Open item: understand also defends; it makes progress visible over weeks.

items.label: Points for logging in every day
items.why: Serves no objective: rewards showing up.

items.label: A badge when a task is applied at work and a colleague confirms it
items.why: Tied to a real result at work.

items.label: A leaderboard of total points
items.why: Serves no objective: ranks activity, not learning.

items.label: A hint that gives a clue before the answer
items.why: Supports understanding without giving the answer away.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · Mechanics and learning objectives
fields.teaching: There is no single right grid. Item 4 is the open one (continue or understand). Items 5 and 7 serve no objective and are dropped. Each bin must be used at least once. Plan: item 3, the link to learning objectives.

fields.label: Pick one mechanic: which objective does it serve, and how would you know it works?
fields.help: Name the mechanic, the objective and a result you could watch that is about learning, not about clicks. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: pick one mechanic and say which objective it serves and how you would know it works
fields.model: The check question after each section serves remembering and understanding. I would know it works if learners who answer it do better in the end-of-unit task than those who skip it, which is a result about learning, not about clicks.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a badge for applying a task at work serves applying the idea. I would know it works if more learners report using the idea in their job a month later, a result about learning, not clicks.
guide.why: A mechanic is linked to a learning objective and checked by a result about learning (Materi B1).
lookFor: Names the mechanic and the objective.
Names a result about learning, not clicks.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 4 and 5 and the additional requirement · a risk analysis (perverse incentives, over-motivation), prioritised measures, a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: perverse incentives and over-motivation
fields.help: Imagine the strategy has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the strategy fails

options.label: A perverse incentive: learners found a way to collect rewards without learning.
options.why: The perverse-incentive pole. Action: reward only results shown by a task or a check; notice it when points rise and results do not.

options.label: Over-motivation: pressure from streaks and ranks caused stress, and learners studied for the reward.
options.why: The over-motivation pole. Action: no penalties, no public ranking; notice it in complaints and in drop-out after a missed day.

options.label: The reward crowded out interest: learners lost interest in the content when the rewards stopped.
options.why: Action: keep rewards small and tied to progress; notice it in activity after a reward ends.

options.label: We copied competitors' mechanics with no link to our learning goals.
options.why: Action: every mechanic needs an objective before it is built.

options.label: We measured activity, not learning, so we could not tell whether it worked.
options.why: Action: measure task results and retention, not clicks.

fields.model: r1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: perverse incentives and over-motivation
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the learner would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007). The plan names perverse incentives and over-motivation.

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I give a reward only when a task or a check shows the objective was reached, and I compare points and task results every month; if points rise while results stay flat, I change the rule that was gamed.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would tie every badge to a checked result, and watch each month whether badges and test scores move together; if not, I change the badge rule.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without proof that a mechanic works here)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to replace the login points with learning-progress indicators and explained feedback first (D1 and D2) and to test a study-group goal before I build it.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example how learners react when points no longer reward a login. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know how many learners will stay when the login points disappear.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of month 3, the share of learners who finish a unit has fallen from 40% to below 35% without a gain in task results, and I restore the login points for one more month.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to stop the point for opening a page and show mastered objectives instead. I do not know how many learners will stay. I reverse if completion falls from 45% to below 40% by the end of month 3 with no gain in test scores.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I give up the public leaderboard with prizes (D6) and the streak with a penalty (D7) this year. The marketing team will miss the contest they planned to advertise, and some competitive learners will miss the ranking.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I give up the monthly prize contest this year and postpone the leaderboard. Marketing will miss the campaign they planned.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say what it does for real learning rather than for the reward. At least 30 characters.

items.name: Replace points with learning-progress indicators
items.what: Progress per objective, based on tasks answered correctly, instead of a point total.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: learning before reward; removes the wrong incentive.

items.name: An explained feedback system with next steps
items.what: A result line after every task: what was right, what to practise, what next.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: feedback that teaches sustains motivation.

items.name: Choice and challenge
items.what: The learner chooses the order of topics and the level of challenge, which rises with ability.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: autonomy and the balance of challenge and ability, at a modest cost.

items.name: A study-group goal board without ranking
items.what: A group works toward a shared goal; the board shows what the group finished.
items.keyWhy: Defends: feeds relatedness without a ranking; best after the first three.

items.name: Test one mechanic against a control group
items.what: Half of the learners get the new progress display, half do not, and task results are compared.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D3: the decision is made without proof, and D5 is how it is checked.

items.name: A public leaderboard with prizes
items.what: A ranking of all learners by points, with monthly prizes for the top ten.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: extrinsic; most learners cannot win; invites gaming (a perverse incentive).

items.name: A daily streak with penalties
items.what: Points are lost for a missed day.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: pressure and anxiety (over-motivation); cheap but harmful.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: learning before the reward system. As long as points are the measure, every other mechanic competes with them. With progress shown as objectives mastered, the feedback of D2 shows real learning, and the choice and challenge of D3 keep learners going without a prize. The three cost €100,000 of the €150,000.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the progress shown as objectives goes first: it replaces points as the thing learners aim at, and the feedback and the choice that follow only make sense once the aim is learning.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: learning > reward system. A different first measure defends if the reason names what it does for real learning (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says what it does for real learning.
Says why the reward system comes later or not at all.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D2, D3 (€100,000 of €150,000, longest 12 weeks). D1 first because learning comes before the reward system. D1, D2, D5 also defends: test one mechanic against a control group, since there is no proof yet that a mechanic works here. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The gamification strategy for the next twelve months

11.caseExport: GameLearn is a learning platform with a lot of activity and little learning: users collect points but learn little, the focus is on reward instead of content, and extrinsic motivation dominates. Users drop out early, the content is complex and the budget is €45,000.

memoSections.title: Risk analysis: perverse incentives and over-motivation
What I give up or postpone

11.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M3 link every mechanic to a learning objective, M1 progress by learning, M2 meaningful feedback, M4 a say for the learner) and cost €37,000 of the case's €45,000 (a Case assumption), longest 4 weeks of 10. The plan's rationale: learning > reward system.

12.heading: Day 12 · Adaptive learning and personalisation

intro.about: Today is about learning platforms that adapt to the learner, and about when that helps and when it only confuses. You learn how an adaptive system works (it collects data, analyses it and adapts), the difference between rules and machine learning, the UX patterns that make personalisation visible, and the risks of over-adaptation and a wrong data basis. You then weigh measures on a platform whose adaptations nobody understands.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is AdaptLearn, an ambitious but ineffective system: it adapts a lot, users do not understand what changes or why, and acceptance is low. The puzzle: with a small data basis and a limited budget, how much technology do you really need, and what must a learner be able to see and steer?

story.question: What do the eight elements of AdaptLearn do to a learner's understanding, which one would you keep, and which four of nine measures fit €60,000 and twelve weeks?

As the Chief Product & UX Officer, how do you build adaptive paths when users must understand them, which patterns and gamification elements join in, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Tell useful personalisation from technology for its own sake
wiifm.payoff: Asking what a learner can see, understand and steer works for any recommendation feature, in learning or in a shop or a news app.

wiifm.skill: Choose between rules and AI by the data you have
wiifm.payoff: A small data basis points to simple rules. The same test saves budget in any project that is tempted by a model.

wiifm.skill: Weigh a personalisation measure
wiifm.payoff: Benefit, effort and risk give you a fair comparison when a clever idea competes with a plain one for the same budget.

wiifm.skill: Design an adaptive path the learner can understand
wiifm.payoff: Showing why something changed, and letting people undo it, builds the trust any automated decision needs.

wiifm.skill: Combine personalisation with gamification
wiifm.payoff: Linking a mechanic to a personal goal, not to a point total, is a rule you can apply to any engagement feature.

wiifm.skill: Decide when the data basis is incomplete
wiifm.payoff: A reversible first step with a figure to watch is a habit worth having for any decision under uncertainty.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

brief1.heading: The case: AdaptLearn, an ambitious but ineffective system
brief1.paragraph: AdaptLearn is a learning platform with a complex adaptive system. It changes the path, the recommendations and the difficulty for every learner, but users do not understand the adaptations, and acceptance is low. A first analysis points to a lack of transparency and a wrong prioritisation of effort. The data basis is small, the users are very different, and the budget is limited. You are part of the UX team and asked to work out which adaptations help, which only confuse, and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four AdaptLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €60,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 12 weeks (Case assumption: the plan gives none)
Heterogeneous users and a small data basis.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: a complex adaptive system, users do not understand the adaptations, low acceptance, a lack of transparency and a wrong prioritisation, heterogeneous users, a small data basis and a limited budget. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €60,000, the 12 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight elements by what they do to the learner's understanding, say which one you would keep and what you would change (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

cats.label: Opaque: the learner cannot see why
cats.hint: Does something change without telling the learner what or why?
cats.test: Could the learner say what changed and why? If something changes with no notice, no reason or no way to see it, the adaptation is opaque.

cats.label: Wrong basis: too little data or too strong a reaction
cats.hint: Does the system decide on thin evidence, or react too strongly?
cats.test: Does the system draw a big conclusion from little data (a few clicks, one wrong answer), or lock the learner into it? Then the data basis is wrong or the adaptation is too strong.

cats.label: Helps: clear and in the learner's hands
cats.hint: Does it adapt in a way the learner can see, understand and steer?
cats.test: Does the learner see what changed, the reason, and a way to change it back or choose? Then the adaptation helps rather than confuses.

facts.text: The path changed overnight, and a notice says only “Your path was updated”.
facts.short: A path that changes with the notice “updated”
facts.clue: Could the learner say what changed, and why?
facts.why: The change is announced but not explained: opaque.

facts.text: Lesson 4 has vanished from the list, and nothing shows which lessons were skipped.
facts.short: A lesson vanishes with no sign of what was skipped
facts.key: nothing shows which lessons were skipped
facts.clue: Can the learner tell what the system left out?
facts.why: Content disappears without a trace: opaque.

facts.text: A card says “Recommended for you” and gives no reason.
facts.short: A recommendation with no reason
facts.clue: Why this lesson, and why now?
facts.why: The learner has to trust the system without a reason: opaque.

facts.text: A learner who passed the advanced test is offered a beginner course, because the system looked only at the last three clicks.
facts.short: A beginner course for an advanced learner, from three clicks
facts.key: only at the last three clicks
facts.clue: How much evidence does the system use for such a big decision?
facts.why: A big conclusion from very little data: wrong basis.

facts.text: After one wrong answer the difficulty drops two levels, and there is no way to go back.
facts.short: Difficulty drops two levels after one mistake, with no way back
facts.clue: Is one mistake enough to judge a learner, and can they undo it?
facts.why: Over-adaptation to one data point, with no escape: wrong basis.

facts.text: A note says “Difficulty lowered: you missed 3 of 4 questions on pricing”, with a button to change it back.
facts.short: A note with the reason and a button to change it back
facts.key: with a button to change it back
facts.clue: Does the learner see the reason and have a say?
facts.why: The reason is shown and the learner can undo it: it helps.

facts.text: A switch lets the learner choose between “Let AdaptLearn decide” and “I choose my path”.
facts.short: A switch: the system decides, or I choose
facts.clue: Who is in control of the path?
facts.why: The learner stays in control: it helps.

facts.text: A new learner is asked three short questions about their goal and prior knowledge before the first lesson, and can change the answers later.
facts.short: Three start questions, which can be changed later
facts.clue: Where does the first adaptation come from, and can it be corrected?
facts.why: It starts from what the learner says and can be corrected: it helps.

12.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto what it does to the learner's understanding, or select it and then a heading. Select a placed one to move it again. One heading per fact: Opaque, Wrong basis or Helps.
12.sortKeyTitle: Eight elements into Opaque, Wrong basis, Helps
12.sortTeaching: The sort is objective in its core: a change with no explanation, a vanished lesson and a recommendation without a reason are opaque; a big conclusion from three clicks or one mistake is a wrong basis or over-adaptation; a reason with an undo button, a switch for control and start questions that can be corrected help. Fact 8 could be argued as wrong basis if the answers were never checked; the test is whether the learner can correct them. A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. Which element to keep, the changes and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, recognising personalisation, advantages and risks.
12.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A1 and A2

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight elements: opaque, wrong basis or helpful?
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight elements and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · which platform is more effective and why, the advantages of personalisation, the risks.

fields.label: Which element is the best example of useful personalisation, the one you would keep unchanged?
fields.help: Choose one. Any of the three helpful ones defends if the reason below says what the learner can see and do.
fields.missing: choose the element you would keep

options.label: 1 · A path that changes with the notice “updated”
options.why: Rejected: the change is not explained.

options.label: 2 · A lesson that vanishes with no sign
options.why: Rejected: content disappears without a trace.

options.label: 3 · A recommendation with no reason
options.why: Rejected: the learner has to trust blindly.

options.label: 4 · A beginner course for an advanced learner
options.why: Rejected: a big conclusion from three clicks.

options.label: 5 · Difficulty drops two levels after one mistake
options.why: Rejected: over-adaptation with no way back.

options.label: 6 · A note with the reason and a button to change it back
options.why: Reference choice: the adaptation is explained and reversible, so the learner stays in control.

options.label: 7 · A switch: the system decides, or I choose
options.why: Defends: control stays with the learner.

options.label: 8 · Three start questions, which can be changed later
options.why: Defends: starts from what the learner says, and can be corrected.

fields.model: f6
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The element to keep
fields.teaching: Elements 6, 7 and 8 all defend; 1 to 5 do not, because the learner cannot see why or cannot undo it. Look at the reason: it should say what the learner can see and do. The plan's goal is to understand personalisation and its risks.

fields.label: Why keep it, and why not one of the others?
fields.help: Say what the learner can see and do with the element you keep, and name one element you would not keep, with the reason. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why you keep that element and why not another
fields.model: Element 6 shows the learner what changed (the difficulty), why (3 of 4 questions missed) and gives a button to change it back, so the adaptation helps and the learner stays in control. Element 5 I would not keep: it drops two levels after one mistake and offers no way back, so one slip decides for the learner.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would keep the switch between “the platform decides” and “I choose”: the learner can use the adaptation or ignore it. A recommendation with no reason I would not keep, because the learner has to trust it blindly.
guide.why: A helpful adaptation is seen, understood and steerable by the learner; an unhelpful one is hidden or irreversible (Materi A1, A2).
lookFor: Says what the learner can see and do.
Names an element that would not be kept, with the reason.

clue.refLabel: How an adaptive system works (Materi A1)
steps: Pick the element and ask: can the learner see what changed, why, and change it back?
Name one element where the answer is no, and say what the learner would feel.

fields.label: What are the advantages and the risks of personalisation here, and what would you change?
fields.help: Compare a platform that gives everyone the same content with one that adapts. Name the element (by number) that each change answers, and start each change with a verb. At least 60 characters in all.
fields.missing: write the advantages and risks of personalisation and what you would change, naming the element each change answers
fields.model: Advantage: a platform that adapts spares an advanced learner the basics and gives a struggling one practice, where identical content bores one and loses the other. Risk: the adaptation can be opaque or based on too little data. 1. Add a reason to every path change (element 1). 2. Show the skipped lessons (element 2). 3. Add a reason to every recommendation (element 3). 4. Let a learner undo a difficulty change and use more than one mistake (element 5).

guide.example: Advantage: learners get what fits their level. Risk: they may not understand why things change. 1. Show a reason for each change (a path that just says “updated”). 2. Offer an “undo” (a change with no way back).
guide.why: The plan asks for the advantages and risks of personalisation. A good answer names both and ties each change to an element (Materi A1 to A3).
lookFor: Names an advantage and a risk.
Names the element each change answers.
Starts each change with a verb.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Strategic decision on adaptive learning: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are planning a new learning platform. The budget is limited, the users are very different and the data basis is small (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A uses standardised learning paths, option B uses simple rule-based personalisation, and option C builds a complex AI-based system.

criteria.label: Benefit
criteria.help: How much it helps learners reach their goal, for many different users.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example a small data basis or a system nobody understands.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your decision: weigh technology against benefit
opts.whyHelp: Say what each option gives and risks, given the small data basis and the different users. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Standardised learning paths
options.keyWhy: Cheap and clear, but the same for everyone: it does not serve very different users.

options.name: Simple personalisation with rules
options.keyWhy: Rules need little data, are easy to explain and fit different users; mid effort, low to mid risk.

options.name: A complex AI-based system
options.keyWhy: A small data basis cannot support it; high effort and risk, and hard to explain.

model.why: I put B first: the users are very different, so identical paths waste their time, and rules need little data and can be explained. A comes second: cheap and clear, but it does not adapt. C comes last: with a small data basis the AI has too little to learn from, it costs the most, and nobody could explain what it does.

guide.example: For LearnLoop with little data I would start with simple rules: they need few examples and I can say what they do. A learning model comes last, because it would have too little data and nobody could explain it.
guide.why: The plan's goal is to weigh technology against benefit. A different first choice defends if the reason names the data basis and the users.
lookFor: Says what each option gives and risks.
Names the small data basis.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Three options for adaptive learning
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €10,000 Low, €10,000 to €25,000 Mid, above €25,000 High), so the check can flag it; benefit and risk are judgements. Weigh technology against benefit: with a small data basis, rules beat AI. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: using personalisation sensibly
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: more technology is not better UX; ask when adaptive UX really pays off; mind the risk of over-engineering and the importance of data quality.

questions.q: Which personalisation brings real added value?
When does standardisation make more sense?
Which decision is sustainable in the long term?

model.a: Starting at the right level and explaining each change, because it saves the learner time and they understand it.
model.b: When the data basis is small or the content is short and the same for everyone, where adaptation adds cost and confusion.
model.c: Simple rules that the team can explain and maintain, with the option to add a model once there is enough good data.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: more technology is not better UX; when adaptive UX pays off; the risk of over-engineering; the importance of data quality. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four problems
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight elements of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A problem is something that makes users not understand the adaptations, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it explains why users do not understand the adaptations, or is only a matter of the courses, the look or a better model.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at an element by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: Lack of transparency: changes are not explained, so users do not know what changed or why.
items.why: Elements 1 to 3 and the case: users do not understand the adaptations.

items.text: Wrong prioritisation: the effort went into a complex system instead of into being understandable.
items.why: The case: a complex system, low acceptance; the plan names a wrong prioritisation.

items.text: A wrong data basis: the system reacts strongly to very little data.
items.why: Elements 4 and 5, and the small data basis of the brief.

items.text: The learner has no control: adaptations cannot be undone or switched off.
items.why: Element 5, against elements 6 and 7.

items.text: There are too few courses.
items.why: A content matter; the case is about understanding the adaptations.

items.text: The screens look out of date.
items.why: A visual matter; nothing printed about the look.

items.text: The system needs a more powerful AI model.
items.why: More technology would add to the complexity that is the problem, and the data basis is small.

causes.whyModel: Element 1: the path changed overnight and the notice says only “Your path was updated”, so the learner cannot say what changed or why.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “Lack of transparency” rests on one printed fact, that a recommendation card gives no reason. The learner cannot tell why the lesson was chosen.
guide.why: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names lack of user comprehensibility as the main problem.
lookFor: Points at an element by number or quotes the case.
Says why it explains the lack of understanding.

causes.teaching: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names a lack of transparency and a wrong prioritisation; the Musterlösung names lack of user comprehensibility as the main problem. The rejected options include the tempting “a more powerful AI model”, which would add to the complexity; none of them explains why users do not understand the adaptations.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four improvements, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which element it answers (by number), what the learner notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the plan's rationale, comprehensibility before complexity: say how your first measure makes the system understandable. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example that the explanation confuses or the rules are too crude.

impact.label: Benefit
impact.help: How much it helps the learner understand and use the adaptation.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: transparent adaptation, simple personalisation, clear structure, targeted feedback; rationale comprehensibility > complexity. The reference set costs €47,000 of €60,000 and takes at most 6 weeks of 12. M5 (learner control) defends in place of M3 if the reason names control. Reference order: M1, M2, M3, M4; M1 first because lack of comprehensibility is the main problem.

measures.name: Transparent adaptation
measures.what: Every change says what changed and why, with a button to change it back.
measures.notice: The learner sees the reason.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers elements 1 to 3: the main problem, lack of comprehensibility.

measures.name: Simple personalisation with three rules
measures.what: A start level from three questions, skip what was passed, repeat what was missed.
measures.notice: The path fits the learner, and the rules can be stated.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Replaces the complex logic with rules that need little data (elements 4, 5, 8).

measures.name: A clear structure
measures.what: One path page in the same order for everyone, with the adapted parts marked.
measures.notice: The learner sees what is adapted.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers element 2: nothing disappears, adapted parts are marked.

measures.name: Targeted feedback
measures.what: After each unit a short note on what changed in the path and what to do next.
measures.notice: Every unit ends with a clear next step.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Closes the loop between the learner's action and the adaptation (element 6).

measures.name: Learner control
measures.what: A switch to turn the adaptation off and to choose the path alone.
measures.notice: The learner decides.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: gives control (element 7) at the lowest cost. A learner who picks it instead of M3 should name control.

measures.name: A full deep-learning recommender
measures.what: A model that predicts the best next lesson for each learner.
measures.notice: Lessons arrive that nobody can explain.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: small data basis; adds complexity and opacity; effort High.

measures.name: Five variants of every lesson
measures.what: Every lesson is rewritten five ways to fit different learners.
measures.notice: Lessons differ from learner to learner.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: multiplies the content with no evidence it helps; effort High; consistency lost.

measures.name: A dashboard of twenty learner metrics
measures.what: Learners see twenty figures about how the system rates them.
measures.notice: A wall of figures appears.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: more information, not more understanding; density against clarity.

measures.name: Badges for following the recommended path
measures.what: A badge for every lesson taken in the order the system suggests.
measures.notice: Badges appear.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: rewards obeying the system, and does not explain it.

reasons.m1: It answers elements 1 to 3: every change says what and why, with a button to change it back. €14,000 lies between €10,000 and €25,000, so effort is Mid. Benefit High: the learner understands the main thing the system does. Risk Low, it adds explanation and removes nothing.
reasons.m2: It replaces the complex logic with three rules that need little data: start level, skip what was passed, repeat what was missed. €16,000, so effort is Mid. Benefit High: the path fits and the rules can be stated. Risk Mid: three rules are crude for some learners.
reasons.m3: It answers element 2: one path page in the same order, with the adapted parts marked, so nothing disappears. At €9,000 it is under €10,000, so effort is Low. Benefit Mid: it gives orientation. Risk Low.
reasons.m4: It closes the loop after each unit: what changed in the path and what to do next. At €8,000 effort is Low. Benefit Mid: the learner always knows the next step. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: the main problem is that users cannot understand the adaptations, and no other fix works while they do not. Comprehensibility comes before complexity: with the reasons shown, the simple rules of M2 can be trusted, M3 gives structure to the path, and M4 closes the loop after each unit. The four measures cost €47,000 of €60,000, with the longest at five weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know how many learners would have been better served by the old fixed path, because the platform has never compared the two. I would compare completion of learners who switch adaptation off with those who keep it, before I spend the last €13,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, a reason on every recommendation costs €7,000, so effort is Low. It answers cards with no reason, so benefit is High. Risk is Low: it only adds words.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). Benefit and risk are judgements: they must name the element the measure answers, what the learner notices, and what could go wrong (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed element the measure answers.
Says what the learner notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop the reason on every recommendation goes first: without it no other change can be trusted. Comprehensibility comes before complexity.
order.why: The plan's rationale: comprehensibility > complexity. A different first priority defends if the reason names what it does for understanding and why it can wait or go first.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Puts comprehensibility before complexity.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know whether learners who switch adaptation off finish more. I would compare their completion with the others' before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

brief2.heading: The situation: AdaptLearn's Chief Product & UX Officer
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief Product & UX Officer of AdaptLearn, which is to build a new learning platform. The users are very different, competitors use adaptive systems, and the data basis is not complete. Management wants a concept for the next 12 months, and expects you to decide how far to personalise, how gamification joins in, and to take responsibility for the system design.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €200,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Data: it is incomplete, and you do not know how your learners will react.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: heterogeneous users, competitors that use adaptive systems, an incomplete data basis, a limited budget. Everything else is made up: the €200,000, the pattern cards, the sketch elements, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the approach to adaptive paths, the UX patterns, the concept sketch and how gamification joins in (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk analysis, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · The approach, the patterns, the concept sketch and gamification
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the approach below, the list of patterns, the sketch board and the fields. Answer in the lists, the board and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 4 · a concept for adaptive learning paths, the integration of gamification, UX design patterns, a low-fidelity concept sketch.

fields.label: The approach to adaptive learning paths
fields.help: Choose the approach you will take to management. A decision with a clear reason counts, whichever you choose.
fields.missing: choose an approach to adaptive learning paths

options.label: Rules first, model later: simple, explained rules now, a data-driven model once there is enough data
options.why: Reference approach: fits the small data basis, is understandable, and keeps the option open.

options.label: A full AI system from the start, as competitors do
options.why: Weak: “competitors do it” is not a reason, and the data basis cannot support it.

options.label: No personalisation: standard paths for all
options.why: Defends if the reason says that the data is too thin and the content short; it gives up the benefit for different users.

options.label: Not yet: test a prototype with real learners first
options.why: Defends: a decision under uncertainty with an evidence step; slower, but cheap.

fields.model: g1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The approach to adaptive paths
fields.teaching: The plan asks for a concept for adaptive learning paths under an incomplete data basis. Approach 1 is the reference; approach 4 also defends (test first); approach 3 defends with a reason; approach 2 is the weakest because its only reason is what competitors do. A decision with a clear reason exports whichever is chosen (CLAUDE.md #38). Plan: item 1.

fields.label: Why this approach, and not the others?
fields.help: Give the reason in terms of the data you have and what the learner can understand, not in terms of what competitors do. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why you chose that approach and not the others
fields.model: I start with explained rules: the data basis is incomplete, so a model would have too little to learn from, and rules can be stated to the learner, which AdaptLearn's own history shows is the missing piece. I keep the option of a data-driven model once enough good data exists, and I do not copy competitors for their own sake.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would use simple rules first: with little data a model would guess, and a learner can understand a rule. I would add a model later, once the data is there.
guide.why: The reason must rest on the data basis and what the learner can understand, not on what competitors do (Materi B1).
lookFor: Gives a reason about data or understanding.
Does not rest on what competitors do.
Says what is kept for later.

fields.label: UX design patterns for personalised paths: choose at least three
fields.help: A pattern is good when the learner can see it, understand it and steer it.
fields.missing: choose at least three UX design patterns

options.label: A recommendation with a reason (“because you missed …”)
options.why: Individual recommendation, explained.

options.label: Adaptive difficulty with a notice and an undo
options.why: Adaptive difficulty the learner can see and reverse.

options.label: A dynamic path shown as a map, with adapted parts marked
options.why: Dynamic path, visible.

options.label: Feedback based on behaviour after each unit
options.why: Behaviour-based feedback.

options.label: A start questionnaire the learner can edit later
options.why: Starts from what the learner says; handles the cold start.

options.label: Silent re-routing with no message
options.why: Rejected: opaque.

options.label: A recommendation with no reason
options.why: Rejected: blind trust.

options.label: A hidden score that ranks learners
options.why: Rejected: opaque, and a ranking that nobody can check.

options.label: Difficulty that drops after one mistake, with no way back
options.why: Rejected: over-adaptation to one data point.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The UX design patterns
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference patterns defend if each is visible, understandable and steerable. The rejected ones are opaque or over-adapt. Plan: item 3, UX design patterns.

fields.label: The low-fidelity concept sketch: place eight elements on the screens
fields.help: Place each element on the screen of the first prototype where it belongs, or under “not in the first prototype” if it can wait or should be dropped.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight elements

items.label: Three questions about goal and prior knowledge
items.why: The first adaptation starts from what the learner says.

items.label: A path map with the adapted parts marked
items.why: Makes the adaptation visible.

items.label: A “Why this lesson?” link
items.why: Open item: the lesson screen also defends; the reason belongs where the choice is shown.

items.label: A difficulty notice with an undo button
items.why: Shown where the change happens.

items.label: A goal bar: lessons toward the learner's own goal
items.why: Gamification tied to a personal goal.

items.label: A “next step” card after each unit
items.why: Behaviour-based feedback at the end of the unit.

items.label: A hidden AI score for each learner
items.why: Opaque; can wait or be dropped.

items.label: A dashboard of twenty learner metrics
items.why: Density against clarity; not needed for a first prototype.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The concept sketch
fields.teaching: There is no single right sketch. Item 3 is the open one (path or lesson). Items 7 and 8 do not belong in a first prototype. Each bin must be used at least once. A low-fidelity sketch keeps only what must be tested first. Plan: item 4, low-fidelity prototype (concept sketch).

fields.label: How does gamification join the personalisation?
fields.help: Name one gamification element, the personal goal it serves, and one risk to watch (Day 11). At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one gamification element, the personal goal it serves and one risk
fields.model: A goal bar that counts lessons toward the learner's own goal, chosen at the start, instead of a point total. It serves the learner's goal, so the personalisation and the motivation point the same way. The risk I watch is that learners aim at the bar and skip understanding, so I count only lessons whose check was passed.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a goal bar toward “apply negotiation at work” serves the learner's own goal. I would watch that learners do not rush through the lessons just to fill the bar.
guide.why: Gamification joins personalisation when it is tied to a personal goal and checked by a result about learning (Day 11, Materi B1).
lookFor: Names one element and the personal goal.
Names one risk.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, item 5 and the additional requirement · prioritised features and a risk analysis, a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: opacity, over-adaptation and a wrong data basis
fields.help: Imagine the platform has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the platform fails

options.label: Opacity: learners did not understand why things changed, and stopped trusting the system.
options.why: The opacity pole. Action: a reason and an undo on every adaptation; notice it in complaints and in learners who switch adaptation off.

options.label: Over-adaptation: the system boxed learners in after a few clicks, and they never saw other content.
options.why: Action: adapt slowly, on more than one data point, and keep the full path visible; notice it in the share of learners who never leave their first path.

options.label: A wrong data basis: the data was too thin or biased, so the adaptations were wrong for many users.
options.why: Action: start with rules that need little data, and check them against a control group; notice it in learners who override the system.

options.label: We built what competitors have, with no link to our learners' needs.
options.why: Action: every feature needs a learner need before it is built.

options.label: Gamification rewarded activity, and learners followed the bar and did not learn.
