options.why: Action: count only checked results; notice it when the bar rises and test results do not.

fields.model: r1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: opacity, over-adaptation and a wrong data basis
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the learner would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007). The plan names risks from wrong personalisation.

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I show a reason and an undo button on every adaptation, and I watch each month the share of learners who switch adaptation off; if it passes one in five, I rewrite the explanations.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would add a reason to every recommendation, and watch each month how many learners ignore the recommendations; if it is most of them, I change the wording.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without a complete data basis)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to build explained rule-based paths first (D1 and D2) and to test the three rules in a prototype with eight learners before I build them.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example whether learners accept being adapted at all. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know whether learners will follow an adapted path or switch it off.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of month 3, more than 30% of learners have switched the adaptation off, and I return to the standard path for them while I rewrite the explanations.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to add reasons to every recommendation first. I do not know whether learners read them. I reverse if fewer than one in four open a reason by the end of month 3.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I give up the full AI recommender (D5) this year. The data science team will miss the project they wanted, and sales will have no “AI-powered” line to match competitors.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I postpone the learning model for a year. The data team will miss it, and marketing cannot say “AI”.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say what it does for the learner's understanding rather than for the technology. At least 30 characters.

items.name: Transparent adaptive paths
items.what: Every adaptation says what and why, shows the adapted parts on a path map, and can be undone.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: comprehensibility before complexity.

items.name: Rule-based personalisation for start level and difficulty
items.what: A start questionnaire, skipping what was passed, repeating what was missed, with the rules stated.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: needs little data and can be explained.

items.name: Gamification tied to the learner's own goal
items.what: A goal bar chosen at the start and filled by checked lessons, with no ranking.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: joins motivation to personalisation (Day 11), at a modest cost.

items.name: A low-fidelity prototype tested with eight learners
items.what: The concept sketch is tested on paper or clickable screens before anything is built.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D3: the decision is made without a full data basis, and D4 is how it is checked.

items.name: A full AI recommender
items.what: A model that chooses the next lesson for each learner from behaviour data.
items.keyWhy: Rejected for now: the data basis is too small, it is hard to explain, and the cost is highest.

items.name: A personalised leaderboard with prizes
items.what: Learners are ranked against others like them, with prizes for the top.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: extrinsic; most cannot win; invites gaming (Day 11).

items.name: Automatic adaptation with no learner control
items.what: The system adapts silently and the learner cannot see or change it.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: opaque; the problem the case started with.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: comprehensibility before complexity. If learners cannot see why the path changes, nothing else is trusted. With the adaptations explained, the simple rules of D2 can be tested honestly, and the goal bar of D3 joins motivation to the personal goal. The three cost €145,000 of the €200,000.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the explained paths go first: they make every other adaptation understandable, and the rules and the goal bar only make sense once learners can see what the system does.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: comprehensibility > complexity. A different first measure defends if the reason names what it does for understanding (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says what it does for understanding.
Says why the technology comes later or not at all.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D2, D3 (€145,000 of €200,000, longest 16 weeks). D1 first because comprehensibility comes before complexity. D1, D2, D4 also defends: test the concept in a prototype first, since the data basis is incomplete. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The personalisation strategy for the next twelve months

12.caseExport: AdaptLearn is an ambitious but ineffective adaptive learning system: it adapts a lot, users do not understand what changes or why, and acceptance is low. The data basis is small, the users are very different and the budget is €60,000.

memoSections.title: What I give up or postpone

12.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 transparent adaptation, M2 simple personalisation, M3 clear structure, M4 targeted feedback) and cost €47,000 of the case's €60,000 (a Case assumption), longest 5 weeks of 12. The plan's rationale: comprehensibility > complexity.

13.heading: Day 13 · Inclusive UX/UI and WCAG

intro.about: Today is about learning platforms that everyone can use, whether they see poorly, cannot use a mouse, or find complex pages hard to follow. You learn what inclusive design is and how it differs from classic usability, the four principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust), the key requirements of the WCAG standard, and how to build accessibility into the design process. You then weigh measures on a platform full of barriers.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is AccessLearn, a platform with barriers: users with impairments cannot use it, complaints are increasing, and legal risks are growing. The puzzle: with a limited budget, time pressure and a lot of existing content, which barriers do you remove first, and how do you stop new ones from appearing?

story.question: Which of the eight facts about AccessLearn are barriers, for whom, which one stops a learner completely, and which four of nine measures fit €50,000 and ten weeks?
As the Chief Accessibility Officer, how do you implement WCAG step by step, how do you build it into the UX process, how do you measure it, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Spot a barrier and say who it stops
wiifm.payoff: Asking who cannot use a page, and why, is the first step in checking any website, document or app you are responsible for.

wiifm.skill: Use the four principles of accessibility
wiifm.payoff: Perceivable, operable, understandable and robust give you a checklist that works for any digital product, far beyond learning.

wiifm.skill: Prioritise accessibility measures
wiifm.payoff: Impact, effort and risk give you a fair comparison when many fixes compete for a small budget.

wiifm.skill: Plan a step-by-step WCAG implementation
wiifm.payoff: Starting where most users meet the barrier is a way to plan any large compliance programme.

wiifm.skill: Build accessibility into a process
wiifm.payoff: A check at design review stops barriers cheaply, which is the idea behind any quality gate.

wiifm.skill: Make accessibility measurable
wiifm.payoff: Choosing indicators that management can read is how a goal becomes something a team can be held to.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Find the barriers, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight facts about AccessLearn by the user group they affect, say which one stops a learner completely and what you would change, then choose four of nine measures within €50,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 13 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application
route1.h1: Accessibility: find the barriers, then choose the measures
route1.order: Materi A (all five cards, four are core) → the UX Analysis task, one case in two parts (find the barriers, choose measures), with two core blocks. Every section stays open, so you can start anywhere.
route1.taskSub: UX Analysis File: find the barriers, choose the measures

route2.title: Decide the accessibility strategy
route2.blurb: Level 3 in the Chief Accessibility Officer's chair: a strategy to implement WCAG, how accessibility joins the UX process, how to measure it, three prioritised measures, a risk analysis of costs against benefits, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up.
route2.h1: An accessible UX strategy according to WCAG: the strategy, the process, the measures, the evaluation, the risks, and what you give up
route2.order: Materi B (three cards) → the UX Strategy task, one frame with two core blocks and a memo that builds below. Route 1 is a good start but not needed; every section stays open.
route2.materiSub: Level 3 · accessibility as a strategic quality
route2.taskSub: UX Strategy Memo: decide as Chief Accessibility Officer

brief1.heading: The case: AccessLearn, a platform with barriers
brief1.paragraph: AccessLearn is a learning platform that people with impairments cannot use properly. Complaints are increasing and legal risks are growing. A first analysis points to a missing implementation of WCAG and to no inclusive UX in the design. There is a lot of existing content, time is short and the budget is limited. You are part of the UX team and asked to work out which barriers exist, whom they stop, and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four AccessLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €50,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 10 weeks (Case assumption: the plan only says “time pressure”)
Many existing content items.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: users with impairments cannot use the platform, complaints are increasing, legal risks, a missing WCAG implementation, no inclusive UX, a limited budget, time pressure and many existing content items. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €50,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight facts by the user group they affect, say which one stops a learner completely and what you would change (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

cats.label: Visual: seeing the page
cats.hint: Does it make the page hard or impossible to see or to hear described?
cats.test: Would a learner with low vision, colour blindness or blindness (who uses a screen reader) be blocked or slowed by it? Contrast, text size, images without a text alternative belong here.

cats.label: Motor: using the controls
cats.hint: Does it make controls hard to reach or to hit without a mouse or a steady hand?
cats.test: Would a learner who uses only a keyboard, a switch, or has a tremor be blocked or slowed? Menus that need a mouse, tiny buttons and keyboard traps belong here.

cats.label: Cognitive: understanding and following
cats.hint: Does it make the page hard to understand, remember or follow?
cats.test: Would a learner with dyslexia, ADHD, an anxiety about time, or simply a tired mind be lost? Deep navigation, long unstructured text and fixed time limits belong here.

facts.text: The lesson text is light grey on a white background, with a contrast ratio of 2.1 : 1.
facts.short: Light grey text, contrast 2.1 : 1
facts.clue: Who would struggle to read this, and in what light?
facts.why: Low contrast hits learners with low vision: a visual barrier.

facts.text: The text is 10 px, and when it is enlarged the page breaks and text is cut off.
facts.short: 10 px text that breaks when enlarged
facts.key: when it is enlarged the page breaks
facts.clue: What happens to a learner who needs larger text?
facts.why: Small, unscalable text hits learners with low vision: a visual barrier.

facts.text: A chart that carries the lesson's key message has no text alternative.
facts.short: A key chart with no text alternative
facts.clue: What does a learner who uses a screen reader hear here?
facts.why: A blind learner misses the content entirely: a visual barrier.

facts.text: The course menu opens only when the mouse hovers over it, and cannot be reached with the Tab key.
facts.short: A menu that opens only on mouse hover
facts.key: cannot be reached with the Tab key
facts.clue: Can a learner who does not use a mouse reach the courses at all?
facts.why: A keyboard-only learner cannot open the menu: a motor barrier that stops use completely.

facts.text: The quiz answer buttons are 18 px high and sit close together.
facts.short: 18 px quiz buttons close together
facts.key: 18 px high and sit close together
facts.clue: Who would hit the wrong button, and how often?
facts.why: Tiny targets hit learners with a tremor or on a phone: a motor barrier.

facts.text: A lesson sits seven levels deep, and the same page can be reached from three different menus.
facts.short: Seven levels deep, three menus to the same page
facts.clue: Could a tired learner find lesson 3 again?
facts.why: Complex navigation overloads learners who find structure hard: a cognitive barrier.

facts.text: Instructions run as long paragraphs with unexplained abbreviations and no headings.
facts.short: Long paragraphs, abbreviations, no headings
facts.clue: Can a learner skim this to find the step they need?
facts.why: Unstructured text hits learners with dyslexia or limited attention: a cognitive barrier.

facts.text: Each quiz has a fixed 60-second time limit that cannot be extended.
facts.short: A fixed 60-second quiz limit
facts.clue: Who needs more than a minute, and what happens to them?
facts.why: A fixed limit penalises learners who read or respond more slowly: a cognitive barrier.

13.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto the user group it affects most, or select it and then a heading. Select a placed one to move it again. One heading per fact: Visual, Motor or Cognitive.
13.sortKeyTitle: Eight barriers into Visual, Motor, Cognitive
13.sortTeaching: The sort is objective in its core: low contrast, small text and a missing text alternative are visual; a mouse-only menu and tiny buttons are motor; deep navigation, unstructured text and a fixed time limit are cognitive. Several barriers affect more than one group (small buttons also matter for low vision; a time limit also matters for motor impairments); the test is whom it hits first. A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. Which barrier stops a learner completely, the changes and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, identify barriers, user groups affected, improvements.
13.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A1 and A2

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight barriers: who do they affect, and which one stops a learner?
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight facts and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · identify five barriers, which user groups are affected, which improvements.

fields.label: Which barrier stops a learner from using the platform at all?
fields.help: Choose one. A barrier that slows is not the same as one that stops. The reason below says whom it stops and why.
fields.missing: choose the barrier that stops a learner completely

options.label: 1 · Light grey text, contrast 2.1 : 1
options.why: Slows: the text can be read with effort, or with a zoom or a high-contrast setting.

options.label: 2 · 10 px text that breaks when enlarged
options.why: Slows or blocks for low vision; defends if the reason says the page breaks.

options.label: 3 · A key chart with no text alternative
options.why: Defends: a blind learner misses the content, though the rest of the page works.

options.label: 4 · A menu that opens only on mouse hover
options.why: Reference choice: a keyboard-only learner cannot reach any course, so use stops completely.

options.label: 5 · 18 px quiz buttons close together
options.why: Slows: errors, but a learner can still try.

options.label: 6 · Seven levels deep, three menus to one page
options.why: Slows: findable with effort.

options.label: 7 · Long paragraphs, abbreviations, no headings
options.why: Slows: harder to read, not impossible.

options.label: 8 · A fixed 60-second quiz limit
options.why: Defends: a learner who needs longer cannot finish the quiz.

fields.model: f4
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The barrier that stops a learner
fields.teaching: Elements 3, 4 and 8 can all stop a learner completely; the others mostly slow. Element 4 is the reference because every course sits behind the menu. Look at the reason: it should say whom it stops and why they cannot go around it. The plan's goal is to raise awareness of barriers.

fields.label: Whom does it stop, and why is it worse than a barrier that only slows?
fields.help: Name the user group, say why they cannot get around it, and name one barrier that only slows, with the reason. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say whom that barrier stops and why it is worse than one that only slows
fields.model: Element 4 stops learners who use only a keyboard, for example because of a motor impairment: the menu opens only on mouse hover and cannot be reached with Tab, so they cannot reach any course. Element 1, low contrast, only slows: the text is hard to read, but a learner can still zoom or change the colours and go on.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a video with no captions stops a deaf learner from getting the content at all. A video with poor sound quality only slows a hearing learner, who can turn up the volume.
guide.why: A barrier that stops leaves the learner no way around it; one that slows can be worked around with effort (Materi A1).
lookFor: Names the user group.
Says why there is no way around it.
Names a barrier that only slows.

steps: Pick a barrier and ask: is there any way around it for this learner?
If there is none, it stops; if there is, it slows.

fields.label: Which user groups are affected, and what would you change?
fields.help: Name the group, and for each change the barrier (by number) it answers, starting each change with a verb. At least 60 characters in all.
fields.missing: write which user groups are affected and what you would change, naming the barrier each change answers
fields.model: Affected: visual (1 to 3), motor (4, 5) and cognitive (6 to 8). 1. Make the menu open with the keyboard as well as the mouse (barrier 4). 2. Raise the text contrast to at least 4.5 : 1 (barrier 1). 3. Add a text alternative to the chart (barrier 3). 4. Add headings and shorter paragraphs (barrier 7). 5. Let learners extend the quiz time (barrier 8).

guide.example: Affected: visual and motor. 1. Add a visible focus outline to every link (links with no focus sign). 2. Enlarge the buttons to at least 44 px (buttons 18 px high).
guide.why: The plan asks which user groups are affected and which improvements. A good answer names the groups and ties each change to a barrier (Materi A1 to A3).
lookFor: Names the user groups.
Names the barrier each change answers.
Starts each change with a verb.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Prioritising WCAG measures: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to make a learning platform accessible. The budget is limited, time is short and there are many existing content items (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A improves the contrasts, option B simplifies the navigation, and option C provides alternative content, such as text for images.

criteria.label: Impact
criteria.help: How many learners it frees from a barrier, and how badly they were blocked.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example that it is not finished in time or does not remove the barrier.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your prioritisation: prioritise practical implementation
opts.whyHelp: Say what each option frees learners from and what it costs, given the time pressure and the amount of content. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Improve the contrasts
options.keyWhy: Cheap and quick, with no risk: one change in the style sheet helps every page at once.

options.name: Simplify the navigation
options.keyWhy: A big effect: it removes the keyboard and cognitive barriers behind every course; mid effort.

options.name: Provide alternative content for all existing items
options.keyWhy: Necessary for blind and deaf learners but large: many existing items make it costly and slow.

model.why: I put A first: it costs €6,000 and two weeks, nothing can go wrong, and one change helps every page, which suits the time pressure. B comes second: it removes the barriers behind every course and is worth the mid effort. C comes last: it is needed, but with many existing items it costs the most and takes the longest, so I would do the most-used content first and the rest later.

guide.example: For LearnLoop with little time I would start with the quick fix that helps every page: larger text. Alternative text for every image comes last, because there are hundreds, but I would do the most-viewed ones first.
guide.why: The plan's goal is to prioritise practical implementation. A different first choice defends if the reason names the time pressure and the budget.
lookFor: Says what each option frees learners from.
Names the time pressure or the amount of content.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Three options for WCAG measures
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €8,000 Low, €8,000 to €18,000 Mid, above €18,000 High), so the check can flag it; impact and risk are judgements. Prioritise practical implementation: a cheap fix that helps every page first. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: accessibility as quality and compliance
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: accessibility is not an add-on but a standard; WCAG is a minimum requirement, not a goal; inclusion improves UX for all users; its strategic importance lies in law, market and reputation.

questions.q: Who is currently being excluded?
Which measure has the greatest effect?
Which risks arise from non-compliance?

model.a: Keyboard-only learners, learners with low vision, blind learners, and learners who need more time or a simpler structure.
model.b: A keyboard-operable menu and clear structure, because they open every course for several groups at once.
model.c: Complaints, legal action and fines, loss of customers and public bodies, and damage to the reputation.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: accessibility is a standard, not an add-on; WCAG is the minimum, not the goal; inclusion improves UX for all; the strategic importance lies in law, market and reputation. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four central barriers to the platform
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight facts of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A problem is something that keeps learners with impairments from using the platform, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it explains why users with impairments cannot use the platform, or is only a matter of the learners' skills or the platform's look.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at a fact by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: WCAG is not implemented: there are no rules for contrast, text alternatives or keyboard use.
items.why: Facts 1, 3 and 4 and the case: a missing WCAG implementation.

items.text: There is no inclusive UX: accessibility was not considered when the screens were designed.
items.why: Facts 4 to 8 and the case: no inclusive UX.

items.text: The barriers hit several user groups at once: visual, motor and cognitive.
items.why: Facts 1 to 8 cover all three groups.

items.text: Nobody tests the platform with a keyboard, a screen reader or users with impairments.
items.why: Facts 3 and 4: barriers that a simple test would have shown.

items.text: Learners with impairments are not skilled enough with technology.
items.why: It blames the learner; the facts show barriers in the platform.

items.text: The platform's colours need a new brand design.
items.why: A look matter; contrast is only one fact of eight.

items.text: Users with impairments should be given a separate simplified version.
items.why: It is a remedy, not a problem, and it contradicts inclusive design.

causes.whyModel: Fact 4: the course menu cannot be reached with the Tab key, which is a missing WCAG requirement and a barrier a keyboard test would have found.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “No inclusive UX” rests on one printed fact, that a video has no captions. Nobody asked what a deaf learner would need when the video was made.
guide.why: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the lack of accessibility as the main problem.
lookFor: Points at a fact by number or quotes the case.
Says why it explains the barrier.

causes.teaching: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names a missing WCAG implementation and no inclusive UX; the Musterlösung names the lack of accessibility as the main problem. The rejected options include the tempting “a separate simplified version”, which is a remedy that contradicts inclusive design; none of them explains why users with impairments cannot use the platform.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four UX measures, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which fact it answers (by number), whom it helps, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the plan's rationale, accessibility is usability is success: say how your first measure helps most learners soonest. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example that it takes longer than planned or covers only part of the content.

impact.label: Impact
impact.help: How many learners it frees from a barrier, and how badly they were blocked.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: improve contrast, simplify navigation, provide alternative content, clear structure; rationale accessibility = usability = success. The reference set costs €46,000 of €50,000 and takes at most 6 weeks of 10. M5 (a check with assistive technology and users) defends in place of M4 if the reason names evidence. Reference order: M1, M2, M3, M4; M1 first because it is the cheapest change that helps every page.

areas.alternatives: Removes: barriers for blind and deaf learners

measures.name: Improve contrast and text size
measures.what: Raise all text to a contrast of at least 4.5 : 1 and let text be enlarged without breaking the page.
measures.notice: Text is readable on every page.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1 and 2: cheap, quick and no risk, helping every page at once.

measures.name: Simplify the navigation
measures.what: One menu, at most three levels deep, operable with the keyboard.
measures.notice: Every course can be reached with the keyboard.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 4 and 6: removes the barrier that stops keyboard users.

measures.name: Alternative content for the most-used items
measures.what: Text alternatives for the 40 most-viewed images and charts, and captions for the 10 most-viewed videos.
measures.notice: Blind and deaf learners get the key content.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 3 for the content that matters most, within the budget.

measures.name: Clear structure
measures.what: Headings, short paragraphs and plain labels on the lessons that are used most.
measures.notice: Lessons can be skimmed.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 7: removes a cognitive barrier at low cost.

measures.name: A check with assistive technology and users
measures.what: Test the platform with a keyboard, a screen reader and five users with impairments.
measures.notice: The team sees the barriers for itself.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: the plan's analysis found no testing; it gives evidence. A learner who picks it instead of M4 should name evidence.

measures.name: An accessibility overlay
measures.what: A plug-in that adds a toolbar and promises to fix the page automatically.
measures.notice: A toolbar button appears.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: it does not remove the barriers underneath, and users and experts criticise overlays.

measures.name: A separate accessible version
measures.what: A second, simplified copy of the platform for users with impairments.
measures.notice: There are two platforms.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: separate is not inclusive, doubles the upkeep, and the effort is High.

measures.name: Fix all 2,000 content items at once
measures.what: Every lesson, image and video is reworked in one programme.
measures.notice: Nothing changes for months, then everything.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: over the budget, effort High, and learners wait ten weeks for any gain.

measures.name: An accessibility statement on the website
measures.what: A page that describes the platform's accessibility and a contact for complaints.
measures.notice: A new page appears in the footer.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected as a stand-alone: required but removes no barrier.

reasons.m1: It answers facts 1 and 2: contrast of at least 4.5 : 1 and text that can be enlarged. At €6,000 it is under €8,000, so effort is Low. Impact Mid: it helps learners with low vision and anyone in bright light. Risk Low, one change in the style sheet.
reasons.m2: It answers facts 4 and 6: one menu, three levels, keyboard-operable. €14,000 lies between €8,000 and €18,000, so effort is Mid. Impact High: it opens every course to keyboard users and helps cognitive load. Risk Mid, because a new menu may confuse regular users at first.
reasons.m3: It answers fact 3 for the content that matters most: 40 images and 10 videos. €18,000 is at the top of the Mid band, so effort is Mid. Impact High: blind and deaf learners get the key content. Risk Mid, because the rest of the 2,000 items stay open.
reasons.m4: It answers fact 7: headings, short paragraphs and plain labels on the most-used lessons. €8,000 is at the lower edge of Mid, so effort is Mid. Impact Mid: lessons can be skimmed. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: it costs €6,000 and two weeks, nothing can go wrong, and one change helps every page at once, which suits the time pressure. Accessibility is usability is success: with the contrast fixed, M2 opens every course to keyboard users, M3 gives blind and deaf learners the key content, and M4 makes the lessons easier for everyone. The four measures cost €46,000 of €50,000, with the longest at six weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know how many learners with impairments actually use the platform or leave it, because nobody has tracked or asked them. I would run a keyboard and screen-reader check and ask the five users who complained, before I spend the last €4,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, captions for the ten most-viewed videos cost €9,000, so effort is Mid. They answer videos with no sound access, so impact is High for deaf learners. Risk is Low: it only adds text.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). Impact and risk are judgements: they must name the fact the measure answers, whom it helps, and what could go wrong (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed fact the measure answers.
Says whom it helps.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop larger text goes first: it costs little, helps every page and cannot go wrong. Accessibility is usability is success, and a quick win builds support for the larger work.
order.why: The plan's rationale: accessibility = usability = success. A different first priority defends if the reason says whom it helps soonest and why it can go first.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Says whom it helps soonest.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know how many learners use a screen reader. I would ask the support team and run a screen-reader check before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

brief2.heading: The situation: AccessLearn's Chief Accessibility Officer
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief Accessibility Officer of AccessLearn. The platform must become accessible, the budget is limited and the requirements are increasing. Management wants a strategy for the next 12 months and expects you to decide how to implement WCAG, how to build accessibility into the UX process, how to measure progress, and to take responsibility at management level.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €180,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Requirements are increasing, and nobody can say exactly how much of the platform fails them.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: the platform must become accessible, a limited budget, increasing requirements. Everything else is made up: the €180,000, the process steps, the indicators, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the strategy for WCAG, the integration into the UX process, and the evaluation approach (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk analysis of costs against benefits, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · The WCAG strategy, the process and the evaluation
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the strategy below, the list of process steps, the indicator board and the fields. Answer in the lists, the board and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1, 3 and 4 · a strategy for implementing WCAG, integration into UX processes, an evaluation approach (measurability).

fields.label: The strategy for implementing WCAG
fields.help: Choose the approach you will take to management. A decision with a clear reason counts, whichever you choose.
fields.missing: choose a strategy for implementing WCAG

options.label: Step by step: WCAG 2.2 level AA on the most-used courses first, then build it into the process
options.why: Reference strategy: starts where most learners are, and stops new barriers from appearing.

options.label: Everything at once: all 2,000 items in one programme
options.why: Weak: over the budget, slow, and learners wait for any gain.

options.label: Only the legal minimum, fixed when a complaint arrives
options.why: Weak: reactive; treats WCAG as the goal, not the minimum; the risk stays.

options.label: Audit first: test the whole platform, then decide
options.why: Defends: a decision with an evidence step; slower, but cheap.

fields.model: g1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The strategy for WCAG
fields.teaching: The plan asks for a strategy for implementing WCAG within a limited budget. Strategy 1 is the reference; strategy 4 also defends (audit first); strategy 3 is the weakest because it treats WCAG as the goal and leaves the risk. A decision with a clear reason exports whichever is chosen (CLAUDE.md #38). Plan: item 1.

fields.label: Why this strategy, and not the others?
fields.help: Give the reason in terms of reach, cost and risk, not only in terms of what the law demands. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why you chose that strategy and not the others
fields.model: I implement WCAG step by step, starting with the most-used courses: the budget is limited, so fixing everything at once is not possible, and the most-used courses reach the most learners soonest. I then build accessibility into the process so that new content does not bring new barriers, because WCAG is the minimum and not the goal.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would fix the most-visited pages first: they reach the most learners and fit a small budget. Then I would add a check at design review, so new pages start accessible.
guide.why: The reason must rest on reach, cost and risk, and on WCAG as a minimum, not only on what the law demands (Materi B1).
lookFor: Gives a reason about reach, cost or risk.
Treats WCAG as a minimum.
Says what comes after the first step.

fields.label: Integration into the UX process: choose at least three steps
fields.help: A step is good when it stops a barrier early, where it is cheap, and does not depend on one person.
fields.missing: choose at least three process steps

options.label: Accessibility criteria in every design brief
options.why: Early: the barrier is stopped before it is designed.

options.label: A check at every design review
options.why: A quality gate that does not depend on one person.

options.label: A keyboard and screen-reader test before every release
options.why: Catches what automated tools miss.

options.label: Training for designers and content authors
options.why: People who make the content know the rules.

options.label: Accessible components in the style guide
options.why: Every new page starts from accessible parts.

options.label: A test only before the launch of a big change
options.why: Rejected: too late and too rare.

options.label: An overlay plug-in as the fix
options.why: Rejected: does not remove the barriers underneath.

options.label: A separate team that fixes problems afterwards
options.why: Rejected: late, costly, and teams keep creating new barriers.

options.label: Automated tests only
options.why: Rejected: automated tools find only a part of the barriers.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The process steps
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference steps defend if each stops barriers early and does not depend on one person. The rejected ones are late, narrow or do not remove the barrier. Plan: item 3, integration into UX processes.

fields.label: The evaluation approach: place eight indicators
fields.help: Place each indicator under the way it is best measured or used, or under “does not show accessibility” if it tells nothing about it.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight indicators

items.label: The share of pages that pass the contrast check
items.why: A tool can count it.

items.label: The share of images with a text alternative
items.why: A tool can count it; whether the text is useful needs a person.

items.label: Can a keyboard-only user finish a lesson?
items.why: Only a person trying it can tell.

items.label: How long a screen-reader user needs to find lesson 3
items.why: A task test with a real user.

items.label: Accessibility complaints per month
items.why: A figure management reads; open item: it also shows where to test.

items.label: Open barriers by severity, reported each quarter
items.why: The progress view for management.

items.label: The number of pages on the platform
items.why: Says nothing about accessibility.

items.label: A published statement that the platform “is accessible”
items.why: A claim, not a measurement.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The evaluation indicators
fields.teaching: There is no single right grid. Item 5 is the open one (report or test). Items 7 and 8 do not show accessibility. Each bin must be used at least once. A good approach mixes automatic counts, tests with users and a figure for management. Plan: item 4, evaluation approach (measurability).

fields.label: Which measure has the greatest reach, and who else gains?
fields.help: Name the measure, the user groups it reaches, and one group beyond people with impairments who also gain. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name the measure with the greatest reach and who else gains
fields.model: A keyboard-operable menu and clear structure reach the most learners: keyboard-only and screen-reader users, and learners who find structure hard. Everyone else gains too: a learner on a phone, in a hurry, or with a broken mouse also finds courses faster, which shows that inclusion improves UX for all.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, captions reach deaf learners, and also anyone watching on a train with the sound off. That shows that a measure built for one group often helps everyone.
guide.why: The plan's Level 3 input asks for the measure with the greatest reach; inclusion improves UX for all (Materi B1).
lookFor: Names the measure.
Names the groups it reaches.
Names a group beyond people with impairments.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 2 and 5 and the additional requirement · prioritised measures, a risk analysis of costs against benefits, a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: costs against benefits
fields.help: Imagine the programme has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the programme fails

options.label: Non-compliance: we did too little, and a complaint led to legal action and lost customers.
options.why: The non-implementation pole. Action: fix the most-used courses first and publish a dated plan; notice it in the complaint count.

options.label: Cost overrun: retrofitting the old content cost far more than planned.
options.why: Action: fix the most-used content first and set a cap; notice it in cost per item after the first month.

options.label: A one-off project: new content brought new barriers, and the gains faded.
options.why: Action: build checks into the process; notice it in the share of new pages that fail.

options.label: We fixed what automated tools found, but real users still could not use the platform.
options.why: Action: test with real users each quarter; notice it in task results.

options.label: The team lacked the skills, and the fixes were wrong.
options.why: Action: train designers and authors; notice it in failed checks.

fields.model: r1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: costs against benefits
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the team would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007). The plan's Level 3 input asks which risks arise from non-implementation.

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I fix the most-used courses first and publish a dated plan for the rest, and I count accessibility complaints each month; if they do not fall after the first three months, I move budget to the barrier they name most.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would fix the most-visited pages first, and count complaints each month; if they stay level for a quarter, I look at the barrier they name most.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without knowing how much of the platform fails WCAG)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to start with WCAG 2.2 AA on the twenty most-used courses (D1) and to build checks into the design review (D2), before I audit the rest.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example how many barriers the remaining courses have. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know how many barriers the other courses have.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of month 4, the audit of ten further courses shows more than five serious barriers per course, and I widen the first step to the audit's worst courses.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to fix the ten most-visited pages first. I do not know how bad the rest are. I reverse if an audit of five more pages shows more than five barriers each by the end of month 3.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I postpone the accessibility of the rarely used courses and I do not buy an overlay this year. The authors of the old courses will miss a quick fix, and sales cannot yet claim that every course is accessible.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I postpone the old archive of courses for a year. The team that owns it will miss the fix, and sales cannot say “fully accessible”.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say whom it reaches and what it prevents. At least 30 characters.

items.name: WCAG 2.2 AA on the most-used courses
items.what: Contrast, keyboard use, text alternatives, structure and time limits fixed on the twenty courses most learners use.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: removes the barriers where most learners meet them.

items.name: Accessibility built into the UX process
items.what: Criteria in every brief, a check at design review, accessible components in the style guide.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: stops new barriers from appearing, cheaply, early.

items.name: Measurement: automated checks and quarterly user tests
items.what: Automatic counts of contrast and text alternatives, and a keyboard and screen-reader test with users each quarter.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: makes progress visible to management.

items.name: Training for designers and authors
items.what: Workshops on WCAG and accessible writing for the people who create the courses.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D3: builds skills so fewer barriers are made, though progress is harder to show.

items.name: An accessibility overlay
items.what: A plug-in with a toolbar that promises to fix every page.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: does not remove the barriers underneath, and gives a false sense of safety.

items.name: A separate accessible version
items.what: A second platform for users with impairments.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: separate is not inclusive, doubles the upkeep, and the cost is the highest.

items.name: Fix only what complaints report
items.what: A team that reacts to each complaint as it arrives.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: reactive; the risk stays, and learners who do not complain stay excluded.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: it removes the existing barriers where most learners meet them, which also lowers the legal risk soonest. With the first courses fixed, D2 stops new barriers from appearing, and D3 shows management the progress. Accessibility is usability is success, so the order goes from fixing to preventing to measuring. The three cost €140,000 of the €180,000.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the fixes on the most-used courses go first: they reach the most learners and lower the legal risk soonest. Preventing new barriers and measuring progress only make sense once the first courses are fixed.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: accessibility = usability = success. A different first measure defends if the reason names whom it reaches and what it prevents (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says whom it reaches.
Says what it prevents or why the others can wait.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D2, D3 (€140,000 of €180,000, longest 20 weeks). D1 first because it removes existing barriers where most learners meet them. D2, D1, D3 also defends: process first, so that new content stays accessible while old content is fixed. D1, D2, D4 defends if the reason names skills. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The accessibility strategy for the next twelve months

13.caseExport: AccessLearn is a learning platform with barriers: users with impairments cannot use it, complaints are increasing and legal risks are growing. WCAG is not implemented and there is no inclusive UX. The budget is €50,000, time is short and there is a lot of existing content.

memoSections.title: What I give up or postpone

13.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 improve contrast, M2 simplify navigation, M3 alternative content, M4 clear structure) and cost €46,000 of the case's €50,000 (a Case assumption), longest 6 weeks of 10. The plan's rationale: accessibility = usability = success.

14.heading: Day 14 · Plain language, usability and testing

intro.about: Today is about learning platforms that people understand at first sight. You learn the principles of plain language (short sentences, clear terms, no jargon), what makes a learning environment intuitive (clear structure, navigation, less complexity, and three usability principles), how to test with different user groups, and how to improve continuously. You then weigh measures on a platform that users do not understand.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is ClearLearn, a complex platform with low usage: users do not understand the content, the navigation is unclear, and the drop-out rate is high. The puzzle: with time pressure, do you simplify, restructure or add functions, and how do you know whether it worked?

story.question: Which of the eight facts about ClearLearn are hurdles to understanding, which would make learners give up first, what would a plainer text say, and which four of nine measures fit €45,000 and ten weeks?

As the Chief Usability & Experience Officer, how do you simplify, how do you reshape the information architecture, how do you test and keep improving, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Rewrite a text so that more people understand it
wiifm.payoff: Short sentences, clear terms and no jargon work on an email, a contract summary or a slide, not only on a screen.

wiifm.skill: Use three usability principles as a checklist
wiifm.payoff: Efficiency, error prevention and consistency show you in minutes where any form or tool is likely to fail.

wiifm.skill: Weigh a simplification measure
wiifm.payoff: Impact, effort and risk give you a fair comparison when a new function competes with a plainer text for the same budget.

wiifm.skill: Plan how to test understanding, not opinion
wiifm.payoff: Asking people to explain something back tells you more than asking whether they like it, in any product or training.

wiifm.skill: Reshape an information architecture
wiifm.payoff: One place for each thing and one name for each action is a rule for any intranet, website or document system.

wiifm.skill: Decide how much to simplify
wiifm.payoff: Naming what complexity is necessary protects you from simplifying away what experts need.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Find the hurdles, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight facts about ClearLearn by the kind of hurdle, say which would make learners give up first, write a plainer version of a text, then choose four of nine measures within €45,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order, define two test methods and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 14 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application
route1.h1: Plain language and usability: find the hurdles, then choose the measures
route1.order: Materi A (all five cards, four are core) → the UX Analysis task, one case in two parts (find the hurdles, choose measures), with two core blocks. Every section stays open, so you can start anywhere.
route1.taskSub: UX Analysis File: find the hurdles, choose the measures

route2.title: Decide the usability strategy
route2.blurb: Level 3 in the Chief Usability & Experience Officer's chair: how to simplify, how to reshape the information architecture, how to test and keep improving, three prioritised measures, the risk of too much and too little simplification, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up.
route2.h1: A UX optimisation strategy for an understandable platform: simplify, restructure, test, prioritise, and what you give up
route2.order: Materi B (three cards) → the UX Strategy task, one frame with two core blocks and a memo that builds below. Route 1 is a good start but not needed; every section stays open.
route2.materiSub: Level 3 · comprehensibility as a strategic quality
route2.taskSub: UX Strategy Memo: decide as Chief Usability & Experience Officer

brief1.heading: The case: ClearLearn, a complex platform with low usage
brief1.paragraph: ClearLearn is a learning platform that users find too complex. They do not understand the content, the navigation is unclear, and usage is low. A first analysis points to a lack of comprehensibility and poor usability. The drop-out rate is high and time is short. You are part of the UX team and asked to work out where users get lost, and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four ClearLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €45,000 (Case assumption: the plan gives none)
Time: 10 weeks (Case assumption: the plan only says “time pressure”)
A high drop-out rate, and users who do not understand the content.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: users do not understand the content, the navigation is unclear, low usage, a lack of comprehensibility, poor usability, a high drop-out rate and time pressure. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €45,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight facts by the kind of hurdle, say which would make learners give up first and write a plainer text (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, define two test methods, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

cats.label: Language: the words are hard
cats.hint: Is the text hard to read or understand?
cats.test: Would a learner understand it if the sentences were shorter and the terms were everyday words? Long sentences, jargon and cryptic messages belong here.

cats.label: Structure: where things are is unclear
cats.hint: Does the learner not know where to go or where to find something?
cats.test: Would a learner find it if there were one clear place and one clear name? Menus with too many entries and the same thing in several places belong here.

cats.label: Usability: efficiency, errors, consistency
cats.hint: Is it slow, error-prone or inconsistent to use?
cats.test: Does the task take too many steps (efficiency), let a mistake happen that could be prevented (error prevention), or call the same action by different names (consistency)?

facts.text: The welcome text is one sentence of 52 words with four subordinate clauses.
facts.short: A 52-word welcome sentence
facts.clue: Could a learner read this once and say what it asks them to do?
facts.why: A very long sentence is hard to follow: a language hurdle.

facts.text: It uses unexplained terms such as “asynchronous modality” and “learning taxonomy level”.
facts.short: Unexplained terms: “asynchronous modality”
facts.clue: Which words would a new learner not know, and who explains them?
facts.why: Jargon without an explanation keeps newcomers out: a language hurdle.

facts.text: An error message reads “Error 4012: invalid payload”.
facts.short: An error message: “Error 4012: invalid payload”
facts.clue: Does the message tell the learner what went wrong and what to do?
facts.why: A technical message says nothing to a learner: a language hurdle.

facts.text: The menu has eleven entries on one level, with labels such as “Hub” and “Resources 2”.
facts.short: Eleven menu entries, labels “Hub” and “Resources 2”
facts.clue: Could a learner guess what is behind “Hub”?
facts.why: Too many entries with vague names: a structure hurdle.

facts.text: The same course can be found under “Learn”, “Library” and “Pathways”, each with different content.
facts.short: One course in three places with different content
facts.clue: Where would a learner look, and would they find the same thing?
facts.why: The same thing in several places confuses: a structure hurdle.

facts.text: A learner can send in an assignment with no file; the error appears only after the upload.
facts.short: An assignment can be sent with no file
facts.clue: Could the system have stopped the mistake before it happened?
facts.why: A preventable mistake is allowed: an error-prevention hurdle.

facts.text: The save action is called “Save” on one page, “Submit” on another and “Apply” on a third.
facts.short: One action named “Save”, “Submit” and “Apply”
facts.clue: Does a learner know that these three do the same thing?
facts.why: The same action under different names: a consistency hurdle.

facts.text: To mark a lesson as done, a learner needs five clicks.
facts.short: Five clicks to mark a lesson done
facts.clue: How many steps does the most common action take?
facts.why: A common action takes too many steps: an efficiency hurdle.

14.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto the kind of hurdle it is, or select it and then a heading. Select a placed one to move it again. One heading per fact: Language, Structure or Usability.
14.sortKeyTitle: Eight hurdles into Language, Structure, Usability
14.sortTeaching: The sort is objective in its core: a long sentence, jargon and a cryptic error message are language; a crowded menu with vague labels and the same course in three places are structure; a preventable mistake, one action under three names and five clicks for a common task are usability (error prevention, consistency, efficiency). Fact 3 could also be argued as error prevention; the test is whether the words alone are the problem. A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. Which hurdle makes learners give up first, the plainer text and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, comprehension hurdles, which users, a more understandable version.
14.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A1 and A2

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight hurdles: which kind, which one first, and a plainer text
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight facts and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · identify five comprehension hurdles, for which users the text is problematic, formulate a more understandable version.

fields.label: Which hurdle would make most new learners give up first?
fields.help: Choose one. Think of a new learner in the first minute. The reason below says why that one comes before the others.
fields.missing: choose the hurdle that would make learners give up first

options.label: 1 · A 52-word welcome sentence
options.why: Reference choice: it is the first thing every learner reads, and nobody can act on what they do not understand.

options.label: 2 · Unexplained terms
options.why: Defends: it is on the same first screen and keeps newcomers out.

options.label: 3 · An error message “Error 4012”
options.why: Defends later: it appears only when something goes wrong.

options.label: 4 · Eleven menu entries
options.why: Defends: if the learner cannot find the course, they stop.

options.label: 5 · One course in three places
options.why: Slows after the first minute.

options.label: 6 · An assignment with no file
options.why: Later: reached only after learning has started.

options.label: 7 · One action under three names
options.why: Later: noticed only across several pages.

options.label: 8 · Five clicks to finish a lesson
options.why: Later: reached only after a lesson.

fields.model: f1
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The hurdle that comes first
fields.teaching: Elements 1, 2 and 4 all defend as the first hurdle; 3 and 5 to 8 come later in a learner's path. Element 1 is the reference because every learner reads the welcome text first. Look at the reason: it should say why this comes before the others, for a new learner. The plan's goal is to develop an awareness of language.

fields.label: Why does it come first, and for which users is it most problematic?
fields.help: Say why it comes before the others, and name the user groups it hurts most (for example new learners, non-native speakers, learners with dyslexia). At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why that hurdle comes first and for which users it is most problematic
fields.model: The 52-word welcome sentence comes first because every learner reads it before anything else, and a learner who does not understand the first screen has no reason to go on. It is most problematic for new learners, non-native speakers and learners with dyslexia, who need short sentences and everyday words.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the unexplained abbreviation on the first page would come first: everyone sees it, and a newcomer cannot guess it. It hurts new learners and people who speak another language at home most.
guide.why: The reason must say why the hurdle comes before the others in a learner's path, and name the user groups it hurts (Materi A1, A2).
lookFor: Says why it comes before the others.
Names the user groups.

clue.refLabel: Plain language and who it helps (Materi A1)
steps: Walk a new learner through the platform and ask where they meet each hurdle.
The earliest one that blocks all of them comes first.

fields.label: Write a more understandable version of the welcome text
fields.help: Use short sentences, everyday words and no jargon. Say what the learner can do first. At least 60 characters.
fields.missing: write a more understandable version of the welcome text
fields.model: Welcome to ClearLearn. Here you learn at your own pace, in short lessons. Start with “My first lesson”. You can stop at any time, and we save where you were.

guide.example: “Hello! You can learn here at your own pace. Pick your first course below. If you stop, we keep your place.” Short sentences, everyday words, one thing to do.
guide.why: The plan asks for a more understandable version. A good answer has short sentences, everyday words, no jargon and a clear first step (Materi A1).
lookFor: Short sentences.
Everyday words and no jargon.
A clear first step for the learner.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Prioritising UX simplification: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to optimise a learning platform. Users do not understand the content, the drop-out rate is high and there is time pressure (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A simplifies the content, option B improves the navigation, and option C adds additional functions.

criteria.label: Impact
criteria.help: How much it helps learners understand and keep going.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example that it adds complexity or does not reach the cause.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your decision: weigh comprehensibility against functionality
opts.whyHelp: Say what each option does for understanding and what it costs, given the time pressure. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Simplify the content
options.keyWhy: It goes to the cause: users do not understand; moderate cost and quick.

options.name: Improve the navigation
options.keyWhy: It helps learners find things; useful, but it does not make the content understandable.

options.name: Add additional functions
options.keyWhy: It adds complexity to a platform that is already too complex; high effort and risk.

model.why: I put A first: users do not understand the content, so simplifying it goes to the cause, it costs €9,000 and takes three weeks, which suits the time pressure. B comes second: finding things is part of the problem, but a clear menu does not help if the content is still hard. C comes last: more functions add complexity to a platform that is already too complex, and cost the most.

guide.example: For LearnLoop with users who leave early I would simplify the text first: it goes to the cause and is quick. A new feature comes last, because it would make a confusing platform more confusing.
guide.why: The plan's goal is to weigh comprehensibility against functionality. A different first choice defends if the reason names the cause and the time pressure.
lookFor: Says what each option does for understanding.
Names the cause or the time pressure.

opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €7,000 Low, €7,000 to €15,000 Mid, above €15,000 High), so the check can flag it; impact and risk are judgements. Weigh comprehensibility against functionality: complexity is UX's greatest enemy. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: comprehensibility as a strategic quality
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: complexity is UX's greatest enemy; simple systems are more successful; usability determines usage; testing is a continuous process.

questions.q: Where do users not understand the system?
Which simplification has the greatest effect?
Which complexity is necessary?

model.a: At the first screen (a long welcome text with jargon), at the menu (too many entries) and at the error messages.
model.b: Plain language on the first screens and in the messages, because every learner reads them.
model.c: The depth of the subject itself: an expert course can be demanding, as long as the interface around it is clear.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: complexity is UX's greatest enemy; simple systems are more successful; usability determines usage; testing as a continuous process. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four central problems
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight facts of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A problem is something that makes users not understand the platform or leave it, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it explains why users do not understand the platform, or is only a matter of missing functions or price.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at a fact by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: The language is too complex: long sentences and technical terms keep users from understanding.
items.why: Facts 1 to 3 and the case: lack of comprehensibility.

items.text: The navigation is unclear: too many entries, vague labels and the same thing in several places.
items.why: Facts 4 and 5 and the case: navigation unclear.

items.text: The usability is poor: preventable errors, inconsistent names and too many clicks.
items.why: Facts 6 to 8 and the case: poor usability.

items.text: Complexity has not been reduced: the platform shows everything at once, and nobody has tested it with learners.
items.why: The plan's main problem, complexity; no test is mentioned.

items.text: The platform has too few functions.
items.why: More functions would add to the complexity that is the problem.

items.text: The learners are not motivated.
items.why: The facts show hurdles in the platform, not in the learners.

items.text: The subscription price is too high.
items.why: A business matter; nothing printed.

causes.whyModel: Fact 1: the welcome text is one sentence of 52 words, so a learner cannot understand what to do, which is the lack of comprehensibility the case names.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “Poor usability” rests on one printed fact, that an error message says only “code 12”. The learner cannot tell what went wrong.
guide.why: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names complexity as the main problem.
lookFor: Points at a fact by number or quotes the case.
Says why it explains the lack of understanding.

causes.teaching: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names a lack of comprehensibility and poor usability; the Musterlösung names complexity as the main problem. The rejected options include the tempting “too few functions”, which would add complexity; none of them explains why users do not understand the platform.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four UX measures, two test methods, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which fact it answers (by number), what the learner notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the plan's rationale, comprehensibility, then usage, then success: say how your first measure helps learners understand. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example that it removes information some learners need.

impact.label: Impact
impact.help: How much it helps learners understand and keep going.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: plain language, clear structure, intuitive navigation, usability tests; rationale comprehensibility → usage → success. The reference set costs €35,000 of €45,000 and takes at most 4 weeks of 10. M5 (explanations for technical terms) defends in place of M1 only if the reason says why a rewrite is not possible. Reference order: M1, M2, M3, M4; M1 first because lack of comprehensibility is the first hurdle.

measures.name: Plain language
measures.what: Rewrite the 30 most-used screens and all error messages with short sentences and everyday words.
measures.notice: Texts can be understood at first reading.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1 to 3: the first hurdle, and the cheapest cure.

measures.name: Clear structure and consistent names
measures.what: One name for each action, the same place for the same button, and fewer clicks for the common tasks.
measures.notice: The same thing is always called the same.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 6 to 8: consistency, efficiency and error prevention.

measures.name: Intuitive navigation
measures.what: One menu of six entries, each course in one place, and a path above every page.
measures.notice: Learners know where they are and where to go.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 4 and 5: too many entries and the same course in three places.

measures.name: Usability tests
measures.what: Three rounds of tests with eight learners, among them learners with impairments, who do tasks while someone watches.
measures.notice: The team sees where learners get stuck.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. The plan's analysis found no testing; it gives evidence at low cost.

measures.name: A hover explanation for technical terms
measures.what: Every technical term gets a small explanation that opens when the learner selects it.
measures.notice: A term can be looked up on the spot.
measures.keyWhy: Defends in place of M1 only for terms that cannot be replaced; it explains rather than simplifies.

measures.name: Add chat, forum and calendar
measures.what: Three new functions, each with its own menu entry.
measures.notice: Three new menu entries appear.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: adds complexity to a platform that is already too complex; effort High.

measures.name: A new visual style
measures.what: New colours, fonts and icons across the platform.
measures.notice: The platform looks different.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: the problem is understanding, not the look; effort High.

measures.name: A 40-page user manual
measures.what: A manual that explains how to use the platform.
measures.notice: A manual link appears.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: intuitive use means understandable without explanation; a manual explains instead of fixing.

measures.name: Cut half of the content
measures.what: Remove every second lesson to make the platform smaller.
measures.notice: Lessons disappear.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: removes necessary content; the aim is to clarify, not to delete.

reasons.m1: It answers facts 1 to 3: short sentences and everyday words on the 30 most-used screens and every error message. €9,000 lies between €7,000 and €15,000, so effort is Mid. Impact High: every learner reads those screens. Risk Low, it only changes words.
reasons.m2: It answers facts 6 to 8: one name for each action, the same place for the same button, fewer clicks. €8,000 is in the Mid band. Impact Mid: it removes friction rather than a first hurdle. Risk Low.
reasons.m3: It answers facts 4 and 5: one menu of six entries, each course in one place, a path above every page. €12,000, so effort is Mid. Impact High: learners find their way. Risk Mid, because a new menu may disturb regular users at first.
reasons.m4: It gives evidence: eight learners, among them learners with impairments, do tasks while someone watches. At €6,000 it is under €7,000, so effort is Low. Impact Mid: it shows what to fix next. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: the first hurdle is language, and a learner who cannot understand the first screen needs nothing else until that is fixed. Comprehensibility leads to usage and usage to success: with plain language in place, M2 and M3 make the platform easy to use and to find one's way in, and M4 shows what to fix next. The four measures cost €35,000 of €45,000, with the longest at four weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know where exactly learners stop, because nobody has watched them. I would run a first test with five learners and compare drop-out by screen, before I spend the last €10,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, replacing the error codes with plain sentences costs €6,000, so effort is Low. It answers messages that say only “code 12”, so impact is High. Risk is Low: it only changes words.
