reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). Impact and risk are judgements: they must name the fact the measure answers, what the learner notices, and what could go wrong (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed fact the measure answers.
Says what the learner notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop plain language on the first screens goes first: everyone reads them, and nothing else helps while they are not understood. Comprehensibility leads to usage.
order.why: The plan's rationale: comprehensibility → usage → success. A different first priority defends if the reason says what it does for understanding and why it can go first.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Says what it does for understanding.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know on which screen most learners stop. I would watch five learners do a task and compare drop-out by screen before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

b22.afterNote: The plan also asks for two test methods. Choose exactly two, the ones that would show you whether learners now understand.

after.label: Define two test methods
after.help: A good test method shows whether people understand, not whether they like it. Choose exactly 2.

options.label: A usability test: five to eight learners do set tasks while someone watches
options.why: Shows where learners get stuck, with real users.

options.label: A five-second test: show a screen for five seconds, then ask what it was about
options.why: Defends: shows whether a screen is understood at a glance.

options.label: A comprehension check: ask readers to explain a text back in their own words
options.why: Shows whether the plain version is understood.

options.label: Ask the managers whether the platform looks clear
options.why: Rejected: the managers are not the users and know the platform.

options.label: Count page views each month
options.why: Rejected: shows use, not understanding.

options.label: A survey: “Do you like the new design?”
options.why: Rejected: opinion, not understanding.

after.teaching: Exactly two. Any two of the three reference methods defend (usability test, five-second test, comprehension check); they test understanding, with real users. The rejected ones ask the wrong people, count use or ask for opinions. Plan: Level 2, define two test methods.

brief2.heading: The situation: ClearLearn's Chief Usability & Experience Officer
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief Usability & Experience Officer of ClearLearn. The platform is too complex, users do not understand the content, and the drop-out rate is rising. Management wants an optimisation strategy for the next 12 months and expects you to decide how to simplify, how to reshape the structure, how to test and keep improving, and to take responsibility for user success.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €170,000 (Case assumption: the plan gives none)
The drop-out rate is rising, and nobody knows exactly where learners stop.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: the platform is too complex, users do not understand the content, a rising drop-out rate. Everything else is made up: the €170,000, the structure steps, the testing activities, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the strategy for simplifying, the optimisation of the information architecture, and the testing concept (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk of too much and too little simplification, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · The simplification strategy, the information architecture and the testing concept
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the strategy below, the list of structure steps, the testing board and the fields. Answer in the lists, the board and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 3 · a strategy for simplifying content, the optimisation of the information architecture, a testing and optimisation concept.

fields.label: The strategy for simplifying
fields.help: Choose the approach you will take to management. A decision with a clear reason counts, whichever you choose.
fields.missing: choose a strategy for simplifying

options.label: In steps: plain language and a clear structure first, then test and adjust
options.why: Reference strategy: goes to the first hurdles, and learns from users before the next step.

options.label: Simplify everything to the minimum at once
options.why: Weak: risks removing what some learners need, with no test.

options.label: Keep the platform as it is and add a help centre
options.why: Weak: explains the complexity instead of reducing it.

options.label: Test first: find where learners stop, then decide
options.why: Defends: a decision with an evidence step; slower, but cheap.

fields.model: g1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The strategy for simplifying
fields.teaching: The plan asks for a strategy for simplifying content. Strategy 1 is the reference; strategy 4 also defends (test first); strategy 2 risks over-simplification; strategy 3 is the weakest because it leaves the complexity. A decision with a clear reason exports whichever is chosen (CLAUDE.md #38). Plan: item 1.

fields.label: Why this strategy, and not the others?
fields.help: Give the reason in terms of comprehensibility, usage and the risk of simplifying too much. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why you chose that strategy and not the others
fields.model: I simplify in steps: the first hurdles are the language and the structure, and both are cheap to fix, so I start there. I then test with learners and adjust, because simplifying everything at once could remove what some learners need, and a help centre would only explain the complexity instead of reducing it.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would fix the first screens first: everyone reads them. Then I would test and adjust, so I do not remove what experts need.
guide.why: The reason must rest on comprehensibility and usage and name the risk of simplifying too much (Materi B1, B2).
lookFor: Gives a reason about comprehensibility or usage.
Names the risk of too much simplification.
Says what comes after the first step.

fields.label: Optimising the information architecture: choose at least three steps
fields.help: A step is good when it gives each thing one place and one name, and shows learners where they are.
fields.missing: choose at least three information architecture steps

options.label: One menu with at most six entries
options.why: Fewer choices; less to scan.

options.label: Each course in exactly one place
options.why: One place for each thing.

options.label: A path above each page (“you are here”)
options.why: Orientation.

options.label: A “continue where you stopped” card on the home page
options.why: Efficiency for the most common return.

options.label: The same label for the same action everywhere
options.why: Consistency.

options.label: A mega menu that lists every course
options.why: Rejected: brings back too many choices.

options.label: Three menus that lead to the same page
options.why: Rejected: the same thing in several places.

options.label: Labels in internal words such as “Hub”
options.why: Rejected: jargon in the navigation.

options.label: A search box as the only way to find things
options.why: Rejected: needs the right word, which newcomers do not know.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The information architecture steps
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference steps defend if each gives a thing one place and one name, or shows where the learner is. The rejected ones add choices, duplicate places or use jargon. Plan: item 2, optimisation of the information architecture.

fields.label: The testing and optimisation concept: place eight activities
fields.help: Place each activity where it belongs in the loop, or under “does not show understanding” if it tells nothing about it.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight activities

items.label: A card sort of the menu labels with learners
items.why: Finds the labels before they are built.

items.label: Test the first draft of a rewritten text with five learners
items.why: Tests the draft with real readers.

items.label: Ask learners to explain a screen back in their own words
items.why: A comprehension check.

items.label: Compare first-week drop-out before and after the change
items.why: A data-based check of the effect.

items.label: Track support questions about the same screen each month
items.why: Continuous evaluation.

items.label: An A/B test of two menu versions
items.why: Open item: during the rollout also defends; compares two versions with real use.

items.label: The number of page views per month
items.why: Shows use, not understanding.

items.label: The team's opinion of whether the text sounds good
items.why: The team knows the platform; not a test of understanding.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The testing and optimisation activities
fields.teaching: There is no single right grid. Item 6 is the open one (during the rollout or after). Items 7 and 8 do not show understanding. Each bin must be used at least once. A good concept tests before, during and after, and repeats. Plan: item 3, testing and optimisation concept.

fields.label: Which complexity is necessary, and which would you remove?
fields.help: Name one kind of complexity you would keep because learners need it, and one you would remove, with the reason. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one necessary complexity and one you would remove
fields.model: I keep the depth of the expert courses: the subject is demanding, and cutting it would take away what advanced learners need. I remove the complexity around it: eleven menu entries, jargon on the first screens and three names for one action, because they add effort that teaches nothing.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I keep the detailed legal course, because the subject is complex. I remove the long menu, because it only makes people search.
guide.why: The plan's conflict is simplicity against information content: separate the complexity of the subject from the complexity of the interface (Materi B2).
lookFor: Names a necessary complexity.
Names an unnecessary one.
Gives the reason.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 4 and 5 and the additional requirement · prioritised measures, a risk analysis of too much against too little simplification, a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: too much against too little simplification
fields.help: Imagine the strategy has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the strategy fails

options.label: Too much simplification: we removed information that some learners needed, and experts left.
options.why: The over-simplification pole. Action: separate the subject's complexity from the interface's and test with experts too; notice it in complaints from advanced learners.

options.label: Too little simplification: learners still did not understand, and drop-out stayed high.
options.why: The under-simplification pole. Action: test understanding after each step; notice it in first-week drop-out.

options.label: An uneven rollout: some screens became clear while others stayed as they were, so the platform felt inconsistent.
options.why: Action: a style guide and one team that owns the words; notice it in the share of screens that follow it.

options.label: We tested opinion, not understanding, so we did not see that learners still got lost.
options.why: Action: use task tests and comprehension checks; notice it when ratings rise and drop-out does not.

options.label: The platform grew complicated again within a year, because nobody kept the rules.
options.why: Action: make a clarity check part of every release; notice it in new screens that fail the check.

fields.model: r1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: too much against too little simplification
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the team would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007). The plan names too much against too little simplification.

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I keep the expert courses untouched and simplify only the interface around them, and I ask advanced learners to test every change; if their complaints rise in the first two months, I roll the change back.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would simplify the menu but not the course content, and ask a few experienced learners to try each change; if they complain, I look again.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without knowing where learners stop)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to start with plain language on the thirty most-used screens (D1) and a first test with eight learners, before I rebuild the menu.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example on which screen most learners stop. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know on which screen most learners stop.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of month 3, first-week drop-out has not fallen from 40% to below 35%, and I look at the structure before I rewrite more text.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to rewrite the welcome screen first. I do not know whether the text is the main reason people leave. I reverse if first-week drop-out has not fallen from 30% to below 27% by the end of month 2.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I postpone the new chat, forum and calendar (D5) and I do not cut any content this year. The community team will miss the functions they planned, and some editors will miss the chance to remove old lessons.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I postpone the planned forum for a year. The community team will miss it, and users who asked for it must wait.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say what it does for understanding and usage. At least 30 characters.

items.name: A plain-language programme
items.what: A style guide, a rewrite of all learner-facing text and a review step for new text.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: goes to the first hurdle and is the cheapest cure.

items.name: A new information architecture
items.what: One menu, each course in one place, clear paths, built after a card sort with learners.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: gives each thing one place and one name.

items.name: A continuous testing and optimisation loop
items.what: A usability test every quarter and monthly data on drop-out and support questions.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: testing as a continuous process; it shows whether the others worked.

items.name: Training authors in plain language
items.what: Workshops for the people who write the courses and the interface text.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D3: builds skills so new text stays plain, though progress is harder to show.

items.name: New functions: chat, forum and calendar
items.what: Three new features with their own menu entries.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: adds complexity, and the cost is highest.

items.name: A help centre and a manual
items.what: A place that explains how to use the platform.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: explains the complexity instead of reducing it.

items.name: Cut half of the content
items.what: Remove every second lesson.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: removes necessary content, the over-simplification risk.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: the first hurdle is language, and plain language is the cheapest cure and reaches every learner. Comprehensibility leads to usage and usage to success: with the words fixed, D2 gives each thing one place and one name, and D3 shows with tests and data whether it worked and what to fix next. The three cost €130,000 of the €170,000.

guide.example: At LearnLoop plain language goes first: it is the cheapest cure and every learner meets it. Structure and testing only make sense once the words can be understood.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: comprehensibility → usage → success. A different first measure defends if the reason names what it does for understanding (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says what it does for understanding.
Says why the others can wait.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D2, D3 (€130,000 of €170,000, longest 14 weeks). D1 first because comprehensibility leads to usage and success. D3, D1, D2 also defends: test first, since nobody knows where learners stop. D1, D2, D4 defends if the reason names skills. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The usability strategy for the next twelve months

14.caseExport: ClearLearn is a complex learning platform with low usage: users do not understand the content, the navigation is unclear, the drop-out rate is high, and time is short. The budget is €45,000.

memoSections.title: Risk analysis: too much against too little simplification
What I give up or postpone

14.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 plain language, M2 clear structure, M3 intuitive navigation, M4 usability tests) and cost €35,000 of the case's €45,000 (a Case assumption), longest 4 weeks of 10. The plan's rationale: comprehensibility → usage → success.

15.heading: Day 15 · Mobile learning and cross-device UX

intro.about: Today is about learners who study on a phone, on the go, with little time and many distractions. You learn what is different about mobile use, how microlearning works and where it can go wrong, how responsive design prioritises content, and how to keep the experience whole across devices. You then weigh measures on a platform that was built for the desktop.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is MobileLearn, a platform optimised for the desktop, while mobile use is rising sharply and learners drop out on their smartphones. The puzzle: with a limited budget and complex content, is the answer to shorten, to copy the desktop, or to build something separate, and how do you keep one learner's experience whole across devices?

story.question: Which of the eight facts about MobileLearn are problems of length, adaptation or continuity, which would you fix first for a learner on the move, which content belongs on a phone, and which four of nine measures fit €50,000 and ten weeks?

As the Chief Mobile Experience Officer, what is your mobile strategy, what does your microlearning concept look like, how do you keep one experience across devices, how do you test and optimise, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Design for the context of use, not for a smaller desktop
wiifm.payoff: Asking where, when and with how much attention people use something works for any app, intranet or training, not only on phones.

wiifm.skill: Cut content into units that stand alone
wiifm.payoff: One objective per unit is a rule for any short training, newsletter or help article.

wiifm.skill: Weigh a mobile measure
wiifm.payoff: User value, effort and risk give you a fair comparison when a separate app competes with a cheap fix.

wiifm.skill: Plan a mobile strategy from the context
wiifm.payoff: Starting from how people really use a product is how you decide between responsive, separate and native.

wiifm.skill: Keep one experience across devices
wiifm.payoff: Syncing progress and keeping the same names is a rule for any service that people use on more than one device.

wiifm.skill: Decide before you have the device data
wiifm.payoff: A reversible first step with a figure to watch is a habit worth having for any decision under uncertainty.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Find the problems, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight facts about MobileLearn by the kind of problem, say which you would fix first for a learner on the move and which content belongs on a phone, then choose four of nine measures within €50,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 15 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application

brief1.heading: The case: MobileLearn, a platform with poor mobile usage
brief1.paragraph: MobileLearn is a learning platform that was optimised for the desktop. Mobile use is rising sharply, and the drop-out rate on smartphones is high. A first analysis points to content that is too long and to no adaptation for the phone. The content is complex and the budget is limited. You are part of the UX team and asked to work out what goes wrong for a learner on the move, and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four MobileLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €50,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 10 weeks (Case assumption: the plan gives none)
Complex content, and rising mobile use.

brief1.assumption: The brief says: a platform optimised for the desktop, mobile use rising sharply, a high drop-out rate on smartphones, content too long, no mobile adaptation, complex content and a limited budget. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the numbers on them, the €50,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight facts by the kind of problem, say which you would fix first for a learner on the move and which content belongs on a phone (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

cats.label: Length: too much for one short session
cats.hint: Does it ask for more time or attention than a session on the move allows?
cats.test: Could a learner finish the unit in the few minutes they have, and leave without losing the work? Long videos, long texts and all-or-nothing quizzes belong here.

cats.label: Adaptation: not made for a phone
cats.hint: Is the layout or the media not fitted to a small screen or the setting?
cats.test: Would it work on a small screen, one-handed, in a noisy or quiet place? A shrunk desktop menu, tables that scroll sideways and video with no captions belong here.

cats.label: Continuity: breaks between devices
cats.hint: Does the learner lose their place or progress when they change device?
cats.test: When a learner moves from phone to laptop, does the platform know where they were? Progress that does not sync and a lost place belong here.

facts.text: A lesson is one 40-minute video with no pause points.
facts.short: One 40-minute video, no pause points
facts.clue: Could a learner on a short break finish this, or stop and return?
facts.why: It cannot be used in a few minutes: a length problem.

facts.text: A text page has 1,800 words, and a phone shows about 150 words at a time.
facts.short: An 1,800-word page; the phone shows 150 at a time
facts.clue: How many screens must a learner scroll, and do they know where they are?
facts.why: A text far too long for one sitting: a length problem.

facts.text: The desktop menu is shrunk onto the phone, and its links are 16 px apart.
facts.short: A shrunk desktop menu with links 16 px apart
facts.clue: Can a thumb hit the right link on a moving train?
facts.why: The layout was not made for a thumb: an adaptation problem.

facts.text: A table with nine columns must be scrolled sideways.
facts.short: A nine-column table that scrolls sideways
facts.clue: Can a learner read a whole row at once?
facts.why: Content was not reduced for a small screen: an adaptation problem.

facts.text: Progress made on the phone does not appear on the laptop.
facts.short: Phone progress is missing on the laptop
facts.key: does not appear on the laptop
facts.clue: Would a learner trust the progress bar after switching?
facts.why: Progress is not synchronised: a continuity problem.

facts.text: On the laptop the learner must find the lesson again, starting at the home page.
facts.short: On the laptop the learner searches again from the home page
facts.clue: Does the platform remember where the learner stopped?
facts.why: The place is lost between devices: a continuity problem.

facts.text: A quiz has twelve questions that must be finished in one go; leaving loses every answer.
facts.short: A twelve-question quiz that loses all answers on leaving
facts.clue: What happens when the train arrives at question seven?
facts.why: It demands one long sitting: a length problem.

facts.text: The videos have no captions, and the sound is needed to follow them.
facts.short: Videos with no captions, sound needed
facts.clue: What does a learner do in a quiet carriage with no headphones?
facts.why: It ignores the setting where phones are used: an adaptation problem.

15.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto the kind of problem it is, or select it and then a heading. Select a placed one to move it again. One heading per fact: Length, Adaptation or Continuity.
15.sortKeyTitle: Eight problems into Length, Adaptation, Continuity
15.sortTeaching: The sort is objective in its core: a 40-minute video, an 1,800-word page and a twelve-question quiz that must be finished in one go are length; a shrunk menu, a nine-column table and videos with no captions are adaptation; progress that does not sync and a lost place are continuity. Fact 7 could also be argued as continuity because answers are lost; the test is whether the session is too long for the situation. A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. Which problem to fix first, the content for a phone and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, what problems arise, what users expect, which content makes sense.
15.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A1 and A2

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight problems: which kind, which first, and what belongs on a phone
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight facts and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · which problems arise for a learner on the move, what the user expects, which content makes sense.

fields.label: Which problem would you fix first for a learner on a crowded train?
fields.help: Choose one. Think of someone with five minutes and one hand free. The reason below says why that one comes first.
fields.missing: choose the problem to fix first for a learner on the move

options.label: 1 · One 40-minute video, no pause points
options.why: Reference choice: it cannot be used in a few minutes at all, so the learner leaves before learning anything.

options.label: 2 · An 1,800-word text page
options.why: Defends: far too long for a phone, though a learner can scroll and stop.

options.label: 3 · A shrunk desktop menu
options.why: Defends: hard to hit with a thumb on a moving train.

options.label: 4 · A nine-column table
options.why: Slows: affects only the lessons with a table.

options.label: 5 · Progress missing on the laptop
options.why: Later: noticed only when the device changes.

options.label: 6 · Searching again on the laptop
options.why: Later: noticed only when the device changes.

options.label: 7 · A twelve-question quiz that loses answers
options.why: Defends: it punishes leaving, which a commuter must do.

options.label: 8 · Videos with no captions
options.why: Defends: unusable in a quiet carriage, though readable text remains.

fields.model: f1
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The problem to fix first
fields.teaching: Elements 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 all defend; 4, 5 and 6 come later. Element 1 is the reference because a learner with five minutes cannot use a 40-minute video at all. Look at the reason: it should say why this comes first for someone on the move. The plan's goal is to develop an understanding of the context of use.

fields.label: Why does it come first, and what does a learner on the move expect?
fields.help: Say why it comes before the others for someone with little time, and name what such a learner expects (speed, simplicity, clarity). At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why that problem comes first and what a learner on the move expects
fields.model: A 40-minute video comes first because a learner on the move has a few minutes, so nothing in the lesson is usable. Such a learner expects speed, simplicity and clarity: something short that works at once, that can be stopped and picked up later, and that makes sense with one hand and many distractions.

guide.example: At LearnLoop a one-hour webinar recording would come first: a commuter has ten minutes, so none of it can be used. They expect something short that works at once and that remembers where they stopped.
guide.why: The reason must say why this problem comes before the others for a learner with little time, and name what such a learner expects (Materi A1).
lookFor: Says why it comes before the others.
Names what a learner on the move expects.

clue.refValue: on the go, little time, low attention
steps: Picture a learner on a train with five minutes and ask which fact makes the platform unusable for them.
The one that blocks everything comes first.

fields.label: Which content makes sense on a phone, and which does not?
fields.help: Name at least one kind of content that belongs on the phone and one that is better on a laptop, with the reason, and the fact (by number) it answers. At least 60 characters.
fields.missing: write which content makes sense on a phone and which does not, with the reason and the fact it answers
fields.model: On the phone: short units of three to five minutes with one objective (fact 1), a quick quiz of three questions that keeps its answers (fact 7), and videos with captions (fact 8). Better on a laptop: the nine-column table and long reading with notes (facts 2 and 4), and the project work with a file upload, because they need a large screen and a long sitting.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, a three-minute tip and a short check question belong on the phone. A long case study with a spreadsheet is better on a laptop, because it needs a big screen and time.
guide.why: The plan asks which content makes sense. A good answer separates what fits a short session on a small screen from what needs a large screen and a long sitting (Materi A1, A2).
lookFor: Names content for the phone and content for the laptop.
Gives the reason.
Names the fact each answers.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · Deciding on a mobile UX strategy: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to optimise a learning platform. Mobile use is increasing, the budget is limited and the content is complex (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A shortens the content significantly for mobile (microlearning), option B adopts the desktop version as it is, and option C develops a separate mobile UX.

criteria.label: User value
criteria.help: How much it helps a learner on the move, and how many such learners it reaches.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example that knowledge is fragmented or two products must be kept up.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your choice: develop a mobile strategy
opts.whyHelp: Say what each option gives a learner on the move and what it costs, given the complex content and the limited budget. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Shorten the content significantly for mobile (microlearning)
options.keyWhy: It fits the context of use: short sessions, one objective each; the risk is fragmentation of knowledge.

options.name: Adopt the desktop version as it is
options.keyWhy: Cheapest, but it ignores the context of use and the problem stays.

options.name: Develop a separate mobile UX
options.keyWhy: It can fit the phone well, but doubles the upkeep and strains the limited budget.

model.why: I put A first: mobile use is rising and learners have only a few minutes, so short units fit the context of use, at €15,000 and five weeks. The risk is that knowledge is cut into pieces, which I would manage by giving each unit one objective. C comes second: it could fit well but costs €42,000 and doubles the upkeep. B comes last: it is cheap but ignores the context, so the drop-out stays.

guide.example: For LearnLoop with rising phone use I would shorten first: learners have minutes, not hours. Copying the desktop comes last, because it is cheap but changes nothing.
guide.why: The plan's goal is to develop a mobile strategy. A different first choice defends if the reason names the context of use and the budget.
lookFor: Says what each option gives a learner on the move.
Names the context of use or the budget.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Three options for a mobile UX strategy
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €8,000 Low, €8,000 to €16,000 Mid, above €16,000 High), so the check can flag it; user value and risk are judgements. Mobile is not a smaller desktop: the context of use decides. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: mobile UX means understanding the context
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: mobile is not a “smaller desktop”; the context of use determines the design; microlearning answers limited attention; cross-device is a strategic advantage.

questions.q: When does the user use which device?
Which content belongs on mobile, and which does not?
Where do breaks in the user experience occur?

model.a: The phone on the way and in short breaks, the laptop at a desk for long work and writing.
model.b: Short units, quick checks and reminders belong on mobile; long reading, big tables and projects with files do not.
model.c: When the device changes: progress that does not sync, a lost place, and different names or menus on each device.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: mobile is not a smaller desktop; the context of use determines the design; microlearning answers limited attention; cross-device is a strategic advantage. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four central problems
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight facts of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A problem is something that makes learners drop out on a smartphone, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it explains why learners drop out on phones, or is only a matter of discipline or of desktop features.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at a fact by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: The wrong context of use was taken into account: the platform was designed for a desk and is used on the go.
items.why: The case: optimised for desktop, mobile use rising; the plan's main problem.

items.text: The content is too long for short sessions: a 40-minute video, an 1,800-word page, a quiz that must be finished in one go.
items.why: Facts 1, 2 and 7 and the case: content too long.

items.text: There is no mobile adaptation: a shrunk desktop menu, sideways tables and videos with no captions.
items.why: Facts 3, 4 and 8 and the case: no mobile adaptation.

items.text: The experience breaks between devices: progress and the learner's place are not carried over.
items.why: Facts 5 and 6: a continuity break.

items.text: A phone screen is too small for learning at all.
items.why: The facts show missing adaptation, not a limit of the phone.

items.text: Learners lack the discipline to study on a phone.
items.why: It blames the learner; the facts show problems in the platform.

items.text: The desktop version has too few features.
items.why: A desktop matter; the case is about phones.

causes.whyModel: Fact 1: a lesson is one 40-minute video with no pause points, which shows that the platform was built for a long sitting at a desk, not for a learner on the move.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “The wrong context was taken into account” rests on one printed fact, that lessons are hour-long webinars. They were made for people with an hour at a desk.
guide.why: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the wrong context of use as the main problem.
lookFor: Points at a fact by number or quotes the case.
Says why it explains the drop-out.

causes.teaching: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names content that is too long and no mobile adaptation; the Musterlösung names the wrong context of use as the main problem. The rejected options include the tempting “the phone screen is too small”, which blames the device instead of the design; none of them explains why learners drop out on phones.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four UX measures, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which fact it answers (by number), what the learner notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the plan's rationale, context, then design, then usage: say how your first measure fits the context of use. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example that knowledge is cut into pieces or progress goes wrong.

impact.label: User value
impact.help: How much it helps a learner on the move.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: microlearning units, mobile optimisation, simplified navigation, progress synchronisation; rationale context → design → usage. The reference set costs €49,000 of €50,000 and takes at most 5 weeks of 10. M5 (a test on learners' own phones) defends in place of M3 if the reason names evidence. Reference order: M1, M2, M3, M4; M1 first because microlearning answers the context of use.

measures.name: Microlearning units
measures.what: Split the 20 most-used lessons into units of three to five minutes, each with one objective and a short check.
measures.notice: A learner can finish a unit in a short break.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1, 2 and 7: the content fits a short session.

measures.name: Mobile optimisation
measures.what: A phone-first layout with large targets, text that fits the screen, tables that become cards, and captions on videos.
measures.notice: The pages work with one thumb.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 3, 4 and 8: the layout and media fit a phone.

measures.name: Simplified navigation
measures.what: A “continue” card on the home page and a bottom bar of three entries.
measures.notice: The next step is one tap away.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 3 and the little time a learner has.

measures.name: Progress synchronisation across devices
measures.what: Progress, bookmarks and the place where a learner stopped are saved to the account and shown on every device.
measures.notice: The learner picks up where they stopped, on any device.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 5 and 6: the experience stays whole across devices.

measures.name: A mobile usability test on learners' own phones
measures.what: Eight learners do three tasks on their own phones, some of them on the move, while someone watches.
measures.notice: The team sees the real context.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: it gives evidence about the context of use at low cost. A learner who picks it instead of M3 should name evidence.

measures.name: A separate native phone app
measures.what: An app for iOS and Android, built apart from the website.
measures.notice: There are two products.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: effort High, doubles the upkeep and strains the limited budget.

measures.name: A push reminder every day
measures.what: A message to every learner's phone each evening.
measures.notice: A message arrives each evening.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: adds interruptions to a context that already has many; it does not fix the content.

measures.name: Shrink the text so the page fits
measures.what: Smaller type on phones so that the desktop page fits the screen.
measures.notice: The text becomes very small.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: shrinking is not adapting; the text becomes hard to read.

measures.name: Rewrite everything for the phone and drop the desktop layout
measures.what: All content is reworked for phones only.
measures.notice: Desktop learners lose their layout.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: effort High, and it breaks the experience for desktop learners.

reasons.m1: It answers facts 1, 2 and 7: units of three to five minutes with one objective and a short check. €14,000 lies between €8,000 and €16,000, so effort is Mid. User value High: a learner can finish a unit in a break. Risk Mid, because knowledge can be cut into pieces that do not add up.
reasons.m2: It answers facts 3, 4 and 8: a phone-first layout with large targets, tables as cards and captions. €16,000 is at the top of the Mid band, so effort is Mid. User value High: the pages work with one thumb. Risk Low.
reasons.m3: It answers fact 3 and the little time a learner has: a “continue” card and three entries at the bottom. €9,000, so effort is Mid. User value Mid: the next step is one tap away. Risk Low.
reasons.m4: It answers facts 5 and 6: progress and the place where a learner stopped are shown on every device. €10,000, so effort is Mid. User value Mid: it keeps the experience whole. Risk Mid, because a sync error can show wrong progress.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: the main problem is the wrong context of use, and microlearning answers it directly, because learners on the move have minutes and not an hour. Context leads to design and design to usage: with short units in place, M2 makes them work on a phone, M3 makes the next step one tap away, and M4 keeps the experience whole when the device changes. The four measures cost €49,000 of €50,000, with the longest at five weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know how many learners actually study on a phone and when, because the platform has not separated its data by device. I would split the drop-out data by device and test with eight learners on their own phones, before I spend the last €1,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, three-minute units for the ten most-used lessons cost €12,000, so effort is Mid. They answer hour-long webinars, so user value is High. Risk is Mid: the units must still add up to the course.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). User value and risk are judgements: they must name the fact the measure answers, what the learner notices, and what could go wrong (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed fact the measure answers.
Says what the learner notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop short units go first: learners on the move have minutes, so everything else depends on content that fits. Context leads to design, and design to usage.
order.why: The plan's rationale: context → design → usage. A different first priority defends if the reason says how it fits the context of use and why it can go first.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Says how it fits the context of use.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know how many learners use a phone. I would split the usage data by device and test with a few learners on their own phones before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

brief2.heading: The situation: MobileLearn's Chief Mobile Experience Officer
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief Mobile Experience Officer of MobileLearn. Mobile use is growing strongly, the platform is not optimised for it, and competitors are better on mobile. Management wants a strategy for the next 12 months and expects you to decide how mobile and desktop work together, what microlearning looks like, how to test and optimise, and to take responsibility for the cross-platform UX.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €190,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Data: the platform has not separated its data by device, so you do not know exactly how learners use the phone.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: mobile use is growing strongly, the platform is not optimised, competitors are better on mobile. Everything else is made up: the €190,000, the concept cards, the placement board, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the mobile strategy, the microlearning concept, the cross-device approach and the testing strategy (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk analysis, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · The mobile strategy, microlearning, cross-device and testing
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the strategy below, the list of concept elements, the placement board and the fields. Answer in the lists, the board and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 4 · a mobile learning strategy, a microlearning concept, a cross-device UX approach, a testing and optimisation strategy.

fields.label: The mobile learning strategy
fields.help: Choose the approach you will take to management. A decision with a clear reason counts, whichever you choose.
fields.missing: choose a mobile learning strategy

options.label: One platform, designed from the phone context first: short units on the phone, depth on the desktop, one account
options.why: Reference strategy: starts from the context of use and keeps the experience whole.

options.label: Keep the desktop platform and add a small, separate mobile site
options.why: Weak: two products to keep up, and the experience breaks between them.

options.label: Build native apps for iOS and Android
options.why: Defends if the reason names a need that a website cannot meet (offline, notifications); expensive and slow.

options.label: Study first: split the data by device and watch learners before deciding
options.why: Defends: a decision with an evidence step; slower, but cheap.

fields.model: g1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The mobile learning strategy
fields.teaching: The plan asks for a mobile learning strategy. Strategy 1 is the reference; strategy 4 also defends (study first); strategy 3 defends only with a named need; strategy 2 is the weakest because it splits the experience. A decision with a clear reason exports whichever is chosen (CLAUDE.md #38). Plan: item 1.

fields.label: Why this strategy, and not the others?
fields.help: Give the reason in terms of the context of use, the budget and the learner's experience across devices. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why you chose that strategy and not the others
fields.model: I design one platform from the phone context first: mobile use is growing and learners have minutes, so short units belong on the phone, and the depth stays on the desktop. One account keeps progress whole across devices. A separate site or two apps would double the upkeep on a limited budget and break the experience between the products.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would keep one platform and design the short units for the phone first, with one account for all devices. A separate app would double the work and split the experience.
guide.why: The reason must rest on the context of use, the budget and the experience across devices (Materi B1).
lookFor: Gives a reason about the context of use.
Names the budget or the upkeep.
Mentions the experience across devices.

fields.label: The microlearning concept: choose at least three rules
fields.help: A unit is good when it can be finished in a short break, serves one objective, and still fits the whole course.
fields.missing: choose at least three microlearning rules

options.label: Each unit has exactly one learning objective
options.why: Focus: the learner knows what the unit is for.

options.label: A unit takes three to seven minutes
options.why: Fits a short break.

options.label: Each unit works alone but shows its place in the course
options.why: Answers the risk of fragmentation.

options.label: A short check at the end of each unit
options.why: Shows the learner what they took away.

options.label: A “continue” card that remembers where the learner stopped
options.why: Makes returning easy.

options.label: Cut long lessons into five-minute pieces at arbitrary points
options.why: Rejected: pieces with no objective do not teach.

options.label: Units that only work if the previous unit is open
options.why: Rejected: a unit must stand alone.

options.label: One-hour videos with chapter markers
options.why: Rejected: still a long sitting.

options.label: A forced daily streak
options.why: Rejected: pressure, not microlearning (Day 11).

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The microlearning rules
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference rules defend if each makes a unit finishable in a break and keeps it tied to an objective and to the course. The rejected ones cut without an objective, create dependencies or keep the long sitting. Plan: item 2, microlearning concept.

fields.label: The cross-device approach: place eight pieces of the experience
fields.help: Place each piece where it belongs, or under “not needed” if it should not exist.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight pieces

items.label: A three-minute unit with one objective
items.why: Made for short sessions.

items.label: Long reading with notes in the margin
items.why: Needs a large screen and a long sitting.

items.label: Progress and bookmarks
items.why: Must be identical on every device.

items.label: A quick quiz of three questions
items.why: Fits a short break.

items.label: A project with a file upload and a long form
items.why: Needs a keyboard and time; open item: a phone can start it.

items.label: The same login and the same lesson names
items.why: Consistency across devices.

items.label: A sidebar with twenty links
items.why: Complexity on every device.

items.label: A separate phone-only course catalogue
items.why: A second product that splits the experience.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The cross-device placement
fields.teaching: There is no single right grid. Item 5 is the open one (desktop first, or the same on both with a phone start). Items 7 and 8 are not needed. Each bin must be used at least once. A good approach sets what is phone first, desktop first and identical everywhere. Plan: item 3, cross-device UX approach.

fields.label: How will you test and keep optimising on real phones?
fields.help: Name one test with learners on their own phones, one figure you will watch by device, and how often you repeat it. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: describe how you will test and keep optimising on real phones
fields.model: Each quarter I test with eight learners on their own phones, some of them on the move, doing three tasks while someone watches. Each month I watch drop-out split by device, and I adjust the units that lose the most learners, then repeat.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would watch five learners do a task on their own phones every quarter, and look each month at how many leave a unit on phones against laptops.
guide.why: The plan asks for a testing and optimisation strategy: tests on real phones, a figure by device, and a loop (Materi A3, B1).
lookFor: Names a test on real phones.
Names a figure by device.
Says how often it repeats.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, item 5 and the additional requirement · prioritised measures and a risk analysis, a decision under uncertainty.

fields.label: Risk analysis: what can go wrong with a mobile strategy
fields.help: Imagine the strategy has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the strategy fails

options.label: Fragmentation: the short units did not add up, and learners gained pieces of knowledge, not understanding.
options.why: The fragmentation pole. Action: every unit names its place in the course, with an end-of-course check; notice it in results on the final task.

options.label: The two experiences drifted apart: phone and desktop got different names, menus and progress.
options.why: Action: one component set and one owner; notice it in learners who switch and then leave.

options.label: We designed for an imagined context, not the real one, because we never watched learners on the move.
options.why: Action: test on real phones in real settings; notice it in tasks that fail.

options.label: The cost grew: two products had to be kept up on a limited budget.
options.why: Action: one platform and a cap on the budget; notice it in cost per unit after the first quarter.

options.label: A sync error showed wrong progress and learners lost trust in the platform.
options.why: Action: test the sync before release; notice it in support questions about progress.

fields.model: r1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: fragmentation of knowledge
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the team would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007). The plan names the risk of fragmentation of knowledge.

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: Every unit names the course objective it serves and ends with a short check, and each course ends with a check across its units; if the final-task results of learners who used mostly phone units fall below the others' by the end of month 4, I add a summary unit.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would end each course with one check across all its units, and compare the results of phone learners with others after a quarter; if phone learners do worse, I add a summary.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without the data by device)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to split the data by device first and to build microlearning units for the twenty most-used lessons (D1) before I redesign the whole platform.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example how large the share of phone learners really is. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know how large the share of phone learners really is.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of month 3, drop-out on phones has not fallen from 50% to below 42% for the learners who use the new units, and I look at the layout before I cut more content.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to cut the ten longest lessons into short units. I do not know how many learners use a phone. I reverse if phone drop-out has not fallen from 45% to below 40% by the end of month 3.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I postpone the native apps (D5) and the daily push reminders (D7) this year. The marketing team will miss the app-store presence they wanted, and some learners who asked for reminders will have to wait.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I postpone the planned native app for a year. Marketing will miss the app-store listing, and a few learners who asked for it must wait.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say how it fits the context of use. At least 30 characters.

items.name: Microlearning restructure of the core courses
items.what: The core courses are rebuilt as units of three to seven minutes with one objective, a check and a place in the course.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: answers the context of use directly.

items.name: A phone-first responsive redesign with synchronised progress
items.what: One layout system that prioritises content by device, with progress and place carried across devices.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: makes the units work on a phone and keeps the experience whole.

items.name: Continuous mobile testing and device-level analytics
items.what: A test on real phones every quarter and monthly drop-out data split by device.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: shows whether the others work, and closes the data gap.

items.name: A diary study of when and where learners use which device
items.what: Fifteen learners note for four weeks where, when and on which device they study.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D3: it gives the real context, though it does not track change over time.

items.name: Native iOS and Android apps
items.what: Two apps, built and kept up apart from the website.
items.keyWhy: Rejected for now: the highest cost, two products to keep up, and a one-way door.

items.name: A separate mobile site with reduced content
items.what: A second site for phones with a smaller catalogue.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: two products, and the experience breaks when the device changes.

items.name: Daily push reminders
items.what: A message to every phone each evening.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: adds interruptions and does not fix the content.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: the wrong context of use is the main problem, and microlearning answers it directly, since learners on the move have minutes. Context leads to design and design to usage: with the units in place, D2 makes them work on a phone and keeps progress whole across devices, and D3 shows with tests and data by device whether it worked. The three cost €155,000 of the €190,000.

guide.example: At LearnLoop short units go first: they answer the context of use directly. The redesign and the testing only pay off once the content fits a short session.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: context → design → usage. A different first measure defends if the reason says how it fits the context of use (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says how it fits the context of use.
Says why the others can wait.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D2, D3 (€155,000 of €190,000, longest 16 weeks). D1 first because the context of use is the main problem. D3, D1, D2 also defends: measure by device first, since the data is missing. D1, D2, D4 defends if the reason names the real context. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The mobile learning strategy for the next twelve months

15.caseExport: MobileLearn is a learning platform that was optimised for the desktop. Mobile use is rising sharply and the drop-out rate on smartphones is high, because the content is too long and not adapted for the phone. The content is complex and the budget is €50,000.

memoSections.title: What I give up or postpone

15.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 microlearning units, M2 mobile optimisation, M3 simplified navigation, M4 progress synchronisation) and cost €49,000 of the case's €50,000 (a Case assumption), longest 5 weeks of 10. The plan's rationale: context → design → usage.

16.heading: Day 16 · UX testing, analytics and KPIs

intro.about: Today is about learning from data without being fooled by it. You learn how UX is tested (usability tests, A/B tests, observation, and the difference between qualitative and quantitative), what to track and what data protection asks, how to define KPIs, and how to read data: patterns, causes rather than symptoms, and the misreadings to avoid. You then weigh measures on a platform that has a lot of data and no improvement.
intro.caseLine: The case that runs through the day is DataLearn, a platform with extensive tracking data, a drop-out rate that stays high, and measures that show no effect. The puzzle: with a limited budget and time pressure, is the problem too little data, or the way the data is read, and how do you decide when the causes are unclear?

story.question: Which of the eight facts about DataLearn show a measuring, a reading or a hypothesis problem, which one jumps from a symptom to a cause, which four of nine measures fit €40,000 and ten weeks, and which three KPIs matter?

As the Chief Data & UX Officer, which KPIs are central, how do you analyse and track, which hypotheses do you test, who decides on what evidence, which three measures come first, and what do you give up?

wiifm.skill: Tell a symptom from a cause
wiifm.payoff: “Sales are down” or “drop-out is high” are symptoms in any business. Asking what could cause them before acting saves money in any department.

wiifm.skill: Define a KPI so that it can be checked
wiifm.payoff: A name, a definition and a target turn a vague number into something a team can be held to, in any report.

wiifm.skill: Weigh a data-based measure
wiifm.payoff: KPI impact, effort and risk give you a fair comparison when a showy dashboard competes with a small test for the same budget.

wiifm.skill: Write a hypothesis before you act
wiifm.payoff: “We believe … so we will … and expect …” is a sentence that makes any project reviewable.

wiifm.skill: Plan tracking that respects privacy
wiifm.payoff: Collecting only what a question needs, and saying so, is both good analysis and good data protection.

wiifm.skill: Set up who decides on what evidence
wiifm.payoff: A decision rule that names the figure and the person reduces arguments between data and intuition, in any team.

wiifm.skill: Leave with two reusable documents
wiifm.payoff: A UX Analysis File and a UX Strategy Memo. Keep them as templates for your own platform or course.

route1.title: Read the data, choose the measures
route1.blurb: Levels 1 and 2 on one case: sort eight facts about DataLearn by the kind of data problem, say which jumps from a symptom to a cause and what you would check, then choose four of nine measures within €40,000 and ten weeks, rate them, put them in order, define three KPIs and name what is missing.
route1.kicker: Day 16 · Route 1 · Levels 1 and 2 · Knowledge and application
route1.h1: UX testing and analytics: read the data, then choose the measures
route1.order: Materi A (all five cards, four are core) → the UX Analysis task, one case in two parts (read the data, choose measures), with two core blocks. Every section stays open, so you can start anywhere.
route1.materiSub: Levels 1 + 2 · UX testing, KPIs, data analysis
route1.taskSub: UX Analysis File: read the data, choose the measures

route2.blurb: Level 3 in the Chief Data & UX Officer's chair: the central KPIs, the analysis and tracking strategy, hypotheses for improvement, who decides on what evidence, three prioritised measures, a risk analysis, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up.
route2.h1: A data-driven UX optimisation strategy: the strategy, the tracking, the hypotheses, the decision architecture, the measures, and what you give up

brief1.heading: The case: DataLearn, lots of data but no improvement
brief1.paragraph: DataLearn is a learning platform with extensive tracking data. The high drop-out rate persists, and the measures taken so far show no effect. A first analysis points to a wrong interpretation of the data and to missing hypotheses. The budget is limited and time is short. You are part of the UX team and asked to work out what goes wrong in dealing with the data, and which measures are worth funding.

have.title: What you have
items: Four DataLearn screens in outline, with eight facts about them (Block 1.1).
Three options (optional Block 1.2) and seven possible problems (optional Block 2.1).
Nine measures, each with a cost and weeks (Block 2.2).

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget: €40,000 (Case assumption: the plan only says “limited”)
Time: 10 weeks (Case assumption: the plan only says “time pressure”)
A drop-out rate of 70% and short time spent (figures from the plan).

brief1.assumption: The brief says: extensive tracking data, a high drop-out rate that persists, measures with no effect, a wrong interpretation of the data, missing hypotheses, a limited budget and time pressure; the plan's figures are a 70% drop-out rate and short time spent. Everything else is made up for this exercise: the screens, the other numbers on them, the €40,000, the 10 weeks, and the costs and weeks of the measures.
brief1.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 30 min
run: Block 1.1: sort eight facts by the kind of data problem, say which jumps from a symptom to a cause and what you would check (Level 1).
Block 2.2: choose four of nine measures, rate them, order them, define three KPIs, justify and name what is missing (Level 2).
brief1.runNote: Three more blocks (about 20 min) are optional and folded.

cats.label: Measuring: what is tracked and how
cats.hint: Is the problem in what is measured, how it is defined, or how it is collected?
cats.test: Is it unclear what a number means, are there too many numbers, or is data collected in a way that is wrong or not allowed? Metrics with no definition and tracking with privacy gaps belong here.

cats.label: Reading: how the data is interpreted
cats.hint: Is a conclusion drawn that the data does not support?
cats.test: Does someone treat a symptom as a cause, or compare two periods that are not comparable? Jumping from a number to an explanation belongs here.

cats.label: Hypotheses: no testable guess
cats.hint: Are measures launched without saying what they should change and how much?
cats.test: Is there a written guess of the form “we believe … so we will … and expect …”, and can the effect of one change be told apart? Many changes at once and no expected effect belong here.

facts.text: The dashboard shows 31 metrics, and nothing marks which one matters.
facts.short: 31 metrics, none marked as the one that matters
facts.clue: Which number would a team act on first, and who decided?
facts.why: Too many numbers and no priority: a measuring problem.

facts.text: “Engagement” is the number of clicks, and nobody has written down what it should show.
facts.short: “Engagement” is clicks, with no definition
facts.clue: Does a click mean the learner understood or learned something?
facts.why: A KPI with no definition: a measuring problem.

facts.text: The report says “drop-out is 70%, so the content is too hard”, and no other cause was looked at.
facts.short: “70% drop-out, so the content is too hard”
facts.key: so the content is too hard
facts.clue: What else could make 70% of learners leave?
facts.why: A symptom taken for a cause: a reading problem.

facts.text: A chart compares this month with last month and calls the rise a success, though last month had a holiday.
facts.short: A rise called a success; last month had a holiday
facts.key: though last month had a holiday
facts.clue: Are the two months comparable?
facts.why: Two periods that are not comparable: a reading problem.

facts.text: Five measures were launched in one month, so nobody can say which one had an effect.
facts.short: Five measures in one month, no way to tell them apart
facts.key: Five measures were launched in one month
facts.clue: If drop-out falls, which change should get the credit?
facts.why: Changes cannot be told apart: a hypothesis problem.

facts.text: No measure says what it should change, or by how much.
facts.short: No measure states an expected effect
facts.clue: How would the team know whether a measure worked?
facts.why: No expected effect, so nothing to test: a hypothesis problem.

facts.text: Every click is stored with the learner's name, and the privacy notice does not mention it.
facts.short: Every click stored with a name; the privacy notice is silent
facts.clue: Would the learner expect this, and is it needed to answer a question?
facts.why: Data collected beyond need and without notice: a measuring problem.

facts.text: “Time spent” counts how long a page is open, even if the tab is left open overnight.
facts.short: “Time spent” counts a tab left open overnight
facts.clue: Does the number show attention, or only an open tab?
facts.why: A metric that does not measure what its name says: a measuring problem.

16.sortIntro: Drag a fact onto the kind of data problem it is, or select it and then a heading. Select a placed one to move it again. One heading per fact: Measuring, Reading or Hypotheses.
16.sortKeyTitle: Eight problems into Measuring, Reading, Hypotheses
16.sortTeaching: The sort is objective in its core: 31 metrics, a KPI with no definition, tracking with a name and no notice, and time spent that counts an open tab are measuring; a symptom taken for a cause and a rise compared with a holiday month are reading; five measures at once and no expected effect are hypotheses. Fact 5 could also be argued as reading (the effect cannot be read); the test is whether the problem is in how the change was set up. A learner who argues another placement with a reason defends the choice. Which fact jumps from a symptom to a cause, the checks and the reasons are judged. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, causes, suspected problems, measures.
16.testsLabel: Test questions · taught in Materi A2 and A3

b11.title: Block 1.1 · Eight problems: measuring, reading or hypotheses, and a symptom taken for a cause
b11.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the four drawn screens directly below, then the sort board with the eight facts and the fields under it. Answer on the board and in the fields.
b11.plan: Plan: Level 1, task 1 · possible causes of a 70% drop-out rate with short time spent, which problems you suspect, which measures you suggest.

fields.label: Which fact jumps from a symptom to a cause?
fields.help: Choose one. A symptom is what the data shows; a cause is why. The reason below says what else could explain it.
fields.missing: choose the fact that jumps from a symptom to a cause

options.label: 1 · 31 metrics on the dashboard
options.why: Not a jump: too many numbers, a measuring problem.

options.label: 2 · “Engagement” is clicks
options.why: Not a jump: an undefined metric, a measuring problem.

options.label: 3 · “70% drop-out, so the content is too hard”
options.why: Reference choice: a number (the symptom) is turned into an explanation (the cause) with no check.

options.label: 4 · A rise called a success, vs a holiday month
options.why: Defends: a wrong comparison; the conclusion is drawn from a number that does not mean what is claimed.

options.label: 5 · Five measures in one month
options.why: Not a jump: a set-up problem.

options.label: 6 · No measure states an expected effect
options.why: Not a jump: missing hypotheses.

options.label: 7 · Every click stored with a name
options.why: Not a jump: a data protection problem.

options.label: 8 · “Time spent” counts an open tab
options.why: Not a jump: a metric that does not measure what it says.

fields.model: f3
fields.keyTitle: Block 1.1 · The symptom taken for a cause
fields.teaching: Element 3 is the reference: it turns the symptom (70% leave) into a cause (the content is too hard) with no check. Element 4 also defends, as a misreading from a wrong comparison. Look at the reason: it should name other possible causes. The plan's goal is to develop an intuitive understanding of data.

fields.label: What else could cause a 70% drop-out rate with short time spent?
fields.help: Name at least two other possible causes (for example a long sign-up form, a slow page, learners who expected something else) and say why “too hard” was a jump. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name other possible causes and say why the first explanation was a jump
fields.model: “Too hard” is one guess among many: a long sign-up form, a slow page, a mismatch between the course title and its content, or a mobile layout could all make learners leave early, and short time spent fits all of them. The report looked at none of these, so it took a symptom for a cause.

guide.example: At LearnLoop, “sales of the course are down, so the price is too high” could also be a broken checkout, a competitor's offer or a bad review. The number shows a symptom; the price is only one guess.
guide.why: Data shows symptoms, not causes. A good answer names several possible causes and says that the first explanation was never checked (Materi A3).
lookFor: Names at least two other causes.
Says why “too hard” was a jump.

clue.refValue: what else could explain the number?
steps: Take the number and ask: what are three different reasons it could be this high?
The report looked at one; name two more.

fields.label: Which problems do you suspect, and which measures do you suggest?
fields.help: Name the kind of problem (measuring, reading, hypotheses) for the facts you suspect, and for each measure the fact (by number) it answers, starting each measure with a verb. At least 60 characters in all.
fields.missing: write which problems you suspect and which measures you suggest, naming the fact each measure answers
fields.model: Suspected: reading (facts 3 and 4), hypotheses (5 and 6) and measuring (1, 2, 7, 8). 1. Define three KPIs with a written definition and pick one to watch (facts 1 and 2). 2. Write a hypothesis for each change and launch one at a time (facts 5 and 6). 3. Watch five learners on the screens where they leave, before naming a cause (fact 3). 4. Stop storing names with clicks and update the privacy notice (fact 7).

guide.example: Suspected: reading and measuring. 1. Define what “active user” means (a metric with no definition). 2. Compare the same weekdays, not a holiday week against a normal one (a wrong comparison).
guide.why: The plan asks which problems you suspect and which measures you suggest. A good answer names the kind of problem and ties each measure to a fact (Materi A2, A3).
lookFor: Names the kinds of problem.
Names the fact each measure answers.
Starts each measure with a verb.

opts.title: Block 1.2 · A KPI-based decision: three options
opts.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the three options below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Rate each one, put them in order, and justify your decision.
opts.intro: You are to optimise a platform. The drop-out rate is high, the budget is limited and there is time pressure (Case assumption: the costs). Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5. Option A improves the UX (navigation and structure), option B expands the content, and option C increases the marketing.

criteria.label: KPI impact
criteria.help: How much it would move the drop-out rate or the completion rate.

criteria.label: Effort
criteria.help: By the printed cost, with the rule in Materi A5.

criteria.label: Risk
criteria.help: What could go wrong, for example that it does not reach the cause of the drop-out.

opts.orderHelp: The first is the one you would do first. Move one up or down with the arrows.
opts.whyLabel: Justify your decision: develop a data-based prioritisation
