opts.whyHelp: Say what each option would do to the drop-out rate and what it costs, given the limited budget and the time pressure. At least 30 characters.

options.name: Improve the UX (navigation and structure)
options.keyWhy: It goes to a likely cause of the drop-out; moderate cost, and it can be tested.

options.name: Expand the content
options.keyWhy: More content does not address why learners leave; high effort.

options.name: Increase the marketing
options.keyWhy: More learners arrive into the same drop-out; it raises the number of leavers, not the completion rate.

model.why: I put A first: the drop-out is the problem, and the structure and navigation are likely causes that can be tested, at €13,000 and four weeks. B comes second: more content does not touch why learners leave, but it does little harm. C comes last: more marketing sends more learners into the same drop-out, so the KPI I care about does not improve and the cost is high.

guide.example: For LearnLoop with many early leavers I would fix the sign-up and course page first, because that goes to where learners leave. More advertising comes last: it would bring more people to a door that most walk out of.
guide.why: The plan's goal is to develop a data-based prioritisation. A different first choice defends if the reason names the KPI it would move and the limited budget.
lookFor: Says what each option does to the KPI.
Names the limited budget or the time pressure.

opts.keyTitle: Block 1.2 · Three options for a KPI-based decision
opts.keyTeaching: Effort follows the printed cost by the rule in Materi A5 (under €7,000 Low, €7,000 to €14,000 Mid, above €14,000 High), so the check can flag it; KPI impact and risk are judgements. Data-based prioritisation: ask which KPI each option would move. A different, well-reasoned order exports (CLAUDE.md #38).
opts.reason: Practises the three ratings at small scale; Block 2.2 is answered without it.

reflect.title: Block 1.3 · Coaching reflection: using data correctly
reflect.point: The coaching point of the plan: data shows symptoms, not causes; data and UX understanding are needed together; there is a danger of misinterpretation; data is a basis for decisions, not a substitute for thinking.

questions.q: Which data is really relevant?
Where are we interpreting incorrectly?
Which decision is based on assumptions?

model.a: The few figures that tie to a question: first-week drop-out, completion and where learners leave, not all 31 metrics.
model.b: Where a symptom is called a cause (“too hard”) and where two periods are compared that are not alike.
model.c: The decision to expand content or buy more advertising, which assumes that content or reach is the problem.

reflect.guideWhy: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: data shows symptoms, not causes; data and UX understanding together; the danger of misinterpretation; data as a basis for decisions, not a substitute for thinking. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.
reflect.reason: A reflective bridge between the two levels; your notes appear in the file, and no Core block needs them.

causes.title: Block 2.1 · Four problems in dealing with data
causes.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the case brief above and the eight facts of Block 1.1. Choose four of the seven problems below, then say which printed fact supports your first one.
causes.pickHelp: A problem is something in how the team handles data that keeps the drop-out from falling, and you can point at it in the case or in a fact.
causes.clue: For each problem, find a printed fact that supports it. Ask also whether it explains why measures show no effect, or is only a matter of how much data there is.
causes.whyLabel: Which printed fact supports your first problem?
causes.whyHelp: Quote a line of the case or point at a fact by its number. At least 30 characters.

items.text: The data is interpreted wrongly: a symptom is taken for a cause, and unlike periods are compared.
items.why: Facts 3 and 4 and the case: a wrong interpretation of the data.

items.text: There are no hypotheses: changes are made without saying what they should change.
items.why: Facts 5 and 6 and the case: missing hypotheses.

items.text: The KPIs are unclear: too many metrics, and some with no definition or a misleading one.
items.why: Facts 1, 2 and 8.

items.text: Measures cannot be told apart: several are launched at once, so the effect of each is lost.
items.why: Fact 5 and the case: measures show no effect.

items.text: There is not enough tracking data.
items.why: The case says that extensive data is available; more data would not fix how it is read.

items.text: The analytics tool is the wrong brand.
items.why: A tool matter; the facts point at how data is defined and read.

items.text: Learners are simply not interested in the content.
items.why: That is a cause that was assumed and never tested, which is the problem itself.

causes.whyModel: Fact 3: the report says “drop-out is 70%, so the content is too hard” and looked at no other cause, which is a symptom taken for a cause.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “No hypotheses” rests on one printed fact, that a redesign was launched with no stated goal. Nobody can say whether it worked.
guide.why: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's Musterlösung names the lack of analytical competence as the main problem.
lookFor: Points at a fact by number or quotes the case.
Says why it explains the lack of effect.

causes.keyTitle: Block 2.1 · Four problems in dealing with data
causes.teaching: A problem is defended by a printed fact. The plan's analysis names a wrong interpretation of the data and missing hypotheses; the Musterlösung names the lack of analytical competence as the main problem. The rejected options include the tempting “not enough tracking data”, which contradicts the case; none of them explains why measures show no effect.
causes.reason: Practises pointing at a printed fact for a problem; Block 2.2 reads the facts, not this block.

b22.title: Block 2.2 · Four optimisation measures, three KPIs, rated, ordered and justified
b22.findIt: Route 1 → Task 1 → the nine measures in the list directly below, each with its printed cost and weeks. Answer in the list, the rating rows and the fields under them.
b22.evidenceNote: The facts of Block 1.1 and the case brief are your evidence. Effort follows the printed cost, by the rule in Materi A5.
b22.reasonHelp: Which fact it answers (by number), what the team notices, and what could go wrong. At least 20 characters.
b22.orderWhyHelp: Use the plan's rationale, data, then insight, then decision: say how your first measure turns data into an insight. At least 30 characters.
b22.riskHelp: What could go wrong, for example that the team reads the data wrongly again.

impact.label: KPI impact
impact.help: How much it would move the drop-out rate or the completion rate, or the team's ability to do so.

b22.keyTitle: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
b22.keyTeaching: The plan's Musterlösung: clear KPI definition, a hypothesis-based approach, targeted UX tests, iterative optimisation; rationale data → insight → decision. The reference set costs €37,000 of €40,000 and takes at most 5 weeks of 10. M5 (a cohort analysis of drop-out) defends in place of M4 if the reason names evidence. Reference order: M1, M2, M3, M4; M1 first because without a KPI nothing else can be judged.

measures.name: Clear KPI definition
measures.what: Choose three KPIs, write a definition and a target for each, and show only those on the main dashboard.
measures.notice: The team looks at three numbers it understands.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 1, 2 and 8: too many and undefined metrics.

measures.name: A hypothesis-based approach
measures.what: Every change gets a written hypothesis (“we believe … so we will … and expect …”), reviewed weekly.
measures.notice: Each change says what it should do.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers facts 5 and 6: no expected effect, so nothing to test.

measures.name: Targeted UX tests
measures.what: Five usability tests on the screens where most learners leave, and an A/B test of one change.
measures.notice: The team sees why learners leave.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 3: it finds causes instead of guessing.

measures.name: Iterative optimisation
measures.what: Two-week cycles with one change each, a review of the KPI, and a decision to keep, change or drop.
measures.notice: One change at a time, each judged.
measures.keyWhy: Reference measure. Answers fact 5: changes can be told apart.

measures.name: A cohort analysis of drop-out
measures.what: Drop-out by week of sign-up, device and course, to see where it concentrates.
measures.notice: The team sees where drop-out concentrates.
measures.keyWhy: Defends: gives evidence from the data already held, at low cost. A learner who picks it instead of M4 should name evidence.

measures.name: Track forty more events
measures.what: Forty new click and scroll events are added to the tracking.
measures.notice: More numbers appear in the tool.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: more data is not insight; it adds to the 31 metrics and to the privacy burden.

measures.name: A real-time dashboard with forty charts
measures.what: A wall screen showing every metric live.
measures.notice: A large screen of moving charts.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: more charts, not more insight; effort High.

measures.name: An AI tool that finds insights automatically
measures.what: A tool that scans the data and reports patterns.
measures.notice: Reports of patterns arrive.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: patterns without hypotheses repeat the misreading; effort High.

measures.name: Launch all five ideas at once
measures.what: A redesign, new content, new emails, a new menu and a new price in one month.
measures.notice: Everything changes together.
measures.keyWhy: Rejected: effort High, and the effect of each cannot be told apart.

reasons.m1: It answers facts 1, 2 and 8: three KPIs with a definition and a target each. At €6,000 it is under €7,000, so effort is Low. KPI impact High: without a KPI nothing else can be judged. Risk Low.
reasons.m2: It answers facts 5 and 6: every change gets a written hypothesis. €8,000 lies between €7,000 and €14,000, so effort is Mid. KPI impact High: it makes the effect of each change testable. Risk Low.
reasons.m3: It answers fact 3: five usability tests where learners leave, and an A/B test. €14,000 is at the top of the Mid band, so effort is Mid. KPI impact Mid: it finds causes, but only for the screens tested. Risk Mid, because five learners show the main hurdles, not every one.
reasons.m4: It answers fact 5: two-week cycles, one change each. €9,000, so effort is Mid. KPI impact Mid: changes can be told apart and kept or dropped. Risk Low.

model.orderWhy: M1 goes first: without a defined KPI nothing else can be judged, and the platform shows 31 metrics with no priority. Data leads to insight and insight to a decision: with the KPIs fixed, M2 gives each change a hypothesis, M3 finds the causes by watching learners, and M4 changes one thing at a time so that the effect shows. The four measures cost €37,000 of €40,000, with the longest at five weeks.
model.missingInfo: I do not know on which screens and for which learners the drop-out concentrates, because nobody has split it by sign-up week, device and course. I would run a cohort analysis and watch five learners on the worst screen before I spend the last €3,000.

reason.example: At LearnLoop, writing a hypothesis for each change costs €7,000, so effort is Mid. It answers changes launched with no goal, so KPI impact is High. Risk is Low: it only adds a sentence per change.
reason.why: Effort follows the printed cost (a rule). KPI impact and risk are judgements: they must name the fact the measure answers, what the team notices, and what could go wrong (Materi A5).
lookFor: Names the printed fact the measure answers.
Says what the team notices.
Says what could go wrong, or why risk is low.
Does not contradict the printed cost.

order.example: At LearnLoop defining the KPI goes first: without it, nobody can tell whether any change worked. Data leads to insight, and insight to a decision.
order.why: The plan's rationale: data → insight → decision. A different first priority defends if the reason says how it turns data into an insight and why it can go first.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Says how it turns data into an insight.

missing.example: At LearnLoop I do not know on which page most learners leave. I would split drop-out by page and watch five learners on the worst one before I spend the rest of the budget.
missing.why: The plan's wording is “what information is missing”. A good answer is specific and says how to find it out.
lookFor: Names something specific.
Says how to find it out.

b22.afterNote: The plan also asks for three relevant KPIs. Choose exactly three, the ones that would show you whether learners now finish and stay.

after.label: Define three relevant KPIs
after.help: A good KPI is defined, ties to learner behaviour, and shows an outcome. Choose exactly 3.

options.label: Completion rate: the share of learners who finish a course
options.why: A behaviour that shows an outcome.

options.label: First-week drop-out rate: the share who leave within seven days of signing up
options.why: The plan's own problem, with a clear time frame.

options.label: Seven-day return rate: the share who come back within a week
options.why: Engagement, defined as a return, not as clicks.

options.label: Time per session, split into finished and abandoned sessions
options.why: Defends: time spent, but read together with the outcome.

options.label: Total page views
options.why: Rejected: shows use, not outcome.

options.label: Total registered users
options.why: Rejected: a vanity metric; it only rises.

options.label: The number of dashboards built
options.why: Rejected: measures the team's activity, not the learners'.

after.teaching: Exactly three. The three reference KPIs are completion, first-week drop-out and seven-day return; time per session split by outcome (k4) also defends in place of one of them. The rejected ones show use, only rise, or measure the team. Plan: Level 2, define three relevant KPIs.

brief2.heading: The situation: DataLearn's Chief Data & UX Officer
brief2.paragraph: You are the Chief Data & UX Officer of DataLearn. The platform's performance is declining, a lot of data is available, and the causes are unclear. Management wants a strategy for the next 12 months and expects you to decide which KPIs matter, how to analyse and track, which hypotheses to test, who decides on what evidence, and to take responsibility at management level.

limits.title: The limits
items: Budget for the year: €160,000 (Case assumption: the plan gives none)
The causes of the decline are unclear.
You must decide anyway.

brief2.assumption: The brief says: a platform with declining performance, a lot of data available, unclear causes. Everything else is made up: the €160,000, the tracking rules, the hypothesis grid, and the seven decisions with their costs and weeks.
brief2.runTitle: How the task runs · two core blocks, about 20 min
run: Block 3.1: the data-driven strategy, the analysis and tracking rules, the hypotheses and who decides (draws on B1, B2).
Block 3.2: three prioritised measures, the risk analysis, one decision under uncertainty, and what you give up (draws on B2, B3).

b31.title: Block 3.1 · The strategy, the tracking, the hypotheses and the decision architecture
b31.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the strategy below, the list of tracking rules, the hypothesis board and the fields. Answer in the lists, the board and the text boxes.
b31.plan: Plan: transfer project, items 1 to 3 and 5 · central KPIs, an analysis and tracking strategy, hypotheses for improvement, a decision architecture for data-driven UX.

fields.label: The data-driven strategy
fields.help: Choose the approach you will take to management. A decision with a clear reason counts, whichever you choose.
fields.missing: choose a data-driven strategy

options.label: Hypothesis first: three KPIs, written hypotheses, one change at a time, and tracking only what the hypotheses need
options.why: Reference strategy: turns data into insight and insight into a decision, and respects privacy.

options.label: Track everything and look for patterns
options.why: Weak: more data without questions repeats the misreading, and tracking everything is a privacy risk.

options.label: Decide on intuition, because the data is too noisy
options.why: Weak: gives up the measurable system; the plan wants data as a basis for decisions.

options.label: Audit first: check what the data really measures, then decide
options.why: Defends: a decision with an evidence step; slower, but cheap.

fields.model: g1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The data-driven strategy
fields.teaching: The plan asks for a data-driven optimisation strategy with the causes unclear. Strategy 1 is the reference; strategy 4 also defends (audit first); strategy 2 repeats the misreading; strategy 3 gives up data as a basis for decisions. A decision with a clear reason exports whichever is chosen (CLAUDE.md #38). Plan: items 1 to 3.

fields.label: Why this strategy, and not the others?
fields.help: Give the reason in terms of insight, the unclear causes and privacy, not only in terms of how much data there is. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: say why you chose that strategy and not the others
fields.model: I start from hypotheses: the platform already has a lot of data and its problem is how it is read, so more tracking would only add noise. Three KPIs, a written hypothesis for each change and one change at a time turn the data into insight and the insight into a decision, and tracking only what a hypothesis needs also keeps us on the right side of data protection.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I would write down what I expect before each change and change one thing at a time. More tracking would not help, because the problem is how we read what we already have.
guide.why: The reason must rest on insight, the unclear causes and privacy, not on the amount of data (Materi B1).
lookFor: Gives a reason about insight or causes.
Does not rest on the amount of data.
Mentions privacy or what is tracked.

fields.label: The analysis and tracking strategy: choose at least three rules
fields.help: A rule is good when it keeps tracking tied to a question, makes the analysis fair, and respects the learner.
fields.missing: choose at least three tracking and analysis rules

options.label: Track only events that serve a KPI or a hypothesis
options.why: Keeps the data tied to a question and limits the privacy burden.

options.label: Split drop-out by week, device and course
options.why: Shows where the problem concentrates.

options.label: Combine numbers with tests with real learners to learn why
options.why: Data shows symptoms; tests show causes.

options.label: Say what is tracked and get consent where it is required
options.why: Data protection (GDPR) and trust.

options.label: Write down each KPI's definition and owner
options.why: A KPI nobody owns drifts.

options.label: Track every click with the learner's name
options.why: Rejected: beyond need, and a privacy risk.

options.label: Judge a change after one week of data
options.why: Rejected: too short to tell a change from noise.

options.label: Compare this month with last month without checking holidays
options.why: Rejected: unlike periods.

options.label: Use average time on page as the only measure of success
options.why: Rejected: an open tab counts as success.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The tracking and analysis rules
fields.teaching: At least three; any three of the five reference rules defend if each ties tracking to a question, makes the reading fair, or respects the learner. The rejected ones collect beyond need, judge too fast, compare unlike periods or rely on one misleading number. Plan: item 2, analysis and tracking strategy.

fields.label: Hypotheses for improvement: place eight statements
fields.help: Place each statement where it belongs: a hypothesis you can test, an assumption to check first, a symptom (what the data shows), or not a hypothesis at all.
fields.missing: place every one of the eight statements

bins.label: A symptom: what the data shows

items.label: “We believe the sign-up form has too many fields, so we will cut it to three and expect completion to rise by five points.”
items.why: A change, an expected effect and a figure.

items.label: “Learners leave because the content is boring.”
items.why: A cause that is assumed and has no test yet.

items.label: “Drop-out in the first week is 70%.”
items.why: A figure, not an explanation.

items.label: “If we save a learner's quiz answers when they leave, quiz drop-out on phones will fall.”
items.why: A change and an expected effect; open item: it names no figure, which should be added.

items.label: “We should improve the user experience.”
items.why: No change, no effect, no way to test.

items.label: “More marketing will fix it.”
items.why: An assumed fix with no stated effect or test.

items.label: “Time spent per session is short.”
items.why: A figure, not an explanation.

items.label: “The new menu is better.”
items.why: Better by what measure? Not testable as stated.

fields.keyTitle: Block 3.1 · The hypotheses
fields.teaching: There is no single right grid. Item 4 is the open one (testable, once a figure is added). Items 5 and 8 are not hypotheses. Each bin must be used at least once. A testable hypothesis names a change, an expected effect and, ideally, a figure. Plan: item 3, hypotheses for improvement.

fields.label: Who decides on a change, on what evidence, and what does intuition still decide?
fields.help: Name a role, the figure or test it needs, and one kind of decision that data cannot make for you. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name who decides on what evidence, and what intuition still decides
fields.model: The head of product decides on a change, with the head of learning, on the first-week drop-out and the result of a test with real learners. Data shows what happened, so what to try first, the wording of a message, and what the platform stands for are still judgement: data is the basis of a decision, not a substitute for thinking.

guide.example: At LearnLoop the head of product decides, using the return rate and a test with five learners. Which idea to try first, and how the product should feel, still need judgement that no chart can give.
guide.why: The plan asks for a decision architecture and discusses data against intuition: a role, the evidence, and what data cannot decide (Materi B1, B2).
lookFor: Names a role.
Names the figure or test.
Names something intuition still decides.

b32.title: Block 3.2 · Measures, risk, a decision under uncertainty, and what you give up
b32.findIt: Route 2 → Task 2 → the seven decisions in the list below, each with its printed cost and weeks, then the risk and the fields. Answer in the lists and the text boxes.
b32.plan: Plan: transfer project, item 4 and the additional requirement · prioritised measures, a decision under uncertainty with unclear causes.

fields.label: Risk analysis: where a data-driven strategy goes wrong
fields.help: Imagine the strategy has failed in a year. Which reason is the most likely? Choose one.
fields.missing: choose the most likely reason the strategy fails

options.label: We misread the data again: a symptom was taken for a cause, and the wrong thing was fixed.
options.why: The misreading pole. Action: no cause is named without a test with real learners; notice it when a fix shows no effect.

options.label: Data overload: more tracking than anyone could read, and the team stopped looking.
options.why: Action: three KPIs and tracking only for hypotheses; notice it in dashboards that nobody opens.

options.label: A privacy failure: tracking went beyond need or notice, and learners or a regulator objected.
options.why: Action: data protection review and consent before any new tracking; notice it in complaints.

options.label: We optimised the metric and not the learner: the number rose and learning did not.
options.why: Action: pair every KPI with an outcome and a test; notice it when a KPI rises and results do not.

options.label: Analysis paralysis: we waited for perfect data while drop-out kept growing.
options.why: Action: act on the likely and cheap step with a reversal condition; notice it in the months with no change.

fields.model: r1
fields.keyTitle: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk: misreading the data
fields.teaching: Any of the five defends with a reason and an action. The action should cost less than the risk; ask when the team would notice it. These five are the typical answers of a premortem (Klein 2007). The plan names where data is misinterpreted.

fields.label: What do you do about that risk?
fields.help: One action, and when you would notice the risk. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name one action against that risk and when you would notice it
fields.model: I name no cause until a test with real learners supports it, and every report states the hypothesis beside the number; if a fix shows no effect on the KPI after one cycle of two weeks, I treat the cause as unproven and test the next guess.

guide.example: At LearnLoop every report would show the guess next to the number, and no cause is acted on until five learners confirm it; if the fix does not move the KPI, I drop the guess.
guide.why: One action, and a time when the risk would be noticed (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: One action.
Says when the risk would be noticed.

fields.label: One decision you make under uncertainty (without knowing the causes)
fields.frameLabel: The parts · taught in Materi B3
frameSteps: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
fields.frameNote: The fourth part, what you give up, has its own field below.

parts.label: I decide …
parts.help: What you decide, in one sentence. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I decide to define three KPIs (D1) and to run the first hypothesis test on the sign-up form, before I invest in any new tracking.

parts.label: I do not know …
parts.help: A specific unknown, for example which screen causes most of the drop-out. At least 10 characters.
parts.model: I do not know which screen causes most of the drop-out.

parts.label: I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)
parts.help: A figure you can watch and a time. At least 30 characters.
parts.missing: write “I reverse if … (a figure) … by … (a time)”
parts.model: I reverse if, by the end of month 2, first-week drop-out has not fallen from 70% to below 65% for the learners who see the shorter form, and I test the next hypothesis on the course page.

guide.example: At LearnLoop: “I decide to test the shorter sign-up form first. I do not know whether the form is the main reason people leave. I reverse if first-week drop-out has not fallen from 60% to below 55% by the end of month 2.”
guide.why: Four parts: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it (a figure) and by when, and what you give up (Materi B3).
lookFor: States the decision in one sentence.
Names a specific unknown.
Gives a reversal condition with a figure and a time.

fields.label: What do you give up or postpone?
fields.help: Name something real that someone would miss. A plan that gives up nothing has not decided. At least 30 characters.
fields.missing: name what you give up or postpone
fields.model: I postpone the AI analytics platform (D5) and the real-time board dashboard (D7) this year. The data team will miss the tool they wanted, and the board will not get a live wall of charts.

guide.example: At LearnLoop I postpone the automatic insights tool for a year. The analysts will miss it, and the board will not see live charts.
guide.why: Giving up nothing means you have not decided (Materi B3).
lookFor: Names something real.
Names who would miss it.

decisions.orderLabel: Put the three measures in priority order
decisions.whyLabel: Why does the first measure go first?
decisions.whyHelp: Say how it turns data into an insight. At least 30 characters.

items.name: A KPI framework
items.what: Three core KPIs with a definition, a target and an owner each, and one dashboard that shows only these.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: without defined KPIs nothing can be judged.

items.name: A hypothesis-driven optimisation programme
items.what: A hypothesis log, two-week test cycles with A/B tests, and a review after each cycle.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: turns insight into decisions, one change at a time.

items.name: Privacy-safe tracking and cause analysis
items.what: Only the events a hypothesis needs, consent and retention rules, and cohort analyses of drop-out.
items.keyWhy: Reference pick: gives the data a question and keeps it lawful.

items.name: Qualitative research with learners
items.what: Twenty learner interviews and usability tests, to explain what the numbers show.
items.keyWhy: Defends in place of D3: data shows symptoms, research shows causes; it does not track change over time.

items.name: An AI analytics platform that finds insights automatically
items.what: A tool that scans all data and reports patterns.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: patterns without hypotheses repeat the misreading, and the cost is highest.

items.name: Track every click and keep all data for good
items.what: Every event is stored with the learner's identity, with no limit on time.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: beyond need, a privacy risk, and more noise.

items.name: A real-time board dashboard
items.what: A live wall of charts for the board.
items.keyWhy: Rejected: more charts, not more insight.

model.orderWhy: D1 goes first: without defined KPIs nothing can be judged, and the data has no direction. Data leads to insight and insight to a decision: with the KPIs fixed, D2 turns insight into decisions one change at a time, and D3 gives the data a question and keeps it lawful. The three cost €135,000 of the €160,000.

guide.example: At LearnLoop defining the KPIs goes first: until then nobody knows what to improve. The test cycles and the tracking set-up only help once there is a number to move.
guide.why: The plan's rationale: data → insight → decision. A different first measure defends if the reason says how it turns data into an insight (Materi B1).
lookFor: Says how it turns data into an insight.
Says why the others can wait.

decisions.keyTeaching: Reference order: D1, D2, D3 (€135,000 of €160,000, longest 16 weeks). D1 first because without KPIs nothing can be judged. D4, D1, D2 also defends: explain the numbers with research first, since the causes are unclear. D1, D2, D4 defends if the reason names evidence. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38).

memo.subject: The data-driven UX strategy for the next twelve months

16.caseExport: DataLearn is a learning platform with extensive tracking data, a high drop-out rate that persists and measures with no effect, because the data is interpreted wrongly and there are no hypotheses. The budget is €40,000 and time is short.

memoSections.title: What I give up or postpone

16.mentorNote: The reference four measures are the plan's own (M1 clear KPI definition, M2 a hypothesis-based approach, M3 targeted UX tests, M4 iterative optimisation) and cost €37,000 of the case's €40,000 (a Case assumption), longest 5 weeks of 10. The three reference KPIs are completion rate, first-week drop-out and seven-day return. The plan's rationale: data → insight → decision.

list.title: Structure: information architecture, hierarchy and orientation
Visual design: hierarchy, legibility, consistency and reduction
Interaction and user guidance: operability, calls to action, feedback
Typical UX/UI mistakes and the link to learning psychology
Weighing a design measure: user impact, effort, risk
Design as decision architecture: structure beats surface
Conflicting goals: design against functionality, and too complex against too reduced
Deciding without user tests: a structure, principles and guidance you can check later

A1.idea: The structure of a learning interface has three parts. Information architecture is how the content is organised and named. Hierarchy and navigation logic say what is a main section and what is a detail, and how you move between them. Orientation means that the learner always knows where they are and what comes next.
A1.why: In Task 1 you sort facts about a platform into unclear navigation, visual overload and inconsistent design. The first of these is a structure problem, and the plan's coaching says that structure beats visual design.
A1.picture: The first picture is a LearnLoop lesson screen with three switches: a path above the lesson, a menu that marks the real place, and a Next button. Switch them on one at a time and read how many of the three orientation questions the screen answers. The second picture is a simple information architecture. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: Visual design controls attention. A visual hierarchy uses size, colour, contrast and position so that the most important thing is seen first. Legibility means the text can be read comfortably, consistency means the same thing looks the same everywhere, and reduction means leaving out what does not help the learner's goal on this screen.
A2.why: In Task 1 you decide between simplifying the design and restructuring the navigation. You need to know what a visual change can and cannot do.
A2.picture: Choose “Everything competes” or “One main thing”: the same LearnLoop course page, once with seven colours, three banners and five equal buttons, and once with one main button, quiet links and a progress bar. Read what changed for the learner. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A3.idea: Interaction design has three jobs. Intuitive operability: things look like what they do, so the learner does not have to learn the interface. Clear calls to action: one main button says what to do next. Feedback on actions: when the learner acts, the platform answers at once.
A3.why: In Task 1 you judge screens with several buttons without priority, and you choose measures for action guidance.
A3.picture: A LearnLoop Save button in three versions: it answers within a tenth of a second, it answers after about a second, and it shows nothing for ten seconds. Choose a version and read what the learner does. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: The plan lists three typical mistakes: unclear navigation, visual overload and inconsistent design. It also asks you to link design to learning psychology: structure reduces cognitive load, and visual support helps learning (Day 3). Each mistake takes attention that learning needs.
A4.why: The three mistakes are the three areas Block 1.1 sorts facts into. This card gives you the reason for each.
A4.picture: Three small screens, one for each mistake, with what it costs the learner. Nothing to click.

A5.idea: To choose between design measures, rate each on the same three questions. User impact: how much does it help the learner find, choose and carry on? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €8,000 is Low, up to €15,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example adding more clutter.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: First, three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures. The bars show the cost of each. The coloured bands behind them are the effort rule, and the dashed line is the €30,000 budget. Under the bars, the table gives the rating of each measure; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says design is decision architecture: UI is not about making it pretty but about making it understandable; structure beats visual design; good UX reduces the user's wrong decisions. The chain runs from structure and hierarchy to orientation, from orientation to behaviour, and from behaviour to learning success.
B1.why: Task 2 asks you to propose a basic structure, principles for visual design and a concept for user guidance, in order of priority. This card gives you the logic of the order.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: structure and hierarchy, orientation and guidance, behaviour, learning result. Below it, the four design layers and what each decides for the learner. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 8 are design against functionality, and (in the risk analysis) too complex against too reduced. A designer who removes everything to make the screen calm may also remove what learners need: help, options, power for experts. A designer who keeps everything makes the screen unusable. The aim is to remove clutter and keep guidance and function.
B2.why: Task 2 asks for a risk analysis of too complex against too reduced and for prioritised design measures.
B2.picture: The matrix places five LearnLoop options by the clutter they remove (to the right) and by the guidance and function they keep (upwards). The position is a reading of the example, not a score. The top right is the aim. Select a point to read why it sits there. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B3.idea: The plan asks you to decide under uncertainty, for example without user tests. A decision under uncertainty states four things: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it and by when, and what you give up. For a design decision the usual unknown is how learners will react to a new structure and new names.
B3.why: Block 3.2 asks for exactly this, together with prioritised design measures and a risk analysis.
B3.picture: The four boxes at the top are the parts of the decision, filled in for LearnLoop. The two boxes below are the rule for future decisions. Nothing to click.

list.title: Information architecture: organising content so that it can be found and understood
Navigation in learning platforms: orientation, types and typical mistakes
Interactive elements: quizzes, tasks and clicks as a learning reinforcer
Engagement strategies through interaction: activation, feedback and variety
Weighing a structure or interaction measure: learning impact, effort, risk
Structure guides, interaction activates: orientation, activation, engagement
Conflicting goals: structure against flexibility, and interaction against overload
Deciding without behaviour data: a structure and an interaction plan you can check later

A1.idea: Information architecture is how the content of a platform is organised and named. Its goal is that content can be found and understood. Three principles carry it: clear hierarchies, logical grouping, and a reduction of complexity.
A1.why: In Task 1 you sort facts about a platform into too many options, unclear labels and no orientation. The first two come from a weak architecture.
A1.picture: The same LearnLoop items, once as a flat row with two homes for one course and once grouped under four sections. Choose a version and read what Ana can and cannot find. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: Navigation answers the learner's orientation questions: where am I, and what comes next. There are three kinds: a menu, paths and a progress indicator. The typical mistakes are too many options and unclear labels.
A2.why: Block 1.1 asks you to say where a learner loses orientation and how to improve the navigation, and the three problems of the sort come from this card.
A2.picture: First a menu with 4, 9 or 24 entries: choose a size and read how long it takes Sam to find “Contracts”. Then one lesson screen with its three kinds of navigation labelled. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A3.idea: Interactive elements are quizzes, tasks and click interactions. Using them is active, reading is passive, and active use can reinforce learning. But interaction helps only when it is tied to a goal, makes the learner think and answers back; an interaction that only collects clicks is an end in itself.
A3.why: In Task 1 you choose measures for targeted interaction and feedback, and in Task 2 you decide where in a lesson an interaction belongs.
A3.picture: The same LearnLoop lesson three ways: only read, a question with an explained answer, and rewards for clicks. Choose one and read what Lea does with her mind. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: The plan names three engagement strategies through interaction: activate the user, give feedback and reward, and avoid monotony. Feedback that explains and a reward that is tied to progress keep a learner going; the same task again and again does not.
A4.why: The three parts are the engagement side of the plan's Musterlösung (feedback mechanisms). Feedback and a next step are also taught in A3, so no Core block needs this card.
A4.picture: The end of a LearnLoop lesson with three switches: an explained result, a next step and a different kind of task. Switch them on one at a time. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A5.idea: To choose between structure and interaction measures, rate each on the same three questions. Learning impact: how much does it help the learner find the content and then learn from it? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €7,000 is Low, up to €14,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example that an interaction becomes a burden.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: Three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures, the bars show the cost of each against the effort rule and the €30,000 budget, and the table gives the rating of each; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says that structure guides and interaction activates: without structure, interaction has no effect; navigation is decision guidance; interaction must be goal-oriented; engagement arises from meaningful activation. The chain runs orientation, activation, engagement.
B1.why: Task 2 asks you to design the sections, the navigation and the interaction in order of priority. This card gives you the logic of that order.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: orientation, activation, engagement. Below it, what each step needs and where interaction is overestimated. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 9 are structure against flexibility, and interaction against overload. Too much guidance traps experienced learners; too little loses beginners. Too little interaction leaves learners passive; too much overloads them. The aim is guidance with freedom, and interaction in a dose that serves a goal.
B2.why: Task 2 asks for a risk analysis of over-structuring against over-interaction and for prioritised measures.
B2.picture: The matrix places five LearnLoop designs by the guidance the learner gets (to the right) and the freedom they keep (upwards). The position is a reading of the example, not a score. The top right is the aim. Select a point to read why it sits there. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B3.idea: The plan asks you to decide under uncertainty. A decision under uncertainty states four things: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it and by when, and what you give up. For a structure and interaction decision the usual unknown is how learners will react to a new menu or a question after every section.
B3.why: Block 3.2 asks for exactly this, together with prioritised measures and a risk analysis.
B3.picture: The four boxes at the top are the parts of the decision, filled in for LearnLoop. The two boxes below are the rule for future decisions. Nothing to click.

list.title: Visual feedback: direct and indirect feedback as a tool for motivation and steering
Progress tracking systems: bars, levels and status, and their risks
Responsive design for learning platforms: devices, contexts and priorities
Accessibility in the responsive context: operability, legibility and reach
Weighing a feedback, tracking or mobile measure: impact, effort, risk
UX as a steering and feedback system: transparency, motivation, usage
Conflicting goals: information density against clarity, feedback against overload, flexibility against consistency
Deciding without retention data by device: a system you can check later

A1.idea: Feedback is what a platform tells a learner back after they act. It matters in the learning process because it shows that the action counted and what it means. There are two kinds: direct feedback, such as correct or incorrect, and indirect feedback, such as visible progress. Used well, feedback is a tool for motivation and steering.
A1.why: In Task 1 you sort facts about a platform into missing feedback, unclear progress and poor use on a phone, and you say how they affect motivation. The first of these comes from this card.
A1.picture: The same LearnLoop question three ways: no answer, a bare red cross, and an explained result with a next step. Choose one and read what Kim feels. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: A progress tracking system shows the learner how far along they are, with progress bars, levels or status indicators. It answers “how far along am I?”, which makes the learning process transparent, and it raises motivation and the completion rate. Its risks are a misleading display and demotivation when the learner is overwhelmed.
A2.why: In Task 1 you choose measures for transparency, and in Task 2 you design a tracking strategy and name how it could mislead.
A2.picture: The same course page three ways: no progress, a bar that jumps to 90% and then crawls, and an honest display “3 of 8”. Choose one and read what Raj feels. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A3.idea: Responsive design adapts a platform to different devices (desktop, tablet, mobile) and to the different contexts in which they are used. It prioritises content by device: what is the same everywhere, what comes first on a phone, what only fits a large screen. A learner who studies on a phone in a few free minutes needs a different order than one at a desk.
A3.why: In Block 1.1 a fact about a phone screen is one of the three problems, and in Block 3.1 you place content by device. The coaching says responsive design is not an option, but a prerequisite.
A3.picture: The same LearnLoop lesson on four screens: a phone that was not adapted, a phone that was, a tablet and a desktop. Choose one and read what Nia can do. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: In the responsive context accessibility means three things: operability on all devices (targets large enough to hit), legibility (contrast and text that fits), and interaction that works for more people. It is the link to inclusive design from Day 7, and it means scalability and reach: the same design works for more learners.
A4.why: Block 3.1 asks for an accessibility integration. The core rules (target size, contrast, words as well as colour) are repeated in A3 and B1, so no Core block needs this card.
A4.picture: A LearnLoop phone screen with three switches: large targets, strong contrast and status in words. Switch them on one at a time and read who gains. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A5.idea: To choose between feedback, tracking and mobile measures, rate each on the same three questions. Impact: how much does it do for motivation and for finishing a course? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €8,000 is Low, up to €16,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example a display that misleads or feedback that overloads.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: Three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures, the bars show the cost of each against the effort rule and the €30,000 budget, and the table gives the rating of each; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says that UX is a steering and feedback system: users need orientation and feedback; making progress visible increases motivation; responsive design is not an option but a prerequisite; accessibility means scalability and reach. The chain runs from feedback to visible progress, to motivation, to usage.
B1.why: Task 2 asks you to design the feedback, the tracking, the responsive concept and the accessibility integration as one system, in order of priority.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: feedback, visible progress, motivation, usage. Below it, the parts of a system and the accessibility rules. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 10 are information density against clarity, feedback against overload, and flexibility against consistency. A screen that shows everything is not clear; feedback after every click is overload; a layout tuned to each device can break consistency. The aim is to show what the learner needs to decide the next step, and to give feedback where it counts.
B2.why: Task 2 asks for a risk analysis and for prioritised measures. The rules of this card tell you how to weigh them.
B2.picture: The matrix places five LearnLoop progress screens by the information they show (to the right) and the clarity they keep (upwards). The position is a reading of the example, not a score. The top right is the aim. Select a point to read why it sits there. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B3.idea: The plan asks you to decide under uncertainty. A decision under uncertainty states four things: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it and by when, and what you give up. For a feedback and tracking decision the usual unknown is whether the change raises retention, and whether it does so on phones, where most learners are.
B3.why: Block 3.2 asks for exactly this, together with prioritised measures and a risk analysis.
B3.picture: The four boxes at the top are the parts of the decision, filled in for LearnLoop. The two boxes below are the rule for future decisions. Nothing to click.

list.title: Game elements: points, badges, levels and leaderboards, and what gamification is
Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and the three needs of Self-Determination Theory
Gamification and learning: activity is not learning
Principles of meaningful gamification: link, fairness, challenge
Weighing a gamification measure: motivation, effort, risk
Gamification as a strategic tool: from objective to mechanic to behaviour
Conflicting goals: short-term effect against sustainable learning, motivation against manipulation
Deciding without proof that gamification works: a decision you can check later

A1.idea: Gamification means using elements known from games, such as points, badges, levels, a progress bar or a leaderboard, in something that is not a game, such as a learning platform. Each element does something different to a learner: a point rewards an action, a badge marks an achievement, a level shows a stage, and a leaderboard compares people. Whether the element helps depends on what it rewards.
A1.why: In Task 1 you sort eight elements of a platform by what they do to motivation. You first need to know what each element is.
A1.picture: One LearnLoop lesson screen with four switches: points, badges, a leaderboard and a progress bar. Switch them on one at a time and read what Kim sees. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: Intrinsic motivation means doing something because it is interesting or meaningful in itself. Extrinsic motivation means doing it for a reward or to avoid a penalty. Self-Determination Theory says people stay motivated when three needs are met: autonomy (I choose), competence (I am getting better) and relatedness (I belong). A reward can also crowd out interest that was already there.
A2.why: Task 1 asks you to sort elements into extrinsic, competence and intrinsic, and to say which would last longest. The test question for each comes from this card.
A2.picture: The same learner, Kim, three ways: with a prize in front of her, with the prize gone, and with real interest. Below it, the three needs drawn as three small pictures. Choose one state and read what Kim does. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A3.idea: A platform can be very busy and teach very little. Activity means logins, clicks and points. Learning means that someone now knows or can do something they could not before. A game element helps learning only when it rewards the learning itself, for example progress against an objective, and not the activity around it.
A3.why: In Block 1.1 and Block 2.2 you separate measures that reward learning from measures that reward activity. This is the test for that.
A3.picture: Two bars for the same LearnLoop platform in three set-ups: logins and clicks, and objectives mastered. Choose a set-up and compare the bars. The values are invented to show the idea. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: Three principles make gamification meaningful. First, every element is linked to a learning objective. Second, the rules are visible and fair, so nobody feels tricked. Third, the challenge matches the learner's ability, so the task is neither boring nor too hard. This last idea is called flow.
A4.why: Block 3.1 asks which mechanics are meaningful. The link rule is repeated in A3 and B1, so no Core block needs this card.
A4.picture: Three small pictures: a badge linked to a goal, a rule everyone can read, and a line where challenge rises with ability. Nothing to click.

A5.idea: To choose between gamification measures, rate each on the same three questions. Motivation: how much does it keep the learner going, and for how long? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €7,000 is Low, up to €14,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example that learners chase the reward and learn little.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: Three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures, the bars show the cost of each against the effort rule and the €30,000 budget, and the table gives the rating of each; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says that gamification is a tool, not a goal. A tool serves an objective: you start from what learners should be able to do, choose a mechanic that encourages the behaviour that leads there, and check the result. The chain runs from objective to mechanic to behaviour to result. Motivation is not the same as gamification.
B1.why: Task 2 asks whether to use gamification at all, which mechanics are meaningful, and how they link to learning objectives. This chain answers all three.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: objective, mechanic, behaviour, result. Below it, the test for each link. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 11 are short-term effect against sustainable learning, motivation against manipulation, and engagement against overload. A reward can lift activity at once and still leave nothing behind. A streak that punishes can push people, but it creates pressure and worry. The aim is the combination that keeps learners going and learning.
B2.why: Task 2 asks for a risk analysis, with perverse incentives and over-motivation. The rules of this card tell you how to weigh them.
B2.picture: The matrix places six LearnLoop game ideas by their short-term effect (to the right) and how much sustainable learning they leave (upwards). The position is a reading of the example, not a score. The top right is the aim. Select a point to read why it sits there. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B3.idea: The plan asks you to decide although you have no proof yet that gamification works, and competitors use it heavily. A decision under uncertainty states four things: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it and by when, and what you give up. A cheap test against a control group is the usual way to get proof.
B3.why: Block 3.2 asks for exactly this, together with prioritised measures and a risk analysis.
B3.picture: The four boxes at the top are the parts of the decision, filled in for LearnLoop. The two boxes below are the rule for future decisions. Nothing to click.

list.title: Adaptive learning systems: collect, analyse, adapt
Technology and algorithms: rules, models and their limits
UX patterns for personalised learning paths
Opportunities and risks, and the link to gamification
Weighing a personalisation measure: benefit, effort, risk
Personalisation as a strategic UX option: need, data, technique, explanation
Conflicting goals: UX against technology, personalisation against standardisation
Deciding with an incomplete data basis: a decision you can check later

A1.idea: An adaptive learning system adapts content to what the learner does. It works in three steps: it collects data about behaviour, it analyses it (for example progress and mistakes), and it adapts the content or the difficulty. The goal is a path that fits one person rather than everyone.
A1.why: In Task 1 you sort facts about a platform into changes that are opaque, based on a wrong basis, or helpful. You first need to know what the system does.
A1.picture: The same LearnLoop course three ways: identical for everyone, adapted with a reason, and adapted with no reason. Choose one and read what Ravi sees. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: There are two broad ways to decide how to adapt. Rule-based systems use if-then logic that a person writes, such as “if the test is passed, skip the lesson”. Data-driven systems, such as machine learning, find patterns in large amounts of data. Their limits are data quality, complexity and transparency: a model with too little data guesses, and a learner cannot be told why it chose.
A2.why: Block 1.2 asks you to weigh rules against a complex AI system under a small data basis. This card gives the test.
A2.picture: The same decision three ways: two clear rules, a closed box with lots of data, and a closed box with too little data. Choose one and read what it needs. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A3.idea: A UX pattern is a proven way to show something in an interface. For personalised paths there are four: an individual recommendation, adaptive difficulty levels, a dynamic learning path, and feedback based on behaviour. A pattern works when the learner can see it, understand why it appears, and change it.
A3.why: In Block 1.1 and Block 2.2 you separate patterns that explain themselves from ones that hide. In Block 3.1 you choose patterns.
A3.picture: One LearnLoop path screen with four switches: a recommendation, difficulty, a path and feedback. Switch them on one at a time and read what Ravi can do. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: Adaptive systems offer opportunities (efficiency, motivation and learning success) and risks (opacity, over-adaptation and a wrong data basis). Over-adaptation means the system reacts too strongly to too little and boxes the learner in. Personalisation also links to gamification: a mechanic tied to a personal goal combines motivation with personalisation.
A4.why: Block 3.1 asks how gamification joins the personalisation. The core rules are repeated in A2 and B2, so no Core block needs this card.
A4.picture: Two columns: opportunities on the left, risks on the right. Nothing to click.

A5.idea: To choose between personalisation measures, rate each on the same three questions. Benefit: how much does it help learners reach their goal, for many different users? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €10,000 is Low, up to €25,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example a small data basis or a system nobody understands.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: Three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures, the bars show the cost of each against the effort rule and the €50,000 budget, and the table gives the rating of each; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says that more technology is not better UX. Personalisation is a strategic option, and the chain to design runs from the learner's need, to the data you have, to the technique (a rule or a model), to an adaptation the learner can see and change. Skipping the last step is how a clever system ends up not accepted.
B1.why: Task 2 asks for a concept for adaptive paths, the UX patterns, how gamification joins in, and a low-fidelity sketch. This chain gives you the order.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: need, data, technique, an adaptation the learner can see. Below it, the test for each link. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 12 are UX against technology, and personalisation against standardisation. A technique can be powerful and still not understood. Standardisation is cheap and clear and ignores differences. The aim is the simplest technique that the learner can understand and that fits the data you have.
B2.why: Task 2 asks for a risk analysis and prioritised measures. The rules of this card tell you how to weigh them.
B2.picture: The matrix places six LearnLoop ideas by their technical complexity (to the right) and how well the learner understands them (upwards). The position is a reading of the example, not a score. Select a point to read why it sits there. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B3.idea: The plan asks you to decide although the data basis is not complete, and competitors already use adaptive systems. A decision under uncertainty states four things: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it and by when, and what you give up. A low-fidelity prototype tested with a few learners is the cheapest way to learn what you do not know.
B3.why: Block 3.2 asks for exactly this, together with prioritised measures and a risk analysis.
B3.picture: The four boxes at the top are the parts of the decision, filled in for LearnLoop. The two boxes below are the rule for future decisions. Nothing to click.

list.title: Inclusive design: user groups with different needs, and how it differs from usability
The four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust
WCAG in practice: contrast, text alternatives, structure, keyboard use
Implementation in UX/UI design: plain language, hierarchy, intuitive interaction
Prioritising accessibility measures: impact, effort, risk
Accessibility as a strategic quality: from requirement to priority, process and measure
Conflicting goals: accessibility against cost, standardisation against flexibility
Deciding without knowing how much of the platform fails: a decision you can check later

A1.idea: Inclusive design means designing so that people with different needs can use a product, not only the typical user. Classic usability asks whether a typical user finds a product easy. Inclusion asks who is left out. Three groups of needs matter: visual (seeing the page), motor (using the controls) and cognitive (understanding and following).
A1.why: In Task 1 you sort facts about a platform by the user group they affect, and you say which one stops a learner completely.
A1.picture: One LearnLoop lesson page as three learners meet it: Mia with low vision, Tom with only a keyboard, and Nia who finds long text hard. Choose one and read what happens to them. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: The WCAG standard rests on four principles. Content must be perceivable (people can see or hear it), operable (people can use the controls), understandable (people can follow it) and robust (it works with different browsers and assistive technologies, such as a screen reader). A barrier breaks one of the four.
A2.why: In Block 2.1 and Block 2.2 you name the barriers behind the facts. The four principles are the way to name them.
A2.picture: Four small pictures, one for each principle: an eye, a keyboard key, a short text and a plug that fits. Nothing to click.

A3.idea: WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, turns the principles into testable requirements. Four matter most on a learning platform: sufficient contrast (at least 4.5 : 1 for normal text), a text alternative for every image that carries content, a clear structure and navigation, and keyboard operability, so that everything works without a mouse.
A3.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 ask you to prioritise measures. Each one is one of these four requirements.
A3.picture: One LearnLoop lesson page with four switches: contrast, a text alternative, structure and keyboard use. Switch them on one at a time and read what changes. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: Accessibility is built in the design itself: plain language (short sentences, everyday words, abbreviations explained), a clear visual hierarchy (headings that show what matters), and intuitive interactions (controls that look and behave as people expect). These help everyone and are the cheapest barriers to avoid.
A4.why: Block 3.1 asks how accessibility joins the UX process. The core rules on structure are repeated in A3 and B1, so no Core block needs this card.
A4.picture: A before and after: one block of long text, and the same text with headings and short steps. Nothing to click.

A5.idea: To choose between accessibility measures, rate each on the same three questions. Impact: how many learners does it free from a barrier, and how badly were they blocked? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €8,000 is Low, up to €18,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example that it takes longer than planned.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: Three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures, the bars show the cost of each against the effort rule and the €40,000 budget, and the table gives the rating of each; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says that accessibility is not an add-on but a standard, and that WCAG is a minimum, not a goal. A strategy moves from the requirement to a priority (start where most learners meet the barrier), to a process (so that new content stays accessible), to a measure (so that management can see progress).
B1.why: Task 2 asks for a strategy to implement WCAG, the integration into the UX process and an evaluation approach. This chain gives you the order.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: requirement, priority, process, measure. Below it, the test for each link. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 13 are accessibility against cost, and standardisation against flexibility. A broad programme is expensive, and a cheap overlay does not remove barriers. A fixed standard is reliable, yet some learners need different solutions. The aim is the measures that reach the most learners for the least cost, with the standard as the floor.
B2.why: Task 2 asks for prioritised measures and a risk analysis of costs against benefits. The rules of this card tell you how to weigh them.
B2.picture: The matrix places six LearnLoop measures by their cost (to the right) and the reach, that is how many learners gain (upwards). The position is a reading of the example, not a score. Select a point to read why it sits there. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B3.idea: The plan asks you to decide although you do not know how much of the platform fails WCAG, and requirements are rising. A decision under uncertainty states four things: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it and by when, and what you give up. A short audit of a sample is the cheapest way to find out what you do not know.
B3.why: Block 3.2 asks for exactly this, together with prioritised measures and a risk analysis.
B3.picture: The four boxes at the top are the parts of the decision, filled in for LearnLoop. The two boxes below are the rule for future decisions. Nothing to click.

list.title: Plain language: short sentences, clear terms, no jargon
Intuitive learning environments: structure, navigation and three usability principles
Testing with different user groups: observe, ask, find the hurdles
Optimising inclusive UX: iterate, use data, keep evaluating
Weighing a simplification measure: impact, effort, risk
Comprehensibility as a strategic quality: find the hurdle, simplify, test, adjust
Conflicting goals: simplicity against information, standard against flexibility
Deciding without knowing where learners stop: a decision you can check later

A1.idea: Plain language means writing so that the people who use a platform understand it at first reading. Use short sentences, clear everyday terms and no jargon. The idea in the plan is: language is access, and access is use. A learner who cannot understand the text cannot use the platform.
A1.why: In Task 1 you sort facts by the kind of hurdle, and you write a plainer version of a text. The first of these is the language.
A1.picture: The same LearnLoop welcome text three ways: one long sentence with technical terms, short sentences that keep the terms, and a plain version. Choose one and read what Kim understands. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: An intuitive learning environment is one that people can use without an explanation. It has a clear structure and navigation, and it reduces complexity. Three usability principles help: efficiency (common tasks take few steps), error prevention (the system stops a mistake before it happens) and consistency (the same thing always has the same name and place).
A2.why: In Block 1.1 and Block 2.2 you separate structure hurdles from usability hurdles, and you choose measures for each.
A2.picture: One LearnLoop learning page with four switches: a short menu, a quick common action, error prevention and consistent names. Switch them on one at a time and read what Raj notices. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A3.idea: To know whether a platform is understood, you test it with different groups of users. A usability test means watching people do real tasks, listening to what they say, and noting where they stop. This finds comprehension barriers that the team, who know the platform too well, cannot see.
A3.why: Block 2.2 asks you to define two test methods, and Task 2 asks for a testing concept. This card names the methods.
A3.picture: Three ways of testing the same LearnLoop page: asking a manager, watching one learner, and watching several different learners. Choose one and read what it shows. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: Optimising inclusive UX is not a one-off task. It is a loop: change something, test it, measure the effect with data, adjust, and repeat. Iterative improvement means small steps with checks in between, and continuous evaluation means the loop never stops.
A4.why: Block 3.1 asks for a testing and optimisation concept. The core of the loop is repeated in A3 and B1, so no Core block needs this card.
A4.picture: A loop of four steps: change, test, measure, adjust. Nothing to click.

A5.idea: To choose between simplification measures, rate each on the same three questions. Impact: how much does it help learners understand and keep going? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €7,000 is Low, up to €15,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example that it adds complexity or does not reach the cause.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: Three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures, the bars show the cost of each against the effort rule and the €36,000 budget, and the table gives the rating of each; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says that complexity is UX's greatest enemy, simple systems are more successful, and usability determines usage. A strategy for comprehensibility is a loop: find the hurdle where learners stop, simplify it, test whether it worked with real users, and adjust. The aim is comprehensibility, then usage, then success.
B1.why: Task 2 asks for a strategy to simplify, an optimised information architecture and a testing concept. This chain gives you the order.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: find the hurdle, simplify, test with users, adjust. Below it, the test for each link. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 14 are simplicity against information content, and standardisation against flexibility. Too much simplification removes what some learners need, and too little leaves them lost. The aim is to separate the complexity of the subject, which may be needed, from the complexity of the interface, which should go.
B2.why: Task 2 asks for a risk analysis of too much against too little simplification. The rules of this card tell you how to weigh them.
B2.picture: The matrix places six LearnLoop screens by the information they keep (to the right) and how well a learner understands them at first reading (upwards). The position is a reading of the example, not a score. The top right is the aim. Select a point to read why it sits there. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B3.idea: The plan asks you to decide although you do not know exactly where learners stop. A decision under uncertainty states four things: what you decide, what you do not know, what would make you reverse it and by when, and what you give up. A first test with a few learners is the cheapest way to find out what you do not know.
B3.why: Block 3.2 asks for exactly this, together with prioritised measures and a risk analysis.
B3.picture: The four boxes at the top are the parts of the decision, filled in for LearnLoop. The two boxes below are the rule for future decisions. Nothing to click.

list.title: The mobile context of use: on the go, little time, low attention
Microlearning design: short units with one objective, and its risks
Responsive and cross-device design: prioritise, reduce, synchronise
Testing and optimising mobile learning: real phones, real settings
Weighing a mobile measure: user value, effort, risk
Mobile UX as a strategy of its own: context, design, usage, scale
Conflicting goals: mobile against desktop, content against fit to the situation
Deciding without data by device: a decision you can check later

A1.idea: The context of use is where, when and with how much attention a person uses a product. On a phone it is usually on the go, with little time and low attention, in a place with many distractions. At a desk it is the opposite. Mobile is not a smaller desktop: the context decides the design, and what mobile learners need is speed, simplicity and clarity.
A1.why: In Task 1 you say which problem to fix first for a learner on the move and which content belongs on a phone. Both come from the context of use.
A1.picture: The same learner, Ben, in three contexts: at a desk, on a crowded train and in a five-minute break. Choose one and read what he needs. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A2.idea: Microlearning means short, self-contained learning units, each with one learning objective. Its advantages are flexibility and a better fit with everyday life. Its risk is fragmentation of knowledge: pieces that do not add up. A unit needs one objective, a short check and a visible place in the course.
A2.why: In Block 2.2 and Block 3.1 you choose microlearning measures and rules, and you name the risk of fragmentation.
A2.picture: The same content three ways: one long lesson, the same lesson cut into pieces at arbitrary points, and five short units with a goal each. Choose one and read what Ben gets. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A3.idea: Responsive design adapts a platform to different screen sizes. On a phone it prioritises content, reduces what is shown to the essentials, and makes controls large enough for a thumb. Cross-device optimisation goes further: it keeps the experience whole when a learner changes device, by synchronising progress and keeping the same names and layout logic.
A3.why: Block 2.2 and Block 3.1 ask for mobile optimisation and for progress synchronisation. This card names both.
A3.picture: One LearnLoop phone screen with four switches: prioritised content, large targets, text that fits and a synchronised continue card. Switch them on one at a time and read what Ben can do. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

A4.idea: Mobile learning is tested on real phones in real settings. A mobile usability test means watching learners do tasks on their own phones, some on the move. Analysing the contexts of use means finding out when and where they study, and continuous adjustment means repeating the loop as use changes.
A4.why: Block 3.1 asks for a testing and optimisation strategy. The loop is repeated in B1, so no Core block needs this card.
A4.picture: A learner tests a task on her own phone while a tester watches and notes where she stops. Nothing to click.

A5.idea: To choose between mobile measures, rate each on the same three questions. User value: how much does it help a learner on the move? Effort: money and time, decided here by a rule: under €8,000 is Low, up to €16,000 is Mid, above that is High. Risk: what could go wrong, for example that knowledge is fragmented or two products must be kept up.
A5.why: Block 1.2 and Block 2.2 of the task ask for exactly this. The example uses LearnLoop, so the answer for the task case is not given.
A5.picture: Three small pictures show LearnLoop's three measures, the bars show the cost of each against the effort rule and the €40,000 budget, and the table gives the rating of each; select a cell to read the reason. Press “Walk me through it” for a short story.

B1.idea: The plan's coaching says that mobile is not a smaller desktop, the context of use determines the design, and cross-device is a strategic advantage. A mobile strategy therefore starts from the context, designs for it (short units, a layout that prioritises), checks the usage it produces, and scales the experience across devices. The chain is context, design, usage, scale.
B1.why: Task 2 asks for a mobile strategy, a microlearning concept, a cross-device approach and a testing strategy. This chain gives you the order.
B1.picture: The chain reads from left to right: context, design, usage, scale. Below it, the test for each link. Nothing to click.

B2.idea: The plan's conflicts for Day 15 are mobile against desktop, and information content against fit to the situation. The desktop can show everything, and a phone cannot. The aim is to show on each device what suits its situation, and to keep one experience across both, instead of building two products or copying one onto the other.
